events.title: Hyundai Motor takes full ownership of Boston Dynamics
events.summary: According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17, all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. Hyundai Motor Group now owns 100% of Boston Dynamics after buying SoftBank’s last 9.65% stake, giving it full control of the US robotics unit. Hyundai plans to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot, aiming for 30,000 units a year by 2028 and first using them at its Georgia plant for simple factory tasks. Boston Dynamics’ revenue rose 29% to 136 billion won in the first nine months of 2026, but losses widened to 626.6 billion won; an IPO could come around 2029 or 2030. SEOUL – Hyundai Motor Group has acquired full ownership of its US robotics subsidiary Boston Dynamics, accelerating its push to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot. According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17 , all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. The transaction concludes the buyout of SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake after the Japanese tech conglomerate triggered its put option in July under an earlier shareholder pact. Existing stakeholders – including Hyundai Motor group executive chair Chung Euisun, HMG Global and Hyundai Glovis – acquired the remaining shares, giving Chung and group affiliates 100% ownership of Boston Dynamics. As part of the transaction, Hyundai Glovis injected 46.5 billion won (S$44.8 million) to raise its stake by 1.08 percentage points to 12.47% at the end of the third quarter, following a 63.1 billion won investment in the first half of 2026. Industry insiders say the ownership consolidation marks a pivotal turning point for Hyundai’s robotics push. With little need to balance external shareholder demands, the group can execute capital expenditures, R&D and cross-affiliate collaborations with greater speed and autonomy. Central to this strategy is commercialising the humanoid robot Atlas. Hyundai aims to build an annual production capacity of 30,000 Atlas units by 2028 and deploy them directly into industrial operations. The initial rollout will take place at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia. The robots will first handle relatively low-intensity tasks such as sorting and transporting auto parts before expanding into complex assembly work once the technology is validated. By integrating Boston Dynamics’ AI-powered robotics with its automotive manufacturing and logistics systems, Hyundai seeks to boost factory efficiency while building a new growth engine. After securing full ownership, one key hurdle for Hyundai is to achieve profitability in its robotics unit. While Boston Dynamics’ revenue for the first nine months of 2026 rose 29% year-on-year to 136 billion won, its net loss widened to 626.6 billion won due to heavy R&D and production costs. With governance restructuring now complete, Boston Dynamics is gearing up for a potential initial public offering, which sources suggest could occur around 2029 or 2030 once production ramps up. No official timeline has been set. THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

events.title: UK jobs market is a ‘mixed picture’ as wage growth slows and unemployment falls – business live
events.summary: 2m ago UK interest rate rise in December a 90% chance 25m ago Imperial Brands cutting another 2,500 jobs 34m ago Youth unemployment down to 15.1% 42m ago Vacancies lowest since 2014 49m ago Introduction: UK wage growth slows as payrolls fall UK interest rate rise in December a 90% chance Despite the slowdown in UK pay growth, the Bank of England is still expected to raise interest rates at its next meeting, in December. The money markets this morning indicate there is a 90% probability that the BoE raises UK interest rates to 4.25%, up from 4%. However, there’s little in today’s jobs report to suggest Britain is being dragged into a wage-price spiral, where inflation drives up pay, which drives up inflation…. Zara Nokes, global market analyst at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, says: “Wage growth remains the critical piece of the inflation puzzle for the Bank of England and, so far, this is not proving troublesome. Green shoots had been emerging in the labour market in recent months, but today’s official data suggests that, if anything, the labour market is still hobbling on. Crucially, for the Bank of England, the risk of a damaging wage-price spiral still looks to be minimal. With bargaining power firmly tilted towards employers, not workers, there is little kindling for wage pressures to catch alight, as was the case following the cost shock in 2022, where we saw the broader entrenchment of price pressures. Andrew Hunter , senior economist at Moody’s Analytics, argues that the UK labour market has not shaken off its weakness: Alongside the further slowdown in average weekly earnings growth to only 3.2% year-on-year in September, its lowest in six years, this suggests overall labour market conditions remain loose. With inflation still on the rise, falling real wages are likely to weigh on consumer spending over the winter, while the continued weakness of the labour market more broadly may give the Bank of England reason for pause as it considers further interest rate hikes.” Today’s UK jobs report is “a tale of two halves”, says Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist Sanjay Raja . And he fears that the unemployment rate is going to be pushed higher: The unemployment rate slipped to 4.6% in the three months to September – its lowest rate since April 2025. August HMRC payroll data was also revised higher from +10k to +20k. The bad news? HMRC payroll data showed a whopping 34k fall in September. While payroll data tend to get revised higher over time, the September drop was still the largest since November 2020. Vacancy data also slipped again, falling to 690k in the three months to September – reaching its lowest level since 2014 (outside the pandemic). What does this tell us? The economy was better than we thought – with the stronger backward-looking labour market data chiming with the stronger backward-looking GDP data. But this looks like old news. With financial conditions tightening further, geopolitical uncertainty still elevated, and the cost of doing business still rising, firms will likely cut back on hiring again – as suggested by the more recent HMRC payroll data and survey data (see the latest KPMG/REC survey). So, despite the drop in the jobless rate to 4.6%, there are headwinds emerging in the labour market, which could push the unemployment rate back up over the coming quarters. Ahead of the Milburn Review, there was some positive news on youth unemployment. With close to 1m young people deemed not in employment, education or training, youth unemployment (16-24) fell for a second straight month to 15.1%. That’s the lowest rate we’ve seen since August 2025. Stronger intervention will help support youth jobs but will need to come with equally strong incentives for businesses to hire young workers again – especially as firms move to an increasingly automated, digitalised and AI world. Imperial Brands cutting another 2,500 jobs Tobacco firm Imperial Brands is planning to cut up to 2,500 more jobs by the end of the decade. Imperial told shareholders this morning that it has already rolled out plans to cut 2,100 jobs around the world over the last year. It now expects “a further reduction of between 2,100 and 2,500 roles by the end of 2030,” as it tries to achieve £320m of annual savings by the end of the decade. This was contained within the company’s latest financial results this morning, which show Imperial’s revenues fell by 1.5% in the 12 months to the end of September, with operating profits down 10.2%. Lukas Paravicini, chief executive officer of Imperial , says: “We continue to perform and transform. This is our sixth consecutive year of growth in tobacco & NGP net revenue and adjusted operating profit. In NGP, once again we grew net revenues at double digit and market share in all categories. At the same time, we have made tangible progress on our transformation to become more consumer-centric, agile, data led and efficient.

events.title: Drought, early harvests and wet winters: can an experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
events.summary: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset . Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm “Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director. One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says. The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.” Nestled by the Mendips, the Shiplate orchard, near Bleadon, has more than 65,000 trees across 57 hectares (140 acres) The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.” He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees. Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.” An apple shaker grasps the tree to shake off ripe fruit, which is then collected by the harvester and pressed within hours at the Myrtle Farm mill. The orchard is home to older cultivars such as Somerset redstreak and dabinett, as well as newer ones including three counties and red falstaff Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.” He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.” Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators. Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing. The exhibition orchard has 458 varieties of apples, many of them rare ones such as these leathercoat russets, which date back to the 16th century “We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.

events.title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
events.summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing SHENZHEN, China -- The leaders of China and Canada called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties. The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry. “Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.” Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship. events.title: HSBC offloads US$300m in troubled data centre loan at steep discount
events.summary: HSBC has sold the slice of an US$18 billion financing package for a data centre in New Mexico tied to Oracle. HSBC sold about US$300 million (S$386 million) of a troubled New Mexico data centre loan at a steep discount, showing growing fear over AI-linked debt. The loan was for the Oracle-linked Project Jupiter, an US$18 billion data centre in New Mexico. The sale came after Oracle sent a force majeure notice. The project has faced delays, permit problems and regulatory pushback, raising doubts over the Stargate AI build-out and its future pace. HONG KONG – HSBC Holdings offloaded a roughly US$300 million (S$386 million) piece of a loan to build a troubled New Mexico data centre project at a steep discount, underscoring deepening anxiety surrounding the AI boom. The bank sold the slice of an US$18 billion financing package, which funds construction of the campus in Dona Ana County tied to Oracle, at prices in the mid-80s, according to people familiar with the matter. The sale took place several weeks ago, shortly after Oracle sent a notice to the project’s developer citing force majeure, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. HSBC’s move comes as lenders weigh their exposure to AI debt alongside renewed regulatory pushback following a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections . Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia , a linchpin of AI’s rapid expansion, has also triggered concerns about the pace of AI growth. The massive venture in southern New Mexico, known as Project Jupiter, has been beset by regulatory hurdles and opposition. Oracle sent the force majeure notice to the developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital, in an attempt to put off payments should the venture get derailed, Bloomberg reported in late September. A group of about 20 banks provided the US$18 billion loan to help fund the data centre’s construction, Bloomberg reported in late 2025. The construction financing is referred to as Project Miner. The loan comprises different tranches tied to various buildings at the site. While lenders in the syndicated loan market are generally free to sell their stakes in the secondary market, banks holding construction project financing loans typically keep them on their balance sheets. In some circumstances, they have to wait for a so-called pooled sell-down agreement to expire before they can sell. Banks looking to exit before the completion of a project’s construction will often have to sell their debt at a discount greater than the upfront fees received. Project Jupiter is a major part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out that US President Donald Trump unveiled in early 2025 alongside leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group. But the campus, designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts, has hit serious setbacks, including delays in acquiring air and pipeline permits key to its plans. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Africa’s coasts are the next frontier for UAE climate finance
events.summary: As Cop31 nears its end in Antalya, Turkey, the race for Africa’s resources is accelerating. Washington has raised the investment ceiling of its International Development Finance Corporation to $205 billion and is aiming much of it at Africa's critical minerals , including a planned stake of about 20 per cent in Balama graphite mine in Mozambique. The UAE is already ahead of that curve. It has committed more than $110 billion to projects throughout Africa in recent years, making it one of the continent’s largest investors. Much of that capital sits in ports, logistics, energy and agriculture. Yet many of these assets share a vulnerability that rarely appears in investment memos: an exposed coastline . For instance, more than 60 per cent of Mozambicans live in low-lying coastal areas. In 2023, Cyclone Freddy displaced more than 184,000 people there. Parts of the country’s central coast lost three quarters of their healthy mangrove forests between 1990 and 2024, stripping away the natural buffer that once absorbed storm surges before they reached towns, roads and ports. That creates a business case for UAE investors. Coastal ecosystems are infrastructure. Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz found mangroves prevented $1.5 billion in direct flood damage in Florida during Hurricane Irma in 2017. Mangroves also store three to five times more carbon per hectare than mature tropical forests, which allows restoration to earn revenue from carbon credits. The UAE understands this at home. It has planted about 51 million mangroves towards its target of 100 million by 2030, and it cofounded the Mangrove Alliance for Climate with Indonesia. Through Alterra, the $30 billion climate vehicle launched at Cop28, held in Dubai, it aims to mobilise $250 billion of climate investment by 2030. The question is whether that expertise and capital can be used in Africa in a way that lasts. Experience suggests one factor matters more than any other: the people who live beside the forest. Large carbon concessions negotiated with governments but not with communities have struggled. A high-profile carbon credit deal in Liberia has stalled. Restoration that pays local people, by contrast, tends to hold. A carbon credit is a promise that trees will stand for decades and that promise is only as strong as the incentives of the families who could cut them down. On Idugo Island, on Mozambique’s Zambezia coast, more than 700 families make sea salt. Most used to sell at harvest, when a 50kg bag fetched about 300 meticais ($4.70). With a community warehouse and working capital, financed partly by the UK government’s Coast Facility, they can now hold stock until the lean season, when the same bag can sell for up to 1,800 meticais. Young men who once cut mangroves for income now work in that business. The forest is worth more to them standing than cut. Development agencies are already absorbing much of the early risk. The US Millennium Challenge Corporation’s $500 million Mozambique compact includes $100 million for coastal livelihoods and climate resilience in Zambezia, led by two national institutions, ProAzul and Biofund. That grant-funded groundwork in community consent, land rights and local enterprise is exactly what makes a region investable for the private capital that follows. For UAE businesses, three opportunities stand out. First, infrastructure investors can protect their own assets. A port operator or logistics group that funds the restoration of the coast around its operations is buying insurance against storm damage and disruption, at a fraction of the cost of engineered defences. Second, UAE climate funds can co-invest alongside development finance. Blended structures, in which grants and guarantees absorb the first losses, are the most efficient way to channel Alterra-scale capital into nature-based projects that would otherwise be too small or too risky. Third, UAE companies buying carbon credits to meet their net-zero targets can insist on contracts that share revenue with communities. Credits backed by legally binding benefit-sharing carry lower reversal risk, and therefore deserve a premium. Next year, Addis Ababa hosts Cop32, putting Africa at the centre of the world’s climate talks. The UAE, a bridge between Gulf capital and African growth, is in a strong position to lead a new kind of investment there: one that treats healthy coasts not as a cost of doing business, but as an asset that protects every other investment on the shore. Vahid Fotuhi is founder and chief executive of Blue Forest, a UAE-based developer of mangrove restoration projects in Africa and Asia

events.title: Soros joins family offices selling Nvidia last quarter
events.summary: George Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Soros Fund Management cut its Nvidia stake by almost a fifth in the quarter to 30 Sept, selling about 206,000 shares worth up to US$47.4 million. Several family offices and firms also trimmed Nvidia, while others bought more. They still held more than US$1 billion in Nvidia shares at quarter end. Nvidia remains a key AI stock, but Jensen Huang’s sudden exit as CEO has hit sentiment. The company is searching for a successor and reports earnings on 17 Nov. LONDON – George Soros’ family office joined investment firms for the world’s ultra-rich in trimming Nvidia bets last quarter, locking in gains ahead of Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit from the vaunted chip designer. The billionaire’s namesake money manager cut its stake in Nvidia by almost a fifth in the period ended Sept 30, the biggest disclosed reduction for its Nvidia holding in 2026 after it had previously added to its position, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from quarterly regulatory filings. Michael Platt’s BlueCrest Capital Management, as well as an investment firm for Abu Dhabi ruler Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, also cut their Nvidia stakes during the same period. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s shares were up 22% in 2026 through the end of September, roughly double the gain of the US benchmark S&P 500 Index for the same period. The selling family offices – totalling at least a dozen – all kept at least some shares of Nvidia, with their combined holdings totalling more than US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) at the end of the quarter. For many of those firms, Nvidia remained one of their top US stock positions. Nvidia has ranked among the world’s hottest stocks in recent years as it rapidly became a poster child of the artificial intelligence boom, but Huang’s abrupt departure last week from the company that he has overseen for more than three decades has led to a reckoning. Huang, 63, was ousted as CEO on Nov 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Nvidia employees and a woman suspected by the US Justice Department of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s shares have fallen more than 25% since the New York Times first reported in late October that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot. Nvidia, which reports third-quarter earnings on Nov 17 , has begun its search for a successor, even as some of Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley – and President Donald Trump – are campaigning for his return to the top job. Nvidia’s dominance in the tech boom has made it an important part of many family offices’ investment portfolios, and some of those firms increased their positions in the stock in the third quarter. Among those buying Nvidia were firms managing fortunes on behalf of duty-free shopping tycoon Alan Parker, Brazil’s Moreira Salles finance dynasty and Missouri’s Van Tuyl family. Soros Fund Management, led by former UBS Group AG executive Dawn Fitzpatrick, sold about 206,000 shares in Nvidia last quarter worth as much as US$47.4 million, filings show. Its remaining Nvidia stake was worth nearly US$200 million as of Sept 30. Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Money managers overseeing more than US$100 million in US equities have to file a 13F form within 45 days of the end of each quarter to list their holdings in stocks that trade on US exchanges. It offers one of the few glimpses into how hedge funds and some large family offices invest. Other highlights from the latest 13F filings include: Jeffrey Skoll’s Capricorn Investment Group slashed its biggest holding, selling 9.8 million shares of SpaceX worth almost US$1.5 billion as of Sept 30. Alta Advisers, an investment firm for a branch of Sweden’s Rausing dynasty, increased its number of equity holdings by more than a third last quarter, with 114 new positions including stakes in ExxonMobil, Blue Owl Capital and AMC Entertainment. WIT LLC, which manages a portion of the Walton family fortune, is comprised solely of stakes in exchange-traded funds. It sold 2 million shares of the iShares ESG Aware MSCI EM ETF and bought 2.75 million shares of the Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets ETF. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Bahrain thwarts drone attack, Iran claims targeting US military radar
events.summary: Bahrain thwarts drone attack; Iran claims targeting US military radar The IRGC says the attack is part of efforts to counter ‘hostile activities of US forces in the region’. Bahraini air defence has thwarted a drone attack, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a barrage of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The IRGC said on Tuesday that it carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain. The reported attacks in Bahrain – home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has affected the entire Gulf region and beyond. It is the latest of several Iran-claimed attacks on US radar systems in Bahrain in recent days. The IRGC said the attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, according to a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB. Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital, Manama, after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Ministry of Interior’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”. On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa airbase, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions. On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or casualties. Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

events.title: Which areas have the most jobs for 16-24 year-olds? Use our look-up to find out
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 00:00 GMT If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start. Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say. But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening? There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021. The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted. Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years. Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment. In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008. The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012. Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job. We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education. According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000. Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils. Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs? Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in. The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna. The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work. Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships. Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings. Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts. Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts . Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector. Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880. events.summary: Ronaldo’s mother Dolores Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat after her son had been ‘deceived’ by him. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus believes he will still be responding to questions about Cristiano Ronaldo next year, after he was asked for his thoughts on scathing comments by the football great’s mother. “Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus asked on Tuesday, addressing the media before Portugal’s final Nations League group fixture away to Wales. list 1 of 3 UEFA backs Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency list 2 of 3 Germany thrash Netherlands to book Nations League quarterfinal spot list 3 of 3 Infantino made things worse at FIFA than Blatter, says Jurgen Klopp “I don’t know when it is going to stop. If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.” Jesus’s frustration stemmed from his lingering tensions with Ronaldo following the recent international retirement of football’s all-time greats. The 72-year-old head coach responded to comments from Ronaldo’s mother in the wake of the team’s latest defeat – their first since the 41-year-old forward quit national duties. Jesus wondered when he would stop being peppered about Ronaldo after a 4-1 Nations League defeat to Denmark prompted criticism from the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s mother, Dolores Aveiro. Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat since taking charge after the World Cup as Ronaldo had been “deceived” by the former Benfica boss. Ronaldo’s decision to hang up his boots for country followed a falling out with Jesus , who was previously the superstar’s coach at Saudi club Al-Nassr. The ex-Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus star accused Jesus of broken promises after he was asked to warm up during a match against Norway in September without being introduced as a substitute. Ronaldo left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and a token fine. He apologised and was expected to return to the Portugal squad, but instead brought down the curtain on a 23-year international career. His 234 appearances and 146 goals are both world records in the men’s game. Ronaldo’s lack of mobility was often pinpointed as a factor in a richly talented Portugal squad falling short in recent major tournaments. Jesus’s side had made a perfect start with four consecutive wins prior to Saturday’s shock defeat to the Danes. “After the game against Denmark, everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here,” added Jesus. “We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.” Portugal only need a point in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League group A4 against a Wales side that will finish bottom of the section. “You were all having a go at him for playing, and then as soon as he retires, suddenly it’s all hell breaking loose!” Wales boss Craig Bellamy told the Portuguese media. “He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We’re all going to miss him.”

events.title: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC
events.summary: Nvidia warned customers that a new law could expose them and the chipmaker to "legal action" over Chinese access to chip capacity, sources say. Current U.S. controls restrict shipments of advanced chips to China, while Congress is considering broader authority over remote access to chips hosted in overseas data centers. Nvidia said it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies. Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC. The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China. Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications. It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said. Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas. RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips. Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment. On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China. Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News. In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs. Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

events.title: The new French malaise
events.summary: The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society. Fifty years ago, Alain Peyrefitte, who served as a spokesperson for French President Charles de Gaulle, published a book entitled Le Mal français (The French Malaise). In the book, Peyrefitte wrote that the progress of the French nation was impeded by the lack of trust – within society and between society and state institutions. In reaction, the state exercised excessive control through rules, bureaucracy and centralisation, which resulted in stagnation. Today, the French malaise persists, but its symptoms are quite different from the ones observed by Peyrefitte. We now have the dramatic protests by French students as well as workers and other disaffected groups, which at times have turned violent. But these demonstrations are only the tip of the iceberg. The malaise runs much deeper. Following the events of October 17, in which symbols of state authority were attacked – including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille and an official building in Lyon – and businesses were looted, French President Emmanuel Macron stated that these acts sought “to tear down our institutions”. The use of such strong words reminds one of the rhetoric employed by the French government during the protests of May 1968, when students challenged the established order, and their actions were portrayed as an “attack on the Republic”. There is, in fact, a tendency to compare the current wave of demonstrations with the events of May 1968. Yet the two movements differ. The protesters of 1968 were calling for more freedom, while today’s protesters are demanding equality and dignity. The former demonstrations were led by privileged youth; the latter are driven by those who have been left behind. Perhaps a more relevant episode to examine is the upheaval of 2005 in the suburbs of Paris and other major cities following the deaths of two teenagers, Bouna and Zyed, who were pursued by the police. For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation. Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts. The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality. In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens. It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour. It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right. In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another. This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left). It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around. The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled. In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise. Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty. The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”. And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality.

events.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
events.summary: A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796 My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86. I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang. You’re damned if you do and damned if you don’t. Failure to report an accident, even if it’s minor, not your fault and you don’t plan to claim, could invalidate your policy. The algorithms that insurers use to assess risk tend to assume that one prang makes you statistically more likely to have another, regardless of blame. Plus, you, or the at-fault driver, might later decide to claim for said incident. However, when I asked the AA how it justified doubling your premium, it discovered that its system and the call handler had boobed. It didn’t say what you should have been quoted, but has decided to honour the original £364 to make up for its failings. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
events.summary: New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores S porting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients. But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market . Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says. Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too. Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people. The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers. Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City. UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week. The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout , before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other. They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis , a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area. The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts. In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year. Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.” Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park. Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed. “They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want.

events.title: Honeywell CEO says AI isn’t about replacing workers as C.H. Robinson touts 60% productivity gains: ‘We all have to reskill ourselves’
events.summary: Honeywell Technologies CEO Vimal Kapur says AI isn’t about replacing industrial workers. What it will do, though, is force them to quickly adapt as the technology transforms how companies operate. “It’s about making humans more productive,” Kapur said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. Sharing the stage with Kapur was C.H. Robinson CEO Dave Bozeman, whose 120-year-old logistics company has already seen productivity gains of more than 60% since the end of 2022 as it uses AI and other technologies to automate repetitive tasks. The two CEOs spoke about how AI is transforming some of America’s largest industrial companies, even as the technology fuels anxiety among employees worried their jobs could eventually disappear.  Both CEOs told Fortune ’s Andrew Nusca that AI has the potential to make workers more productive, but that it will also require them to learn new skills and rethink how they’ve traditionally done their jobs. Changing jobs Honeywell is no stranger to change. The industrial giant has operated across a wide range of industries during its 140-year history. In the past two years alone, it has spun off both its advanced materials business and aerospace division to focus on industrial automation. Now, Kapur is using AI to transform its business once again. While much of the attention around industrial automation has focused on AI-powered humanoid robots, such as Tesla’s Optimus, and its potential to replace factory workers , Kapur sees a broader opportunity to help employees do their jobs more effectively. He argued AI could be especially useful for companies struggling to find enough skilled industrial workers, particularly in jobs requiring hands-on labor. Rather than replacing those employees, AI could supplement their expertise and allow them to perform tasks that could require more specialized training. But making workers more productive doesn’t stop at just implementing the technology, Kapur added. Businesses need to redefine entire processes, and then make sure employees have the necessary skills to get the job done. “Next 18 to 24 months, we all have to reskill ourselves. And we take it very seriously because it’s not a small change for myself or for the entire organization,” he said. AI productivity At C.H. Robinson, Bozeman said the company is employing AI agents to take over tasks that previously required employees to manually review millions of transactions. In its “order-to-cash” process, which covers everything from processing customer orders to collecting payments, C.H. Robinson has developed specialized AI agents capable of generating freight quotes, processing shipment orders, and scheduling pickups and deliveries rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all AI system. That has allowed employees to spend less time on repetitive administrative work and more time solving complicated supply-chain problems for customers, Bozeman said. “Our people, when they look at it, do they want to do those mundane tasks every day? No, they don’t,” he said. This kind of automation is especially important as C.H. Robinson prepares to expand through a key acquisition. The company announced in October that it was acquiring rival freight broker RXO for $5.8 billion . The deal, expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, combines two of the country’s largest freight brokerages. Bozeman said the acquisition is “not just a scale play,” but also an opportunity to bring C.H. Robinson’s technology and operating model to a much larger business. The company expects to generate approximately $300 million in annualized cost savings within two years of the deal closing, it said in an October announcement , in part by applying its AI-powered operating model, Lean AI, to RXO’s operations. Learning to adapt Still, changing how employees work isn’t always easy, especially when workers wonder whether implementing technology to make them more productive could actually do away with their own jobs. Kapur said he heard the same concerns in the 1980s, when some warned computers would replace engineers. Instead, the technology changed the way engineers worked without eliminating the profession. For Kapur, creating more AI-fueled efficiencies means company leaders must evolve alongside their employees. In other words, he must also commit to upskiling. “I personally took training on Copilot because if you don’t learn yourself and immerse yourself, you can give a lot of free advice, but you don’t know what the change really means,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: U.S. agencies say they initiated investigation into Nvidia partner Megaspeed in 2024
events.summary: The Commerce and Justice Department said in a joint statement that they had initiated investigations into Megaspeed in 2024. In June 2025, U.S. officials and Singapore police conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang. Singapore has been conducting its own independent investigation and said Alice Huang was not investigated for alleged espionage. The U.S. Commerce and Justice Department on Monday stateside said they had initiated an investigation into Singapore-based company Megaspeed in 2024 to "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia, has been drawn into the fallout surrounding the leadership shake-up at chip giant Nvidia . In a joint release, the departments outlined a timeline of their investigations into Megaspeed, saying the probes began in 2024 over potential export-control violations. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, after Commerce Department investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to the company. In the same month, U.S. officials and Singapore police conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang, who was allegedly involved in a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang. "Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed," the statement said. On Wednesday, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also reposted the statement , adding, "The Department of Commerce works to protect the U.S. economy and our critical industries every day. We are very proud of the work of the Bureau of Industry and Security." In response to the statement, Chris McGuire , senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council of Foreign Relations wrote on X, "Very, very strange statement tonight... about Megaspeed. The facts here just don't add up, and this does nothing to explain why Commerce did not cut Megaspeed off from chips." McGuire said that Megaspeed kept buying chips after Nvidia put them on their no-trade list, and asked if Nvidia also blacklisted Megaspeed's subsidaries Speedmatrix and PT Megaspeed International. "I would bet they did not! If they kept shipping to them after blacklisting Megaspeed, that would be very concerning," McGuire added. The statement comes after Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said the first time authorities there learned of U.S. interest in Megaspeed and Alice Huang was in June . Singapore had already been conducting its own independent investigation and said she was not investigated for espionage. The city-state barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026 after authorities found that she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. Alice Huang was reportedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has not reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week after revelations about multiple extramarital relationships , including with two Nvidia employees. The tech giant has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. The agencies' statement also comes as Nvidia prepares to report its third-quarter results Tuesday afternoon U.S. time, with Kress set to lead her first earnings call. Earlier on Monday in the U.S., the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia 's advanced computing power through data centers in third countries. The interim final rule from the department's Bureau of Industry and Security is aimed at restricting remote access to advanced U.S. computing technology. It also comes amid growing scrutiny of Lutnick for not having done enough to prevent restricted Nvidia chips and computing capacity from reaching Chinese companies. — CNBC's Anniek Bao and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

events.title: Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aboriginal woman Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna found guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna has been found guilty of one count of trespass. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, had pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. While the court agreed she had a cultural obligation to protect forests, it found she did not have a legal excuse to remain on a logging coupe after being asked to leave. The matter has been adjourned until December 18 for sentencing submissions. An Aboriginal woman has been found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging. Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in state's northern midlands. Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania (STT). During hearings earlier this year, Ms Langford argued that STT had failed to comply with their legal obligations to identify and protect Aboriginal cultural heritage. She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered". MP declares shares in data centre developer before calling for moratorium Man charged with murder of two-week-old Hobart baby Hospital worker charged with accessing child abuse material stood down Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna spoke to the media and her supporters outside court. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Ms Langford said she had permission to be on the site from Palawa/Pakana elder Uncle Jim Everett, whom she described as the rightful owner of the cultural landscape. In a written decision handed down on Tuesday, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed that Ms Langford had cultural obligations. "Ms Langford was entitled to engage in cultural practices and prevent the logging contractors from commencing their work," Ms Geason stated. However, she said that once Ms Langford was asked to leave, that entitlement ended. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna was charged with trespassing at an anti-logging protest at Snow Hill. ( ABC News: Paul Yeomans ) Ms Geason said that while it was accepted Uncle Jim was a senior elder, he did not hold the authority to grant lawful permission for Ms Langford to remain at the coupe. "I also acknowledge the evidence of Ms Langford and her witnesses regarding the profound grief and responsibility experienced by Aboriginal people when old-growth forests are cleared. "However, the court is bound to apply the law as enacted by parliament." Ms Geason said, on the balance of probabilities, Ms Langford had not established that her cultural obligations amounted to a "reasonable or lawful excuse" to remain on the land. "As such, the charge of trespass is proved." Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna at the anti-logging protest in January last year. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) Ms Langford told the court she was "exceptionally disappointed". Outside court, Ms Langford addressed the media and her supporters. "And regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in country and country has spoken. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna says she is pleased with some parts of the chief magistrate's decision. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Despite the verdict, she said she was pleased with some parts of the written decision. "In my hands is the written reasons why this court denied my internationally recognised rights as an Aboriginal person," she said. "I am delighted to see that she has clearly recognised that as an Aboriginal woman, I have an obligation to protect country. "That those old trees hold our law, that that law exists, and that in the finding, the magistrate has recognised that that is true." Ms Langford said she would continue to practice her cultural obligations. "We will assert that our law is in country and we are the law holders," she said. In Tasmania, trespassing on land can incur a maximum penalty of six months jail, or a $5,325 fine.

events.title: Will Netanyahu lose this time?
events.summary: The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations before to retain power. But he may find it hard this time. Akiva Eldar is an Israeli author and was formerly an editorial writer and columnist for Haaretz. I have been covering Benjamin Netanyahu for more than 30 years. I was in Washington when, as a young opposition leader, he worked hand in glove with the Republicans to embarrass Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and sabotage the Oslo Accords. I have seen him cornered before. I have never seen him cornered like this. The numbers are merciless. His bloc won 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Sixty-seven members of the new Knesset recommended former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who now has up to 42 days to form a government. For Netanyahu, they may be the longest 42 days of his political life. The stakes are political, but above all personal. His corruption trial continues, and he faces a possible prison sentence. His pardon request has been gathering dust on President Isaac Herzog’s desk for months. Eisenkot’s bloc has already tabled bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and for prime-ministerial term limits. A state inquiry would strip him of the title he covets the most: “defender of Israel”. For Netanyahu, the chair is not a job. It is a lifeline. His trial, under way since May 2020, is in its final stretch. A sitting prime minister can be removed only after a final conviction. From his office, he can stall hearings and lean on the justice system. Out of office, he is just another defendant. To survive, Netanyahu does not need to build a government. He needs time to keep his rivals from building one. To buy it, he is pulling three levers. The first is his proposal for a “national unity government” of all the parties that support Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Translation: the Arab parties, representing 21 percent of the population, are out. The Jewish supremacists, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are in. So are the anti-Zionist Haredi parties. This is unity, Netanyahu-style. He has gift-wrapped the offer in the old rhetoric of the Iranian nuclear threat, with one catch: He would not give up the premiership or agree to a rotation. Eisenkot has called the offer “another spin”, yet he has agreed to negotiate with Likud. He knows a refusal would only feed the spin machine: They will talk to Arab supporters of Hamas, but not to Jewish patriots, the Netanyahu camp would claim. He also knows to beware of a diversion designed to burn through the days the president has allotted him. The second lever is incitement. At the Knesset’s opening session, Netanyahu branded Ra’am and the Joint List “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel”. A government depending on them, he declared, “must not be formed”. The goal is to strangle an Arab-backed government in its cradle, and to scare the Haredi parties, which are currently part of his bloc, away from joining the “enemy”. But this time the incitement has a hole in it. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas says Netanyahu’s confidant Natan Eshel sounded him out on the bill to bar an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi went on live television with WhatsApp messages he said came from Eshel. “Terror supporters”, it seems, are good enough for a quiet chat. The third lever is escalation. According to media reports, Netanyahu has been pressing US President Donald Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran. A return to full-scale war could help him form an emergency government. In a media interview, former Prime Minister Ehud Barak laid out the scenario: a blatant provocation that forces Iran to respond, and a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government. Lebanon, Gaza or the West Bank could serve just as well. The mantra is well-known: The enemy must see that we are united. Here, too, there are limits. A former chief of staff of the army, Eisenkot spent many years in uniform and has no shortage of sources in the army. They are likely telling him there is no urgent need for another round of war with Iran. And Trump has hinted that he wants that war over. If all three levers fail, Netanyahu has a familiar fallback: another election, next spring. Between 2019 and 2022, he dragged Israelis to the polls five times rather than give up the chair. Tibi has revealed that one of Netanyahu’s ministers tried to convince him his party would be better off “going to elections” than joining Eisenkot’s bloc. Eisenkot has a problem of his own. He campaigned on three pledges: no Netanyahu, no Haredi parties, no Arab parties. He cannot keep all three. Politics is the art of choosing which promise to break. The first path available to Eisenkot runs through the Haredim. His bloc has 48 seats; Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) would add 13, for exactly 61, the number he needs to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

events.title: Cognition’s new revenue chief says he came out of retirement because golf and advising was ‘not fulfilling’
events.summary: Cognition's new revenue chief shares how he landed at the AI coding startup after retiring. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Chris Degnan ended his early retirement to join Cognition as CRO. He said that he was not as happy as he expected to be advising startups and playing golf. His move to Cognition sparks a clash with Factory, a rival AI coding startup. Chris Degnan thought he was done with operating jobs after leaving Snowflake. But golf and startup advisory work left him wanting more. “I was done,” Degnan, Cognition’s new chief revenue officer, said on an episode of Kleiner Perkins’ podcast released on Monday. “No intent to take an operating job — none.” But after 18 months away from full time work, he said he was not as happy as he expected to be. “It’s all well and good that I could go and play golf every single day of the week at 10 in the morning,” he said. “It’s not fulfilling.” Degnan joined Cognition , the maker of the AI coding agent Devin, in September after initially declining outreach about the job. The company’s president, Russell Kaplan, eventually persuaded him to take a meeting. After learning more about its growth, Degnan said he woke up the next day with a realization: “Either I’m never going to do another operating job, which was in the cards, or I’m going to do this.” Degnan’s move to Cognition also sparked a public clash with Factory, a rival AI coding startup where he had been an advisor and board observer. In September, Factory CEO Matan Grinberg said the company had terminated Degnan, accusing him of holding undisclosed discussions with Cognition while advising Factory on confidential matters. Degnan denied sharing Factory information, saying Cognition had never asked for it and that he would never provide it. He announced his new role as Cognition’s chief revenue officer shortly afterward. Before he announced his retirement, Degnan was at Snowflake for over a decade, and rose from a sales leader to CRO at the software-as-a-Service company. '10 times more fulfilling' The decision to come to Cognition put him back at the center of the AI frenzy. “You’re in the middle of this insane thing,” he said, referring to the market’s AI momentum. “In a month on the job, it’s 10 times more fulfilling.” Degnan added that the draw to return to work is less financial than personal. “I have the luxury of not having to do these things,” he said. “I’m having a ton of fun doing it.” Degnan is among a growing list of chief executives who have boomeranged back to work after stepping down. Google cofounder Sergey Brin stepped down from a management role at Alphabet in 2019, but later said he was working at Google “pretty much every day,” drawn back by the pace of AI. Michael Dell left the CEO job at Dell in 2004, but resumed it at the board’s request in 2007. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Singapore must stand firm under pressure, cannot be a ‘laundromat for contraband’: George Yeo
events.summary: The Republic must defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, says former foreign minister George Yeo. SINGAPORE – Singapore must be prepared to withstand pressure from bigger powers and defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, former foreign minister George Yeo said. The Republic cannot become a “laundromat for contraband”, he added, stressing that while Singapore must remain flexible in navigating an increasingly fragmented world, there must be limits to how far it is willing to accommodate the demands of other countries. “Being small, we can come under pressure. But beyond a point, we say no. We have to be ourselves,” he said. He was speaking at a panel discussion titled Fault lines: Investing In A Fragmented World, at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026, where he joined fellow panellist Justin Muzinich, chief executive of Muzinich & Co, in looking at the implications of geopolitical tensions, shifting trade relationships and changing investment patterns. Yeo’s remarks come amid growing scrutiny of Singapore’s role as an international financial and wealth management hub , where its reputation for strong institutions, regulatory credibility and the rule of law is central to attracting global capital. He cited the controversy involving Singapore and Alice Huang – a Chinese former executive at Singapore-based firm Megaspeed and alleged spy who former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair with – saying the Government had responded firmly after The Wall Street Journal allegedly distorted the country’s role in the matter. Singapore cannot act on allegations without evidence, Yeo said. “If you tell us it’s contraband, we’ll investigate it, and please give us information. But if it’s just an allegation without proof, then we cannot continue withholding or impounding or detaining someone at your behest,” he added. For a small country deeply connected to the global economy, such situations can put Singapore in a difficult position, particularly when demands come from larger, more powerful nations. But Yeo said the Republic’s credibility depends on its willingness to stand by its principles rather than buckle under pressure. He recalled the 1994 Michael Fay case in which the American teenager was sentenced to caning for vandalism in Singapore. Then US President Bill Clinton appealed for clemency, and Singapore reduced the sentence from six strokes to four. The episode strained bilateral relations, with then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong unable to visit the White House for three years, Yeo said. Singapore paid a price for its position, but the country’s standing among other nations, including China and India, rose because it demonstrated it would not compromise its principles under external pressure. “So we are flexible, but beyond a point, no. And if there’s a price to be paid, so be it,” he said. Yeo said this firmness was not a departure from Singapore’s approach, but a longstanding reason other countries trust the Republic as a jurisdiction. His comments come as the global order becomes increasingly fragmented, with the rivalry between the United States and China reshaping trade, investment flows and the movement of technology and capital. Yeo described the world as undergoing a major transition, with geopolitical fault lines shifting and a new equilibrium gradually emerging. “We are entering an earthquake,” he said, adding that countries would have to remain watchful and careful as the transition unfolds. For Singapore, preserving its ability to manoeuvre will require a combination of flexibility and firmness, particularly as economic relationships become increasingly entangled with national security and political considerations. Yeo also cautioned investors against assuming that existing trends would continue uninterrupted. History, he said, has often been punctuated by sudden disruptions that could produce winners and losers. Investors should therefore consider potential failure scenarios, including a sharp disruption to the US dollar, an artificial intelligence bubble or geopolitical escalation in the Middle East. Yeo urged them to think beyond conventional market projections and consider what could bring entire economic or financial structures down. In an uncertain world, Singapore’s greatest asset may ultimately be the trust it commands. For Yeo, protecting that trust means knowing when to accommodate international pressures – and when to draw the line. Angela Tan is senior correspondent at The Straits Times’ business desk.
