events.title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
events.summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid. With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy. “It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said. Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes : a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand . Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state . Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory. But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility. “There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.” Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems , electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers . As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico , proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities. “There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans. The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017 , which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths . “We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.” There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout. “The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer. Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate. If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available. The experiment has faced challenges.

events.title: Palestine Weekly: Israel’s political reshuffle as the occupation grinds on
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? As Eisenkot’s bloc moves to form a government and courts the ultra-Orthodox, the Gaza genocide and settler pogroms continue. Israel’s parliament speaker is due to be replaced on Tuesday, one of several signs that power is being rearranged as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc angles to lead the government. But for Palestinians, the machinery of occupation, dispossession and deprivation keeps running. Israeli attacks killed at least 37 people in Gaza in the past week, while in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked whole villages with little to stop them. list 1 of 3 Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar list 2 of 3 ‘My arms are empty’: Tragedy strikes Gaza family after baby dies from cold list 3 of 3 Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu? Gaza: Two narratives of daily killing under the “ceasefire” The past week saw numerous Israeli attacks and killings in Gaza, as military claims of targeting fighters were weighed against accounts of people killed in tents, filling water containers and driving to a wedding photo shoot. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as of November 16, Israel has killed 1,650 Palestinians since the October 2025 “ceasefire”. On November 12, an Israeli bomb hit the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis. The hospital’s surgery building was struck, killing six people, including surgeon Rizq Abu Shaira, and wounding dozens. The Israeli military said it targeted Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade commander, Muhammad Abu Ismail, and accused Hamas of running a command centre in the hospital. In the days that followed, the foreign ministers of 18 Arab and Muslim-majority countries condemned the attack as a violation of international humanitarian law. Beyond the hospital bombing, the Israeli military told Israeli media it had killed 10 Hamas operatives in the past week. Among them was Samir Abu Younis, whom the army named as Hamas’s Rafah Brigade commander, killed in a drone strike in al-Mawasi on November 14, which Hamas confirmed. The strike hit a tent for displaced people , wounding two. Over the weekend, in Jabalia camp, two men were killed in a strike the army said targeted “terrorists”, and a separate strike on a Gaza government security post in al-Mawasi, Rafah, killed two people, according to Wafa. At the same time, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in circumstances that offered little indication of any military target: A tank shell hit an apartment in the al-Qastal towers in Deir el-Balah on November 13, where mourners had gathered. Israeli tanks then fired on people fleeing, killing at least three, including 12-year-old Ahmed Abu Daher, and wounding at least 20, according to local activist Hamza al-Masri and Gaza Now. According to Wafa, a man was killed by a drone on November 11 as he filled water containers on his Gaza City roof. The next day, a driver taking a groom to a wedding photo shoot in Deir el-Balah was killed by Israeli fire. On November 16, a man was shot dead at displacement tents in Jabalia, while three people, including a child, were separately wounded by gunfire inside a school south of Khan Younis, Wafa reported. This week, Gaza’s Health Ministry recorded the winter’s first death from hypothermia – a nine-month-old baby – following the devastation of last week’s rains . Israel’s Prime Minister’s Office claimed more than 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks of winter supplies have been delivered, the Times of Israel reported, and blamed Hamas for the suffering. The United Nations, however, reported this week that aid-truck offloads have fallen about 42 percent after Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor. The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Italy called conditions in Gaza “catastrophic” and urged that 150,000 tents be allowed into the territory. West Bank: Settler attacks, closures and two pogroms The most violent olive harvest on record continues in the occupied West Bank, as OCHA counted 410 harvest-related attacks this year as of November 9. The week saw several kinds of attacks by settlers and soldiers unfold repeatedly across the West Bank: Harvest and land: Residents reported settlers attacking pickers at Deir Istiya, Abu Nujeim, Wadi Saif near Beit Fajjar, Beit Dajan and Deir Jarir. On November 10, dozens of masked settlers attacked Rabbis for Human Rights volunteers and farmers at Qusra, injuring six, the Times of Israel reported. Settlers also bulldozed farmland at Marj Arzal and Sinjil and uprooted olive trees at as-Sawiya, according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack and local residents. Arson and vandalism: Settlers burned a Bedouin tent at Deir Qaddis, set a car ablaze in Taybeh while spray-painting “Death to Arabs”, and destroyed beehives at Atara, according to Wafa and Pollack.

events.title: 'Bragyu' beef a milestone for famous outback station
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Remote Bullo River Station producing branded Wagyu Brahman beef Bullo River beef for sale in Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Bullo River Station in the NT has started producing branded beef, using its herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle. The first animals have been processed and are now for sale at some local butcher shops in the north. A butcher from Kununurra says it is the first time he has been able to sell locally produced beef. One of the most remote cattle stations in northern Australia has started producing its own branded beef, which is now being sold in local butcher shops either side of the WA/NT border. Bullo River Station in the Northern Territory is located about 800 kilometres south-west of Darwin and becomes impossible to access via road during the wet season months. Managers Joe and Catherine Atkins run a herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle and said it had been a dream come true to supply local beef to communities in the region. "About six years ago the owners of this station, the Burt family, put this idea together and we started breeding what we've branded the Bragyu," Mr Atkins said. "So this is a long time coming, but it's now on the shelves for local people and it's very exciting." Wagyu Brahman cross cattle at Bullo River Station, NT. ( Supplied: Bullo River ) Mr Atkins said the station sent a trial consignment of animals to the Rum Jungle abattoir near Batchelor for a service kill and would look to ramp up next year if all went to plan. "We want to initially support butchers in Katherine and Kununurra and also give visitors here at Bullo River the paddock to plate experience," he said. "It's a very different game to what I'm used to; I've long done live export, that was my world, but this is exciting. Butcher Murray Salter cutting beef from Bullo River Station. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Murray Salter took over the butcher shop in Kununurra 10 years ago and said being able to sell locally produced beef was a milestone for his business. "I've been waiting 10 years for a moment like this to source local beef for our customers," he said. "The local Brahman stock all get sent to the live export trade, but by crossing them with the Wagyu it's brought a quality meat to the Kimberley. "Our beef supply normally travels 3,000 to 4,000 kilometres to get here, but this is from just down the road, which is nice." Beef from Bullo River Station packaged up, ready for sale. ( Supplied: Tenderspot Kununurra ) Mr Salter said the beef was tender, juicy, could be cut "with a butter knife", and local customers had been excited to support it. The Bullo River beef is the latest in a growing trend of northern cattle stations selling products locally, including KAPCO beef in the Kimberley, Eva Valley Meats in the NT, and the Niceforo family processing its cattle near Katherine for a new Darwin steakhouse. Joe Atkins said in terms of dollars, selling branded beef was not too different to selling direct to the live export trade, but there were other benefits. Bullo River Station is located 800km south-west of Darwin and 200km east of Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) "There's satisfaction for us is supporting local people and not doing live export," he said. "I've lived up here 40 years and have never been able to buy local beef from our local butcher store, so yeah, I think this is the future. "Actually 45 years ago there was a small abattoir here on Bullo River Station, so it's funny how the wheels have turned around and that is definitely our grand plan to have a micro-abattoir on the property.

events.title: Is £750m a week the real cost of rejoining the EU – or the Brexit bus myth all over again?
events.summary: A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign is very selective with its figures A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign has claimed rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750m a week. How did they arrive at these figures – and are they any more reliable than the ones on the side of the bus? What is behind Stay Out’s claim that rejoining the EU would cost '£750m a week'? Stay Out calculates that it would cost £750m a week to rejoin the EU (rounded down from £756m). The campaign group has based its analysis on the European Commission’s proposed long-term EU budget, worth €2tn (£1.66tn) over 2028-34. The group assumes that Britain rejoining the EU would increase the budget and the UK would make a contribution commensurate with its size and wealth. The £750m is a gross figure, excluding funds that would return to Britain, such as farm subsidy payments and scientific grants. It follows the method of Vote Leave, which was reprimanded by the UK Statistics Authority in 2016 for its “misleading” claim that Britain’s EU membership cost £350m a week. That statistic, emblazoned on the side of a campaign bus, did not count the British rebate or EU funds that flowed to the UK. Stay Out’s headline statistic could be seen as repeating the same trick. While its workings document states the £750m is a gross figure, that is not made clear in a campaign video likely to have far greater reach. “£750m a week: that is what the EU will charge us to rejoin” claims the video, replete with portentous music and images of streets on fire. Like the Vote Leave campaign, Stay Out emphasises the costs of payments to the EU budget, overlooking the wider economic impact of better trading links with Britain’s biggest trading partner. John Springford , of the Centre for European Reform (CER), finds the Stay Out figure “misleading” because of its focus on the UK’s potential gross contribution to the EU budget, overlooking returns from EU funds but also the broad economic losses associated with Brexit or potential gains of rejoining. According to his calculations, based on two different studies on the cost of Brexit, the cost of the UK being outside the EU in lost national income adds up to between £3bn to £3.5bn a week, with an additional loss of £1bn-£1.3bn in tax revenue that could have been earned on that lost economic activity. But is £750m correct on its own terms? It is impossible to give a definitive answer, but the figure looks too high. It is based on a number of assumptions: the fair, the bad and the highly questionable. It assumes that the British rebate – the reduction on membership fees negotiated by Margaret Thatcher in 1984 – is not coming back. That is a fair assumption, as senior EU officials, including most recently the former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, have made this point – although some net payers, such as Germany and the Netherlands, still get a rebate, highlighting the complexity of EU budget realities. Other assumptions that underpin the Stay Out calculation are more doubtful. The EU long-term budget 2028-34 is still being negotiated and the final version will almost certainly be lower than the commission’s maximalist €2tn proposal . EU countries are debating a €1.62tn compromise devised by Ireland, the current holder of the EU rotating presidency, although this has not been accepted. One of Stay Out’s more questionable assumptions is that the UK would be obliged to repay the EU’s pandemic recovery loans , which will cost €24bn a year from 2028 – EU borrowing that happened after the UK had left the EU. The Brexit negotiations set a useful precedent for any British government seeking to return to the EU: a government was liable for costs and benefits incurred as a member state. While any negotiation would be unpredictable, any British negotiating team would surely challenge being asked to fund costs incurred during its absence. Are there other estimates of rejoining? Economists have been more preoccupied with counting the cost of Brexit than the gains of rejoining the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the UK’s independent fiscal watchdog, calculated that the British economy would be 4% less productive in the long run because of Brexit. Springford at the CER devised a doppelganger model, which compared British economic performance with a counterfactual British-style economy inside the EU, and found a 5.5% reduction in GDP . The National Bureau of Economic Research concluded Brexit had resulted in a 6-8% hit to GDP by 2025 . Rejoining the EU does not mean an automatic snapback to 2016 or even 2020. Some UK production that served the EU market may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about any British commitment to staying in the EU. Springford thinks it is plausible that the UK will not recoup all the loss of Brexit, but points out overall losses are high and far exceed the cost of the UK contribution to the EU budget.

events.title: Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz
events.summary: Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping. A third U.S. aircraft carrier has arrived in the Gulf, adding to American firepower. Washington may have "misread" Iranians' capacity to resist as Tehran intensifies efforts to disrupt the critical shipping chokepoint: analyst. Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping as a third American aircraft carrier arrived in the Gulf, stoking fears of renewed escalation in the nine-month conflict . Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a "minefield of fire," according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force. Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions." Separately, CNN reported Tuesday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report. The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat. The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week. "We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel. On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity. Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours. The escalation in Tehran's rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down. Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail. After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that it "militarily is effectively over." Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners. The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal. Washington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran's demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon. Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran's maritime and inland trade routes, he said. "The presumption is that eventually Iran can't handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms," Bremmer said, calling that view a "misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist." Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said.

events.title: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
events.summary: The ongoing Israeli assault continues to have disastrous consequences for the people of southern Lebanon. Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children. Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors. list 1 of 3 UNRWA funding cuts deepen hardship for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon list 2 of 3 Flames engulf Syrian refugee camp in eastern Lebanon list 3 of 3 Israeli drone filmed flying low outside homes in southern Lebanon Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible. Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words. Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera. “What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.” More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations. Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023. We have repeatedly filmed children’s clothes, toys and school books among the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes, and repeatedly attended funerals of children killed alongside their parents. It is just as difficult emotionally to talk to survivors who show signs of trauma and tell us they live in fear. In the village of Tibnine, close to the northern edge of the area occupied by the Israeli army, 11-year-old Bannine took us to the second floor of an orphanage, to show us what a nearby Israeli air strike did to their rooms. “We were not here when this happened,” Bannine told us in a room full of debris and broken glass. Stuffed animals and clothes were still scattered on the floor. Hundreds of thousands of people returned to their villages in southern Lebanon because of a reduction in violence in recent months. But there is little sense of security, with Israeli strikes and home demolitions continuing in front line areas. “We wake up and sleep to the sound of bombing and warplanes and irritating drones,” Anaya Sultan told us. Her father was killed when the Israeli military escalated the conflict earlier this year. “He was my soul … he was everything to me,” she added. Some of the girls here are not orphans, but their parents are too poor to care for them. According to Lebanese officials, the region’s economy is in a state of collapse. Recurring conflicts, ruined infrastructure, blocked access to agricultural land, and mass displacement are making it hard for families in southern Lebanon to sustain themselves. The UN identified southern Lebanon – alongside impoverished northern and eastern regions such as Akkar and Baalbek – as areas of greatest concern where families are struggling to survive. According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than 1 million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity. “Unfortunately, so many people are displaced … many of them used to support and help us. They are not present and they themselves are struggling,” Bassima Fawaz, who helps manage the orphanage, told us as we walked through the cold hallways and rooms of the building. “We had to cover the windows with plastic sheeting because there’s no money to replace the glass shattered by Israeli bombardment. One of our girls is in hospital with pneumonia.”

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Large amounts of fencing has been dumped by the roadside in Noranda. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Main Roads says it removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from Perth's road network over the past two financial years. Perth resident Robert Parker says he reported what appeared to be asbestos and fencing dumped on Reid Highway, and blames costly, restrictive tip rules. Main Roads says the dumped material on Reid Highway will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week. Tonnes of rubbish and potentially toxic old building material are being dumped on Perth roadsides and nature strips by what is believed to be contractors and others avoiding council tip fees. WA's Main Roads department says it has removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the Perth metropolitan road network over the past two years. Dianella resident Robert Parker told 102.5 ABC Perth he recently saw what appeared to be 10 tonnes of material by the side of Reid Highway when he was out walking. "There's what appeared to be a bit of asbestos or fencing being dumped in the scrub down there," he said. "Later on, I was driving and [it appeared] a commercial contractor has chosen to use the verge on Reid Highway as his yard and dumped asbestos material and other products that should go to landfill or the appropriate recycling facility." Mr Parker said he reported the dumping to Main Roads, but also believed councils were making it too expensive for people to legally dispose of their hard rubbish. "You go to the tips, and they say, 'Oh no, we don't accept super six fencing here anymore, we don't take hardy fence', or it's only so many sheets per time. Construction waste dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Listeners to 102.5 ABC Radio Perth said there were significant barriers to disposing of rubbish legally. Matt : 'It's very expensive to take waste to the recycling centre. Last week they would not accept some bathroom tiles. They said it was construction waste, and won't be accepted. No wonder people do illegal dumping.' Anon : "It's a no-brainer: getting rid of waste in the community is far too expensive. It should be free and funded by the state government through our taxes, a clean city with proper disposal is good for everyone and everyone should pay through the taxes. Illegal dumping goes away then, and we return to a beautiful litter-free city." Anon : "I took a broken office chair to the local tip. The guy on the gate said it would cost me $45 to dump it. I guess that's why people dump stuff illegally.' Sivwarr : 'I drive up to Gidgegannup quite regularly on Toodyay road the illegal dumping starts at the bottom of the hills and just doesn't stop." Rick : "The reason for illegal dumping is laziness, selfishness and a sense of self-entitlement." Rubbish dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway between Camboon Road and Alexander Drive. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) In a statement, a Main Roads spokesperson said the department was aware of the fencing material on the southern side of Reid Highway. "The material has been programmed for removal and will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week," the spokesperson said. "Across the 2024/25 and 2025/26 financial years, Main Roads removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the metropolitan road network alone." They said the department continued to monitor known dumping hotspots and used "targeted measures" to deter offending.

events.title: Leonid meteor shower 2026: When and where to see it from where you live
events.summary: The Leonids, among the year’s fastest meteors, peak on November 17-18. Find the best time to watch in your city. Some of the fastest meteors in the night sky return this week, as the Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night between November 17 and 18. Racing at about 71km (44 miles) per second, they burn up as bright streaks, sometimes leaving glowing trails that hang in the sky for seconds. In this visual explainer, see how the shower forms as Earth crosses a comet’s dust trail, then search for your city to find the best viewing time. A meteor shower happens when dozens, or sometimes hundreds, of “shooting stars” streak across the night sky. In reality, they are not stars, but tiny bits of space debris burning up in Earth’s atmosphere. Most of this debris comes from comets, which are icy bodies that orbit the sun and shed dust as they get closer to it. When Earth’s orbit crosses one of these dust trails, the particles, called meteoroids, hit the atmosphere at high speed and heat up. They glow as meteors and usually burn up long before reaching the ground. The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, whose dust trail Earth passes through every November. Drag the slider below to follow Earth through 2026 and see when it meets the stream. What makes the Leonid meteor shower special? The Leonids are named after the constellation Leo, the point in the sky from which they appear to come. They are known for fireballs, which are unusually bright meteors from larger bits of debris. They also produce Earth-grazers, meteors that skim the upper atmosphere at a shallow angle and leave long trails near the horizon. What really sets them apart is their storms. Comet Tempel-Tuttle passes close to the sun about every 33 years and leaves debris behind. When that happens, the shower can produce a storm of at least 1,000 meteors an hour. The 1833 storm over North America helped scientists work out where meteors come from. In 1966, thousands of meteors fell every minute for about 15 minutes. The most recent storms came in 1999, 2001 and 2002, and the comet next swings close to the sun in 2031. The Leonids can appear in any part of the sky, so the best approach is to find a dark spot with a wide view, lie back and take in as much sky as you can. If you trace their paths backwards, the meteors all seem to streak out from a single point known as the radiant. This is an effect of perspective: the debris travels along roughly parallel paths, but the meteors appear to spread out from one point, much like railway tracks seem to meet in the distance. For the Leonids, the radiant lies in the constellation Leo, which rises in the east around midnight. When and how to watch from where you live According to the International Meteor Organization (IMO), the Leonids are active from November 6 to 30 and are expected to peak on the night between November 17 and 18, around 23:45 GMT on Tuesday. Under clear, dark skies, the IMO expects up to about 15 meteors an hour at the peak. The best time to watch is between midnight and dawn, as Leo climbs higher in the sky. The moon, which will be about half full on the peak night, sets around midnight in many places, leaving darker skies for the rest of the night. Find a spot away from city lights and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the dark. Use the widget below to find the best viewing times in your city. Can you see the Leonid meteor shower from both hemispheres? Yes. The Leonids are visible from the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere, but conditions are generally better in the north, where Leo climbs higher in the sky. South of the equator, the best chance is in the hour or two before dawn. Will the moon affect the Leonid meteor shower in 2026? Only slightly. The moon reaches its first quarter on November 17 and sets around midnight, so it should not interfere much during the best viewing hours. How do the Leonids compare with other meteor showers? The Leonids are far from the busiest shower. Under ideal conditions, the IMO puts their peak rate at about 15 meteors an hour, compared with about 100 for the Perseids in August and about 150 for the Geminids in December. What they lack in numbers, they make up for in speed and their history of storms.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 10 hours ago Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 15 hours ago Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 16 hours ago HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing 3 days ago Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor 4 days ago The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ® 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? events.title: North Korea is 'honing' its ballistic missiles in Ukraine with dozens of attacks a month, Zelenskyy says
events.summary: Ukraine and South Korea have said for years that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is sending troops and weapons to Russia in exchange for cash and aid, Contributor/Getty Images North Korea is sending Russia a steady monthly supply of ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said. That's allowing Pyongyang to consistently train its program on real combat data in Ukraine. North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 missiles dwindled in war use last year but saw a resurgence this summer. North Korea is sending dozens of ballistic missiles a month to Russia, allowing Pyongyang to train its weapons program on data from the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. "Unfortunately, Russia is receiving dozens of ballistic missiles a month from North Korea. This is a grave threat not only to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in an evening address on Monday. "North Korea is honing its ballistic missiles by having them used in this war. This creates additional challenges for the entire region surrounding Korea," he added. The Ukrainian leader framed the North Korean threat as a need for Europe to supply his country with more weapons for striking Russian ballistic missile launchers. "If Russia has an ally that supplies it with ballistic missiles, then Ukraine also needs clear parity so that we can respond to the Russian threat on equal terms," he added, calling on European allies to discuss providing Kyiv with "comparable weapons." "Responding in kind is fully justified," Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy's statement marks Ukraine's first public indication this year of Russia receiving a monthly supply of North Korean missiles. They were initially used in the war two years ago, but soon saw a hiatus in deployment until a resurgence this summer. Ukrainian forces first reported their use in January 2024, identifying them as the solid-fuel KN-23 and KN-24 tactical short-range ballistic missiles. Kyiv said at the time that the missiles performed poorly, with roughly half of an initial wave detonating midair before reaching their targets. Russia was said to have received scores of such missiles, but reports of their use dwindled by mid-2025. Kyiv said this summer that they had made a comeback, after a deadly strike in July on a village in southeastern Ukraine. North Korea overhauling DMZ launchers The KN-23 is often compared to Russia's Iskander-M missiles and is assessed as capable of carrying a 500-kg warhead about 280 miles or a lighter payload up to 430 miles. The KN-24 is a smaller missile with a roughly 250-mile range, fired from a multiple-launch rocket system, similar to the US-made ATACMS missile. A renewed stream of these North Korean weapons would bolster the Kremlin's own arsenal of ground-launched Iskander-M ballistic missiles, which Ukrainian intelligence estimates Russia produces about 65 a month. A senior Ukrainian intelligence official told Reuters in August that North Korea had sent Russia a missile unit that could be equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers. That month, South Korean military intelligence also said it had assessed that Pyongyang may be improving the accuracy of its missiles based on combat data accumulated from the war, along with support and consultations from Russia. Ukraine said on Sunday that Russia had attacked its cities over the week with 15 missiles of various types, alongside 2,300 attack drones and 1,590 aerial bombs. events.title: US bank outage: What caused Chase problems and Zelle payment delays?
events.summary: A Chase software bug disrupted US banking transactions and delayed some Zelle payments. Here’s what happened. Thousands of customers across the United States reported problems accessing banking services and making payments after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks. The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments. list 1 of 2 Thousands report online outages at major US banks list 2 of 2 Microsoft says affected services fully recovered following worldwide outage So, what caused the US bank outages, which banks were affected, and have services returned to normal? Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks. The disruption extended to customers of at least five other banks, who reported issues accessing services and completing transactions. According to the French news agency AFP, reports on outage-tracking Downdetector peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (19:00 GMT) before declining later in the day. “JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesperson for the bank. Which US banks were affected by the outages? Customers of several major US banks reported problems on Monday. These included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Capital One. However, not all the banks reported problems with their own systems. Chase confirmed experiencing technical problems, while US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected. Capital One and Truist also said their services were operating normally. JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in its internal hardware systems had slowed transaction processing and may have delayed transactions involving other banks. Some customers said they were not able to access accounts and funds, although Chase said customers continued to have access. The bank stressed that the disruption was not systemic and that other banks may have experienced delays when processing transactions involving Chase. Chase is the consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, which holds the most assets of any US bank. It handles payments involving other financial institutions, meaning a technical problem at Chase can also delay transactions for customers at other banks, even if those banks’ systems are operating normally. “This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” Evangelisti added. Zelle is the peer-to-peer third-party payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. It is owned by Early Warning Services, an Arizona-based company that is itself owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo. In the US, some customers also reported problems sending and receiving payments through Zelle. However, Zelle said its network was operating normally. The company said that customers access Zelle through participating banks and credit unions so technical problems at those institutions can affect the ability to make a payment even if Zelle’s own systems are fully operational. US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving other financial institutions could experience delays. JPMorgan Chase said that transactions were processing normally again following the disruption. A Chase spokesperson said that shortly after close of business on Monday, at approximately 6:30pm (23:30 GMT), transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News. However, the restoration of Chase’s transaction processing does not necessarily mean every delayed payment has been completed. Are the bank outages connected to the Microsoft and FAA disruptions? There is no confirmed connection between Monday’s outages and the recent Microsoft outage and disruptions impacting the US government’s transport agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The banking problems followed two major incidents in the US last week. On Thursday, Microsoft experienced a widespread outage that disrupted services including Outlook. A day later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop following a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications. The incidents had different reported causes. JPMorgan Chase said its disruption was due to a software bug, while the FAA disruption involved malfunctioning equipment.

events.title: Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts
events.summary: Bringing the number not in education, employment or training down from a decade high will be tough. Here’s why Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people Almost a million young people – one in eight – in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Having reached the highest level in a decade, the government is seeking to bring that number down after the recommendations made in Alan Milburn’s landmark report. However, the Neet population is not uniform – making Britain’s youth jobs crisis tougher to respond to. Here we outline the diverse backgrounds of the group struggling to make the transition from school to the world of work on a sustainable basis. An estimated 981,000 of 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are Neet, accounting for 13% of that age group, according to official figures – close to the highest level since 2014. Experts say there are myriad reasons for the high numbers, including the legacies of austerity and the Covid pandemic, rising mental ill health, fewer entry-level jobs, rising costs and taxes for businesses, AI disrupting the jobs market, and employers cutting recruitment as the Middle East war damages Britain’s economy. Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment. This has compounded by a drop in entry-level jobs: over the last 20 years the number of mid- and lower-skilled positions has fallen by about 1.6m. Higher-skilled jobs have risen by about 6.3m. The Saturday job has declined, and automation and AI are replacing entry-level roles. The UK has a much higher youth unemployment gap – the rate relative to the rest of the working-age population – than any other G7 country. Job opportunities have deteriorated more and Neet rates have risen. Britain’s headline Neet rate is above average among wealthy countries and has been falling behind. A decade ago the UK was close to the EU average. By 2025, only Romania had a higher rate. The Netherlands is the European gold standard, with a rate of about 5%. Experts say this is down to higher rates of vocational education and prioritisation of work experience in schools. In contrast, work experience participation is below average and overqualification is high in the UK by international standards. The Neet challenge is uneven across the UK – reflecting a lack of job opportunities in places with weaker local economies. Analysis for Milburn’s interim report shows eight of the 10 English local authorities with the highest likelihood of being Neet are in the north of England and the Midlands. In Blackpool, almost a quarter of young people are Neet. In Bath, the rate is fewer than one in 10. The Youth Futures Foundation shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is highest in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford. A report by the IPPR thinktank showed there was also a sixfold gap in job opportunities for young people in Rotherham relative to the Cotswolds. Rising ill health has plagued Britain at large – with long-term sickness among all working-age adults close to a record high. For young people the picture is particularly stark. Almost half of Neets report having a disability, compared with a fifth of the overall youth population. The rates for both have doubled in the past decade. Experts say the rise in ill health among young people since 2015 has been primarily driven by issues with mental health. This is partly explained by improved identification and diagnosis. But wider social and economic factors play a role – including the rise of social media and smartphones. After the turmoil of the Covid pandemic – hitting the critical final years of education for young people – a deterioration that was already under way was accelerated. Figures show a fifth of Neets report issues with depression, mental health and nervous disorders – a sharp rise from just 8% in 2012. The rates for learning difficulties and autism have also tripled. Those with special educational needs or disabilities are about 80% more likely to be Neet. Despite the focus on welfare in Milburn’s report, almost half of Neets (46%) do not claim benefits. Young women were historically more likely to be Neet. But growing difficulties for young men – with health, the erosion of traditional employment routes, and worsening educational outcomes – alongside a sharp drop in teenage pregnancy rates flipped things in the late 2010s. In terms of ethnicity, those from Black, African and Caribbean backgrounds have the highest Neet rate, at just over 15%. Those from Chinese backgrounds have the lowest rate, at just under 9%. The rates are connected significantly with wider socioeconomic factors, highlighting the intersectional nature of Britain’s youth jobs crisis. Young people from disadvantaged backgrounds are at most risk. Those from lower-working class households are more than twice as likely to be Neet than those from higher professional ones.

events.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
events.summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International , which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia , where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said. In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said. “The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said. Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.

events.title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
events.summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger. Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign , export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing. Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms. “For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University. Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan. One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity. “This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan. The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion. The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t. “I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.” Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense. Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said. Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales. Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low. “I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said. Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

events.title: ‘Due for a reset’: Mubadala CEO says global AI economy faces compute shortage
events.summary: The global AI buildout and broader economy is due for “a reset of sorts,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said Monday. Asked whether “winter is coming” — a nod to fears that the AI boom could face a correction — Al Mubarak said it was, but that “winter doesn’t mean minus 30 degrees. It could be a nice pleasant winter,” he said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The AI buildout is part of “a cycle,” Al Mubarak said, adding that the global economy has had “a very good run.” The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund is a major investor in AI infrastructure and software, with big bets on data center developers and both OpenAI and Anthropic, through MGX, a separate funding vehicle it co-founded. Mubadala has become one of the most aggressive Gulf sovereign wealth funds, embarking on a dealmaking spree , tying up with some of the biggest names in global finance, and taking a more active role leading on investments rather than being a passive capital provider. About 44% of Mubadala’s assets are in North America, and it has aligned itself with the US’ efforts to dominate the AI race with China. “There’s no navigating” between the US and China, Al Mubarak said Monday. “You either go US or China, and we’re betting on the US technology stack.” Al Mubarak said he’s “hoping that any US government, Republican or Democrat, is going to be partnership-oriented.” He said he isn’t worried about energy, and that access to capital is “OK,” but that getting enough compute is the biggest challenge. — J.D. Mr Huang was forced to step down amid revelations about affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters. Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return. Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO . Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen". The message "Taiwan heart Jensen" was projected on the Taipei 101 building in Taipei in support of Jensen Huang. ( Reuters: Ann Wang ) It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online. "We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said. The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known. However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back." The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor. Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings. Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said. Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity". Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom. Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan. He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia. "His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said. "But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

events.title: Anthropic's IPO: How do you price the future of AI?
events.summary: Like most AI companies, Anthropic is burning through cash and has not found a path to profitability, which makes its future cash flows hard to forecast. Anthropic wants a market value of up to US$1.4 trillion in its IPO, as investors try to price the future of AI and its uncertain profits. Valuing Anthropic is hard because it is still losing money and has few listed rivals, so bankers and investors are negotiating the price. CEO Dario Amodei said the firm is going public for funding to build advanced AI, but experts warn there is “no guarantee” it will keep growing. WASHINGTON – Speculation over Anthropic’s stock market valuation has highlighted one of the riskiest bets in finance: trying to put a price on the future of artificial intelligence. A few days before its initial public offering, the maker of the AI agent Claude said it was aiming for a market capitalisation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.81 trillion). That figure would put the young company among the largest stock market debuts on record, though it falls short of the US$2 trillion some estimates had floated until a few weeks ago. Since then, concern about AI development and profits has swept the market. OpenAI, a rival which plans to go public in 2027, is valued at US$1.025 trillion on the private market, according to US media reports. There are two main ways to value a company, said Michelle Lowry, a finance professor at Drexel University. The first is to estimate how much cash the company will bring in over the coming years. Money expected far in the future counts for less than money today, especially when it is uncertain, so those future amounts are reduced to work out what the company is worth now. The second compares the company with similar listed firms. If those firms are valued at, say, five times their annual revenue, the same ratio is applied to the company being valued. Both methods are well established, but “in the case of Anthropic, both of these approaches are quite difficult”, Lowry told AFP. It also has few listed peers. The closest is SpaceX, which made a record debut on Wall Street in June with a valuation of US$1.77 trillion. But that comparison is imperfect, since the Elon Musk-led company combines a social network, space operations and an AI lab. SpaceX also rides on Musk’s star power among retail investors. So, how was the US$1.4 trillion figure set? “There’s some back and forth” between companies seeking to go public and institutional investors, said Minmo Gahng, an assistant professor of finance at Cornell University. Investment banks act as intermediaries between the two sides, he said, in a process that can be time-consuming. A company’s valuation is its share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. A company going public wants that price as high as possible, since it determines how much money it raises. But it also has to leave enough room to attract buyers, since weak demand would drag down the stock. Investors, for their part, want to be sure they can later sell their stakes at a profit – and are hoping for a “pop”, or sharp rise in the share price, on the first day of trading. Speaking on Nov 13 with JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, Anthropic co-founder and chief executive officer Dario Amodei cited a company motto when discussing the IPO: “Under-promise and over-deliver.” He also said the company was going public mainly because it needs funding. Anthropic is set to raise a total of US$90 billion through the offering, money it plans to use to develop cutting-edge AI. Jay Ritter, an IPO specialist at the University of Florida, said investors accept such valuations because a handful of companies, such as Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia, have shown “you can earn profits of US$100 billion a year or more without competition eroding those profits”. But there is no guarantee that Anthropic will do the same, he warned. “It could be the case that 10 years from now, Anthropic will have been left in the dust where nobody is using frontier large language models because open-source models are good enough and cheap.” Anthropic’s growth has already shown signs of slowing and 90 pages of its IPO prospectus are devoted to risks facing the future of the company – and even of humanity – depending on the direction AI takes. events.title: S’pore has $7 trillion in assets under management as AI reshapes wealth management: Alvin Tan
events.summary: Singapore is positioning itself as a centre for the research, development and application of AI across industries, including financial services, says Minister of State for Trade and Industry Alvin Tan. Singapore will use AI to grow wealth and protect its role as a global financial centre, while keeping strong safeguards for financial integrity. Alvin Tan said wealth management has reached "$7 trillion" in assets under management, with about 2,000 single-family offices and a financial sector that makes up about 14% of GDP. Singapore will deepen capital markets, support philanthropy, and use AI safely in finance, while planning long term for jobs, innovation and future generations. SINGAPORE – Singapore must harness artificial intelligence to generate new wealth and strengthen its position as a global financial centre, even as it maintains strong safeguards to protect the integrity of its financial system, said Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development Alvin Tan. Speaking at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026 on Nov 17, he said the Republic is not seeking to compete with global technology giants in developing cutting-edge AI models, but positioning itself as a centre for the research, development and application of AI across industries, including financial services. He added that the country’s wealth management industry had grown on the back of trust, with assets under management reaching $7 trillion, and private banking client assets have increased by about 50% over the past five years. Singapore now has about 2,000 single-family offices, reflecting the continued flow of wealth into the Republic. The financial sector contributes about 14 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product and employs about 200,000 people, said Tan, who is a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) board member. He outlined three priorities for Singapore’s development as a wealth centre: growing wealth through trust, generating wealth through innovation, and giving wealth through philanthropy and legacy planning. He said trust and innovation go hand in hand, stressing that Singapore must remain a trusted regulatory hub while ensuring its financial sector remains competitive and responsive to global investors’ needs. AI is expected to play an increasingly important role in this ambition. Tan highlighted five areas where Singapore can apply AI to create economic opportunities: connectivity, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, national development housing projects and financial services. In financial services, AI could significantly improve the way banks serve wealthy clients by reducing the time needed to gather information and prepare investment recommendations. He cited the example of wealth managers preparing annual portfolio reviews for clients. Previously, bankers had to obtain information from different divisions, including investment banking, trading and wealth management, before consolidating the data into a client portfolio presentation – a process that could take several hours. With AI, information from different sources can be pulled together and a presentation prepared in minutes, allowing bankers to spend more time engaging clients. Tan said about 30 financial institutions, including HSBC, had established centres of excellence in Singapore to develop AI capabilities and financial applications. These include tokenised money market funds, agentic commerce and AI-powered advisory services. He also cited Google’s DeepMind AI research lab and OpenAI’s recently announced US$200 million (S$258 million) investment in AI research in Singapore as examples of the growing ecosystem. But the expanding use of AI in finance must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards, particularly as agentic AI takes on more responsibilities in financial transactions and advisory services. Tan said HSBC had been working with MAS on safeguards for agentic finance, including measures to ensure AI systems operate safely at runtime. Beyond AI, Singapore is also seeking to deepen its capital markets and broaden opportunities for wealth creation. Tan pointed to initiatives to strengthen the equities market, establish Singapore as a gold trading hub and develop a growth capital market group to help start-ups raise funds and find exit opportunities in both public and private markets. On the regulatory front, he said Singapore must strike a balance between maintaining rigorous anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing safeguards, and ensuring that legitimate wealth can enter the financial system efficiently. Following past money laundering concerns, the authorities have adopted a risk-proportionate approach to managing fund flows and account openings. He said the Government has been working with the private banking industry and MAS to improve account-opening processes while maintaining the necessary checks on source of wealth and source of funds.
