events.title: Greens offer government a path to pass trusts and capital gains tax changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens narrow demand on trusts and capital gains tax changes David Shoebridge has raised concerns about an exemption to Labor's trust tax for private schools and other tax-exempt entities. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The Greens want the government to commit to reforming charity rules in exchange for passage of its tax bills. A "name and shame" proposal for trusts and beneficiaries is not a red line and the Greens have no major issues with the government's CGT carve-out. The government is trying to pass two tax bills through the Senate by the end of next week. The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector. Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime. The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate. The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC. The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions. But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday. Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal. That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable. Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated". The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods". Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update. Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler. In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns". "Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote. "Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less." In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex. "This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote. He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax. In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model. "I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said. Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment... "The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now.

Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error. We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting. Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us.” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy.” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia. Others will work from India and the Philippines. While Bunnings follows the template of a big box retailer, each of its stores allows charities and community groups to run fundraising barbeques in its forecourt every weekend. Those barbeques are a significant source of income for many non-profits and have earned the chain a broad social license. The hardware barn is so well-known that children’s TV show Bluey – the most viewed program of 2024 and 2025 in the US – gently parodied it as "Hammerbarn" it in an episode. The Register mentions this because we understand the reference to TCS staff helping to deliver the Bunnings experience has gone down badly, as the chain’s employees wonder how offshore workers who have not experienced its stores and atmosphere can deliver a service that preserves its culture. Bunnings says its new IT operating model will commence in July 2027 and that “Impacted team members will be supported in their roles through Christmas, with any changes taking effect in the new year.” The company’s IT team will still employ around 500 people. These job losses add to a rotten year for Australia’s tech scene, which this year saw local heroes Canva and Atlassian farewell hundreds of staff. events.title: Two camps emerge in Silicon Valley: For Jensen Huang, or against
events.summary: Lisi Niesner/Reuters; BI Silicon Valley is divided over Jensen Huang, following his resignation over his infidelity. Some tech leaders, such as former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, want Huang back in charge at Nvidia. Huang is more controversial in the AI community, and with some women in tech. Where do you stand on Jensen ? That question is roiling Silicon Valley as it reckons with the tech titan's fall from grace. Venture capitalists, tech founders, and Nvidia employees are rallying to his defense — and some are pushing to bring him back. But others see the rush to forgive him as a familiar Silicon Valley reflex: excusing a powerful man's conduct while minimizing the damage to the people and institutions around him. The Nvidia cofounder and CEO resigned last week following reports that he had multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and a subordinate. To some, that's overshadowed by his achievements. "Jensen is one of the great builders of our time. We cannot starve the future of his innovation and industrial breakthroughs," reads a comment from Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick on Stand With Jensen , an online petition with more than 186,000 signatures. "To err is human," Kalanick — who said he is crowdsourcing "wild ideas" to get Huang reinstated — added. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider on Monday. Kalanick joins a growing chorus of people in tech defending Huang, including Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Nvidia executives, all of whom have signed the petition. For others, Huang's downfall was well-deserved given the ethical and national security implications of his conduct. Huang has long rankled some corners of tech because of his constant lobbying to sell powerful AI chips to China. One notable venture investor privately disagreed with Huang's friendly approach to China, given the chronic chip shortage in the US. The investor was frustrated that Huang had done little to address the industry's growing compute crisis, with some startups struggling to secure the resources needed to continue scaling. Nvidia had a lot of compute primarily reserved for research and development, the person said. Huang's business tactics are being scrutinized more than ever given his relationship with one of Nvidia's biggest customers, who some in the US government believe was part of an espionage scheme. That's without even mentioning his reported affair with an employee, executive Kimberly Powell, while he painted himself as a family man. One woman VC said Huang's infidelity and potential national security implications have barely surfaced in her Silicon Valley women's group chats. Some women investors, she said, have expressed that they feel sorry for Huang's wife. But, she said, "The general sentiment is, 'He's such a great leader, who cares what he does in his private life?'" Another woman VC said she and other women in venture were hardly surprised by the news, having grown accustomed to such conduct in the Valley. "Any time there is ego, power, and money, this is what happens," she said. "The tech right and founder class is rallying behind Jensen against all reason," Zvi Mowshowitz, who publishes an influential AI Substack, told Business Insider. At stake isn't just whether Huang gets back on top of Nvidia or not — an unlikely prospect — but the legacy of a key figure behind the AI boom. The godfather of the AI boom For years, Nvidia was best known for the graphics cards it sold to PC gamers. Huang was prescient in predicting that the high-powered chips would power the AI revolution. In a fateful moment, he personally delivered an Nvidia supercomputer, the DGX-1, to OpenAI's office in 2016. It was signed by then-OpenAI researcher Dario Amodei, who now runs Anthropic — which is set for a trillion-dollar blockbuster IPO this week. Huang's role in helping birth the thriving AI startup ecosystem is partly why so many venture capitalists are still Huang fans, industry insiders said. Nvidia's rise has been lucrative for them, too. Nvidia often invested in AI startups at high valuations, boosting the value of their portfolio companies by the billions. The funding also benefited Nvidia because it could be used to buy even more Nvidia chips. If the next Nvidia CEO takes a less aggressive investment approach, it could be the beginning of an AI industry correction, some investors cautioned. Tatiana Koffman, a GP at Moonwalker Capital, said Nvidia's board should finish its investigation, and that Huang should be reinstated if it finds no credible proof of a security breach. "We're painting Jensen with a moral brush for something leaders have done time and time again. He's one of the greatest engineers of the last two generations, and few people have done more for American innovation," she said. A divided AI community In the AI policy and safety world, Huang's push to sell Nvidia chips to China raised concerns about giving a US competitor powerful AI hardware. As worries about AI going rogue reached a fever pitch, Huang's staunch defense of the technology also raised eyebrows. "I would say Jensen's views have been at odds with a lot of the AI community," said former OpenAI employee Will Depue. Huang's brash statements annoyed some of the most senior people in the industry. After Huang said that Anthropic was trying to control AI through safety regulations, Amodei called Huang's claim "the most outrageous lie I've ever heard." Lior Susan, founder and CEO of VC firm Eclipse — which has invested in startups that Nvidia has also backed, like autonomous driving company Wayve — said the industry will endure beyond any single man. “Jensen was huge for the industry of AI and robotics, but the rise of robotics did not happen because of one person, and the rapid technological transformations we are witnessing will not slow down,” Susan told Business Insider. “There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made.” Have a tip? events.title: Dubai airport on target for 70 million passengers by year-end amid recovery from war
events.summary: Dubai International Airport (DXB) handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, even as the Iran war disrupted travel. The airport sustained vital connections for tourism, trade and business during the period, with continued investment in artificial intelligence, connected systems and smarter processes aimed at boosting future growth, state-owned operator Dubai Airports said on Tuesday. Passenger traffic in the nine months to the end of September fell 28.1 per cent year on year, while third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, Dubai Airports said. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. The airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, as airlines resume services and its global network strengthens, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year , the highest annual international passenger traffic recorded by any airport. DXB also has delayed its milestone target of 100 million passengers by a year to 2027. “We are focused on continuing to accommodate future growth … innovation is central to that approach,” he said. Return of global airlines The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted air travel this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. Earlier this month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai International Airport after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group also said last week that it would resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. Other airlines are scheduled to resume operations in the weeks ahead, Dubai Airports said. DXB, the world’s busiest international hub for passengers in 2025, is currently served by 57 airlines connecting Dubai to 235 destinations across 101 countries. Mr Griffiths said in September that DXB was determined to hold on to the top spot despite war-related disruption. India was the DXB’s largest country market in the third quarter of this year, accounting for 2.6 million passengers, followed by Saudi Arabia with 1.4 million and the UK with 1.3 million, Dubai Airports aid on Tuesday. London was the leading city destination, with 784,000 passengers, followed by Mumbai with 528,000 and New Delhi with 525,000. Technology leads the way Dubai Airports is investing in AI, predictive analytics and biometric technology to improve passenger flows and increase capacity within existing facilities, it said. The initiatives bring together data and visual feeds from airport systems to give operations teams a real-time view of passenger movements, aircraft activity and airport facilities. AI tools help identify potential bottlenecks and allow staff to address pressure points before they affect operations. “Every process we simplify and every bottleneck we remove helps us use our existing facilities more efficiently,” Mr Griffiths said. “By combining technology with better ways of working, we can unlock additional capacity without expanding the airport’s footprint, while improving the experience for our guests.” Operational performance Aircraft movements fell 27.6 per cent to 243,000 in the first nine months, while cargo volumes declined 23.2 per cent to 1.215 million tonnes. The average passenger load factor stood at 74 per cent, three percentage points lower than a year earlier, Dubai Airports said. The airport processed 48 million bags during the nine-month period, with 91 per cent delivered within 45 minutes of arrival. In the third quarter, 99.9 per cent of passengers waited less than 10 minutes at departure passport control, while the same proportion cleared arrival passport control within 15 minutes, Dubai Airports said.

events.title: Bunnings cuts 230 jobs in partial offshoring of tech services
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bunnings to make 230 jobs redundant amid partial offshoring of tech services Bunnings is planning to cut more than 200 permanent jobs. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Bunnings has announced plans to cut 230 tech jobs and end 120 contractor agreements. The retail giant has signed an agreement with an Indian-based tech firm to offshore some of its tech services. The company says job cuts will begin in the new year. Hardware retailer Bunnings will cut roughly 230 jobs and end 120 contractor agreements as it shifts part of its technology department offshore. The Australian retail giant announced today it had penned a new agreement with Indian-based tech firm Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as part of a restructure of its technology services. Roughly 230 permanent roles will be made redundant and an additional 120 contractor roles will end as a result. Australia cashes in on India's IT jobs machine India has positioned itself as a global hub of skilled, cheap labour, and Australian companies are moving more jobs to its shores. In a statement, Bunnings managing director Mike Schneider said the changes aimed to respond to evolving consumer needs. "This is a necessary but important change. We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us," Mr Schneider said. The transition is due to begin in December and continue through to June next year, the company said. Affected staff will be supported in their roles over Christmas, with job losses to begin in the new year, while the retailer will retain a core in-house technology team of approximately 500 people based in Australia. Remaining services will be delivered by TCS teams based in Australia, India and the Philippines. Mike Schneider says impacted staff are being offered support. ( Supplied: Bunnings ) Mr Schneider said Bunnings would support impacted team members through various means, including redundancy packages. "We know that this is difficult for our Technology team members, particularly those impacted by the change," he said. "We're managing these changes with care and respect, including through redundancy packages, career transition, redeployment wherever possible and wellbeing support." Bunnings is the latest in a growing list of Australian companies , including Qantas, NAB, Officeworks, Woolworths and Coles, to announce plans to outsource jobs overseas. 'Difficult news to share', executive says Staff were given the news earlier today by Bunnings chief information officer Genevie Elliott, who said it was "difficult news to share". In a virtual meeting with employees, Ms Elliott said many of those impacted by today's announcement had helped build up the company's technology services, which remained in use across its network of stores. Bunnings is the latest major Australian company to offshore part of its operation. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I want you to know these changes we're announcing are not a reflection of anyone's performance or their contribution or value," she told staff. "So I think it's really important you all understand why we've made this decision. Over the last two years, we've deliberately strengthened our tech function. "We've evolved our structure, our ways of working, how we prioritise and deliver work, and that structure has served us well. "I don't want anyone thinking those changes didn't work. They did. But this decision that I'm sharing today builds on that work." Ms Elliott said bringing TCS on board would allow the company to drive down business costs and tap into "specialist expertise and global retail experience". "We need a model that allows us to remain competitive without continually increasing our costs. This partnership will help us do that," she said. She said the company had to evolve alongside a rapidly transforming online retail environment impacting how consumers shop. "And we all know that tech is rapidly evolving, and the pace of change is only going to increase. That means we need to respond to keep up.

events.title: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
events.summary: Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region. Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised. list 1 of 4 US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’ list 2 of 4 Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves? list 3 of 4 UN watchdog calls on Iran to reopen nuclear facilities to inspection list 4 of 4 Iran threatens unlimited response over Strait of Hormuz after US attack Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait. The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday. In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman. Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported. It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran. The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone. The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region. In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources. There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident. Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators. The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies. It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups. No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight. The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region. A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

events.title: Robert Pattinson as James Bond throws out the 007 playbook
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts As James Bond, Robert Pattinson prepares to lead his biggest franchise yet Robert Pattinson has capped off a blockbuster year by snagging the coveted role of 007. ( AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision ) Who knew Twilight would have predicted the next 007? Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond , succeeding fellow Englishman Daniel Craig in one of Hollywood's most recognisable roles . But it's a scene from Pattinson's breakout film that has resurfaced for its eerily prophetic nature. In the 2008 vampire hit, the prom theme is Monte Carlo, with the students of Forks High School told to think "gambling, tuxedos and Bond … James Bond". The camera than cuts to Pattinson's Edward Cullen, who steps out of a sleek silver Volvo sporting Ray-Bans and a smirk. Fast forward nearly 20 years and that parallel is now a reality. Pattinson brings maximum star power to the James Bond role, reportedly beating out fellow Brits Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor. "I think Robert Pattinson is one of the most dynamic and most interesting actors working in Hollywood," film critic Luke Goodsell says, noting his roles in this year's Primetime , The Drama and The Odyssey . Several of Robert Pattinson's projects have hit theatres this year, including Primetime. ( Supplied: A24 ) Pattinson's appointment also marks the first time James Bond has been cast since Amazon reportedly paid more than $1 billion for the 007 intellectual property in February last year. The announcement of a new actor to play James Bond gives the franchise an opportunity to reinvent itself for a new audience. "It's been remarked on that it's the first time the Bond franchise has cast a big A-Lister," Goodsell says. "Obviously, Roger Moore was famous for The Saint and Pierce Brosnan was famous to some degree for Remington Steele, but this is the first time they've really gone for an A-list actor. Which is unusual, Goodsell says, because "the former producer Barbara Broccoli was always adamant that the actor should not be bigger than 007". "But I think repeating the same old playbook where they cast a relative unknown would be the least interesting choice at this point in the franchise," Goodsell says. "For them to dive straight in, headlong into a major movie star, and a really interesting and slippery actor who is also a movie star, is a really fascinating choice." Pattinson is no stranger to franchises. One of his first major roles was in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005, where he played the dashing but doomed Cedric Diggory, his death marking the moment the series goes from whimsical to something much darker. But Pattinson was launched to stratospheric levels of fame in 2008 when he landed the role of Edward Cullen in Twilight, the film's success cementing his heart-throb status in Hollywood and making him a household name, in the homes of teenage girls, at least. Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Edward Cullen in Twilight. ( Reuters: Mario Anzuoni ) Despite his fame, Pattinson rallied against his handsome, alluring on-screen persona, instead using his countless interviews on the Twilight press junket to begin a years-long affinity for creating bizarre, fabricated stories. In a 2024 interview with The New York Times , the actor revisited a 2011 interview in which he spoke extensively about watching a clown die in a little-car explosion as a kid. "There was absolutely no hesitation at all [in my voice]," Pattinson said with a combination of "pride and alarm". His reason? Boredom, explaining "the only thing people would ever ask me about was being famous" and "you go into, like, a fugue state". Goodsell says Pattinson's career has been "compelling to watch". Post Twilight, Goodsell says Pattinson and his co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'". With five Twilight movies complete, Pattinson had the freedom to get weird. Robert Pattinson (right) starred alongside Willem Dafoe (left) in The Lighthouse. ( Supplied: Universal ) He dived into independent films, teaming up with David Cronenberg for Cosmopolis, starring in the Safdie brothers' Good Time, and Robert Eggers' psychological horror The Lighthouse. In 2020, he would star in one his most Bond-esque roles to date: Christopher Nolan's Tenet. He even explored voice acting for the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron. "He really kind of, let's just say it, lets his freak flag fly. He loves a weird voice," Goodsell says.

events.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
events.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

events.title: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
events.summary: Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights. “We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.” According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates. Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying. Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not ‌an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Hannity on Fox News. The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. ‌In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage ​involved United’s Unimatic system. The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system. And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

events.summary: Trump administration introduces export licence requirements for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil. United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia. The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia. list 1 of 4 EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria list 2 of 4 Trump departs for ASEAN on summit with Xi and Putin list 3 of 4 Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports list 4 of 4 Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence. BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China. “The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement. While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”. “We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement. “We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.” The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries. The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage. Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”. Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims. Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said. The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement. “The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said. US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session. The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent. The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively. The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

events.title: MP declares shares in data centre developer before calling for moratorium
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts MP Peter George declares shares in data centre developer before calling for Tasmanian moratorium Peter George has been critical of the Tasmanian government's approach to data centres in the state. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmania's parliament is set to debate a bill for a moratorium on new data centre developments until binding rules are put in place. The MP who put forward the moratorium bill — Franklin independent Peter George — has disclosed shares in an Australian property company which has almost 80 per cent of its development pipeline in data centres. Mr George says his interest in Goodman Group centres on its commercial buildings, which have "a wide range of uses". A Tasmanian independent MP who has tabled a bill for a moratorium on new data centres has declared shares in a property giant whose global development pipeline is almost 80 per cent data centres. Franklin MP Peter George listed Sydney-headquartered Goodman Group among the interests in his "retirement plan", previously described as his self-managed super fund. The company was not included in his disclosure 12 months earlier, when the Climate 200-backed MP listed shares in Origin Energy and poker machine venue operator Endeavour Group , both of which he divested as being "inappropriate" to his values. In its full-year results, released in August, Goodman Group outlined that data centre development accounted for more than $15 billion out of its total $19.7 billion global work in progress. The proportion has increased substantially in the past 18 months for the industrial and logistics property group, rising from 57 per cent to 68 per cent by September last year, and now at 78 per cent, building large facilities aimed at cloud and AI customers. Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests Man charged with murder of two-week-old Hobart baby Hospital worker charged with accessing child abuse material stood down Peter George with supporters during his election campaign. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) Mr George has been critical of the Tasmanian government's lack of specific planning controls and broader framework for data centre development in Tasmania, describing "deep uncertainty" about their costs and benefits, with "growing resistance from communities globally". He tabled a bill for a moratorium on data centres on Tuesday until issues around location, energy and water use had been addressed, saying there is concern in Tasmania "about the impact of giant data centres on communities and natural resources". His bill would ensure data centres could only be built in specially designated zones, and that public consultation and appeal rights are retained. Mr George confirmed he bought the shares in the past 12 months and said his interest in Goodman Group was due to its commercial holdings. He said he would review his shares as Goodman "changes its portfolio listings" to ensure he is comfortable with the company's direction. "It just shows that I am technologically neutral," he said. "I am quite happy to engage with a company which, in part, develops data centres but also other commercial undertakings, other commercial buildings at the same time. Goodman Group recently withdrew plans for its proposed $1.2 billion Project Mars facility in Sydney's north shore after community opposition and regulatory changes . It does not have any publicly announced proposals for Tasmania. Mr George said data centres needed to be placed "in the right places and under the right conditions". Approach is 'one of caution', MP says The Tasmanian government last week released an "expectations" document for data centre developments. It included partnering with new renewable energy projects, but not be expected to procure or construct new firming capacity if this was already available from Hydro Tasmania. They would need to "use water efficiently" and minimise water demand through the design phase. Progressive politician has shares in mining, pokies An independent MP who received more than $72,000 in donations from Climate 200 says he will divest his shares in a fossil fuel company, miner and pokies venue operator, as they conflict with his "approach to life". A community benefit fund would also be established, a common method for any new development type involving large companies. The expectations were criticised by Labor and the Greens, who both called for binding rules prior to developments proceeding. They both supported a pause on new data centres until these are in place.

events.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
events.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 4 days ago The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

events.title: S’pore to lead ASEAN association on social security as region tackles ageing population
events.summary: Acting Minister for Manpower and Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Jasmin Lau speaking at the ASEAN Social Security Association conference on Nov 17. Singapore has taken over the ASEAN Social Security Association for 2026/2027. Leaders will share ways to handle ageing, changing work, and digitalisation. At the 43rd ASSA Conference in Singapore, about 90 delegates from 21 groups are discussing stronger safety nets. Lau said ASEAN is at “different stages of demographic transition” and by 2050 all members are expected to be ageing, aged or super-aged, with about one in six people aged 65 or older.. Lau warned that “Digital-first must never mean digital-only” and said members must improve digital safety without excluding seniors. SINGAPORE – Singapore takes the helm of the ASEAN Social Security Association (ASSA) for 2026/2027 from Brunei, at a time when the region is dealing with an ageing population, the changing nature of work and digitalisation. The handover took place at the 43rd ASSA Conference and Meeting, which is being held at Orchard Hotel Singapore from Nov 17 to 19. About 90 delegates from 21 social security organisations across ASEAN, as well as regional and international experts, are attending the three-day conference. They will exchange experiences and explore practical ways to strengthen social safety nets for their populations. Jasmin Lau, Acting Minister for Manpower and Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information noted in her opening speech that the ASEAN countries are at “different stages of demographic transition”. Some still have young populations while others – such as Singapore, with 21.4% of its citizens aged 65 or older – have already crossed the United Nations’ 21 per cent threshold for a super-aged society. She added that by 2050, all ASEAN countries are projected to be ageing, aged or super-aged societies, with around one in six people in the region aged 65 or older. “Longer lives are something for us all to celebrate. But because none of us knows whether we will live to 75 or 95, or whether we will need years of care at the end – that uncertainty is the part that is too much for us to bear, and that is why we pool risk,” she said. CPF LIFE, Singapore’s national longevity insurance annuity scheme, shares the risks across members, so everyone receives a steady monthly payout for life. To ensure these payouts keep pace with inflation, rising living standards and longer lifespans, the Government has been increasing retirement sums by about 3.5% annually from 2023 to 2027. The full retirement sum (FRS) will rise from $220,400 for those turning 55 in 2026 to $228,200 in 2027. The FRS for 2028 and beyond is not yet available as the Government is currently reviewing the figures, Lau said. The nature of work is also evolving as the rise of platform jobs and other non-traditional work arrangements creates new opportunities, while making it more challenging for workers to build up retirement savings. Before January 2025, platform workers contributed only to MediSave for healthcare needs, and lacked mandatory work injury compensation and collective representation. The Government introduced the Platform Workers Act in January 2025 to close these gaps. Under the Act, those born on or after January 1995, or older workers who opt in, make CPF contributions in increments, with their employers having to do so as well. Their contribution rates will reach standard employee-employer rates of 20% and 17% by 2029. This Platform Workers project has been nominated for the Insurance Coverage Recognition Award. During the conference, Singapore will share its learnings in strengthening retirement and housing adequacy for platform workers. Lastly, Lau touched on the digitalisation trend. She said that while technology can speed up transactions – for example, eligible CPF members can now withdraw their CPF savings online almost instantaneously – greater digital convenience also brings more risks. Member organisations will discuss how they strengthen digital safeguards without making the services too difficult for people to use. “Digital-first must never mean digital-only. Not everyone is equally comfortable with technology, particularly our seniors,” Lau added. As ASEAN countries navigate these triple challenges, she sees value in learning from one another. There are hardly perfect solutions to complex problems and Singapore does not claim to have all the answers, she said, adding that the Republic can learn from some of the solutions that ASEAN peers are trying out. Ultimately, it is through mutual learning and sharing that ASEAN can build a resilient social security system that is here to stay. “The real test of a social security system is not whether it works today. It is whether a 25-year-old starting work today can trust that it will work for him when he turns 85,” Lau said. “That is what all of us are building together.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s daughter, a close ally, remains in senior role at Nvidia
events.summary: The continued presence of Madison Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Madison Huang has become a powerful figure at Nvidia, acting like Jensen Huang’s chief of staff and shaping marketing, communications and key decisions. Her temper and direct access to her father have upset staff and helped drive departures, while some executives worry about her loyalties after Jensen Huang’s resignation. Nvidia must now decide Madison Huang’s role, along with other family members, as interim CEO Colette Kress takes control and faces pressure over the company’s future. SAN FRANCISCO – Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive officer Jensen Huang , had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, he had pulled out and tapped a long-time lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place. But Nvidia had not buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Madison Huang. On a call before the event, she berated other employees – including Puri – for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Puri interrupted and told her he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him. Less than six months later, Puri left his role at Nvidia. The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Jensen Huang resigned last week , Madison had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives. That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO, who replaced Jensen Huang after his resignation last week. Kress must quickly determine how much power Madison Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Jensen Huang’s other family members employed at the company: his son, Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez. Huang resigned after revelations that he had had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that US intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Jensen Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang returned to his job. The Huang family – including Jensen, Madison and Spencer, as well as Puri – did not respond to requests for comment. Jensen Huang, who employees say also has a hot temper, was aware of his daughter’s behaviour. He occasionally threatened to sic an angry Madison Huang on other employees and told them to be afraid of her, said two people familiar with the comments. And even senior executives thought they could not disagree with her because of her direct line to the boss. “Nepotism is almost always a bad idea,” said David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who has served on more than dozen corporate boards. “There are few examples of it even working modestly well.” Jensen Huang has said he was not around much as a father. On a podcast recorded in April, he said he “missed a lot” of Madison’s and Spencer’s childhoods, including “all of their karate tournaments”. Jensen Huang’s wife, Lori , an accomplished electrical engineer, left her job to raise their children shortly before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. His children learnt from an early age to care about Nvidia. “Both kids have read every shareholder letter, gone to every shareholder meeting, been to every single conference that I’ve ever done,” Jensen Huang said on the podcast. “Despite the fact that I was gone a lot, they found a way to always love the company.” Huang’s children took winding paths to Nvidia. Madison Huang received her bachelor’s degree from the Culinary Institute of America in 2012 and studied baking and wine at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and London from 2013 to 2015, according to her profile on LinkedIn. She then managed luxury hotels and an Italian pastry shop owned by Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessey for four years. In 2019, she started at London Business School and then joined the family business in 2020. Spencer, 36, received his bachelor’s degree from Columbia College Chicago, an arts school, in 2013, according to his profile on LinkedIn. He then owned a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, called R&D Cocktail Lab for eight years. In 2022, he joined Nvidia, where he is now a director of product management for its robotics efforts. He is considered to be quiet and focused on his responsibilities, said seven people familiar with his work. Caprez, who met Madison Huang at London Business School, joined Nvidia in 2024 and became heavily involved in dealmaking.

events.title: Singapore discussing effect of new chip rules with US, minister says
events.summary: Singapore is pressing Trump administration officials for details on new rules designed to crack down on China’s access to advanced US-made chips, and which pose a potential threat to the country’s booming AI sector. Josephine Teo, Singapore’s minister for digital development and information, said Monday her government is “engaging with our US counterparts as to the scope of implementation.” “I think more importantly, how we can facilitate trusted access to this very important AI infrastructure,” Teo said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, noting she has spoken with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. The new US Commerce Department rules include closing a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced US semiconductors via third-country data centers, which the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, at the center of the Nvidia scandal that took down CEO Jensen Huang, is accused of exploiting. Singapore has also been added to a list of countries that faces export restrictions on advanced chips, a move US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had postponed repeatedly until his agency came under scrutiny in recent days. “Singapore takes very seriously the upholding of the rule of law,” Teo said, noting that there are about 6,000 US companies in Singapore: “We safeguard our integrity in the business environment and we do not condone anyone… violating the laws of other countries.” “If they also violate our laws, they can be very certain that we will actively investigate and also hold them to account,” Teo said. Teo declined to comment on her government’s claim that the US had been unhelpful in the city state’s investigation of Megaspeed — whose former executive, Alice Huang, is accused of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset — but noted that Singapore’s own investigation into the company predated its knowledge of an investigation by the US Bureau of Industry and Security. “Suffice to say, investigations into Megaspeed are still continuing,” Teo said. Teo said the environment in Singapore for AI companies would continue to remain favorable, and pointed out that firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had deepened their presence in Singapore in recent months. “There is positive momentum. We’d like to keep it going.” “I think we will try our best to understand the impact and help ensure that we continue to have trusted access to the critical infrastructure needed for legitimate businesses,” Teo said. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Government backflips on backpacker policy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government backflips on backpacker regional work policy Tony Burke has backed down on proposed changes to backpacker visas. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) The government has backed down on planned changes to working holiday visas. The cap on third-year visas will rise from 5,000 to 25,000, while second-year applicants will have tougher regional work requirements. British backpackers remain exempt from regional work rules. The government has backed down on its planned overhaul of the working holiday-maker program, agreeing to increase the number of backpackers eligible for a third-year visa and tightening regional work requirements. Under changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, working holiday-makers would need to complete 120 days of regional work, up from 88 days, to qualify for a second-year visa. In a major speech in September, Mr Burke had announced third-year visas would be capped at 5,000 places, a reduction on the current level of about 31,000. That cap will now be set at 25,000 places, while the introduction of a ballot system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee has also been delayed to next year after it was originally scheduled to start in November. The shift follows months of pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors over the government's original proposal, with businesses warning it would significantly reduce the supply of seasonal workers and leave them struggling to fill jobs over summer. The new arrangements will apply from March 1, while backpackers who complete their regional work requirements before that date will remain eligible under the existing rules, creating a transition period for those already in the country. A visa is the reason backpackers take on the tough jobs in regional Australia. The cap on second-year places would be set at 45,000. Mr Burke rejected suggestions the government was abandoning its original reforms, arguing the final package had been shaped by consultations with industry and would ultimately deliver more workers to regional Australia. "From the day after the speech … we started consultation with industry to work through what is the best landing place to deliver the total numbers that we're talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry," he said. "This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them." He said the government had been able to refine its approach because of a go-slow in visa processing which had created "head room" to adjust the broader working holiday-maker reforms while still pursuing an overall lower migration number. The number of backpackers getting visas to Australia has fallen dramatically since July, when the go-slow was introduced as a temporary fix designed to put the brakes on international arrivals. Since then, 44,469 visas have been approved, which means a total of 177,876 backpackers would be granted entry to Australia this financial year, if the government maintains its current rate of processing. Last financial year, a record 323,077 backpacker visas were granted in Australia. Mr Burke said Australia would continue to welcome working holiday-makers. "These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term," he said. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the changes were 'complete nonsense'. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Opposition rubbishes changes as 'complete nonsense' Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the proposal as "complete nonsense" and vowed to repeal the changes if the Coalition was elected. "They've created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot. They've said they're going to delay it … they should just axe it," he said. The sentiment was echoed by Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said the backdown was "inevitable" but warned the government had already damaged confidence in the sector. The National Farmers' Federation welcomed the changes but said key questions remained unanswered. "We need more details on the logistical realities of this reform before we can fully throw our support behind it," president Hamish McIntyre said. In WA, Premier Roger Cook acknowledged the federal government's need to bring down net overseas migration, but said he would make sure it "doesn't impact on Western Australia's economy". He said he hoped further adjustment to the system would improve the number of working holiday-makers heading west. "What I want to see is less people going to the east coast and more people coming to the west coast," Mr Cook said.

events.title: The tech industry has a public image problem, Arianna Huffington says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” corporate leaders who “just lack wisdom,” Arianna Huffington said Monday. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. “We see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,” said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. “We need to invest in making humans better.” Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is “ridiculous.” Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isn’t considering it . Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, “doesn’t even come close to computing. You can’t bring Jensen back.” Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public. “The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials “to communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.” Huffington said that people’s anxieties and fears stem from how life — not just the economy — is changing. “There was no effort to really tell a story that would touch people’s hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.” Rattner, who led the Obama administration’s 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldn’t take stakes in AI companies. “We did not to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,” he said. “I think it’s a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.” — J.D. events.title: Asia shares stumble on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
events.summary: Asian shares fell after the US stepped up efforts to curb China’s access to advanced AI chips. Asian shares fell as tech stocks weakened after the US tightened rules on China’s access to advanced AI chips. Nvidia’s earnings are now a key test for AI demand, export risks, and the effect of Jensen Huang’s departure. The market mood turned more negative on AI, with Goldman Sachs saying sentiment is "about as negative as we’ve seen in quite some time“. Copper also dropped, showing wider concern about the AI outlook. The US dollar stayed near its highest since April 2025 as traders bet on more Fed rate hikes. The yen remained near 160, while the Australian dollar was steady after RBA minutes backed a possible rate rise. SINGAPORE – Asian shares followed Wall Street lower on Nov 17, weighed down by weakness in technology companies after the US stepped up efforts to curb China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, escalating the race for technological dominance. South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI slid 2% shortly after the open, while Taiwan stocks fell 1.4%. Japan’s Nikkei eased 1% and MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan extended early losses to last trade down 1.2%. Overnight, Washington said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia. The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to data centres like those in Thailand and Malaysia that Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models. The move came just days after Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with a woman who worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres. It has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China. “This is a meaningful escalation because it extends restrictions from physically buying advanced chips to accessing their computing power remotely,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. “The impact could be significant for providers heavily reliant on Chinese customers training advanced AI models. They could face lower utilisation, weaker pricing and delays to expansion, while licensing uncertainty could make financing new projects harder.” Markets in China and Hong Kong slid, with the CSI300 blue-chip index down 0.5%, while the Shanghai Composite Index lost 0.65%. The Hang Seng Tech Index shed roughly 2%. A key moment for markets on Nov 17 will be Nvidia’s earnings after the bell, with investors watching for signs of whether its debt-fuelled AI spending will continue into 2027 and how Huang’s departure could affect the company’s influence across the AI ecosystem. Torsten Sippel, UBS’s head of voice cash trading for the Americas, said: “With a roughly 7.8% implied move and a strong beat-and-raise already embedded, the bar looks increasingly tied to forward growth, AI ecosystem financing and export-control risk rather than the quarter alone.” US stock futures edged higher in Asia, with Nasdaq futures up 0.35% and S&P 500 futures adding 0.13%. EUROSTOXX 50 futures, DAX futures and FTSE futures slid roughly 0.6% each. Concerns about the AI outlook continued to roil the metals market, with copper prices falling to their lowest levels in more than four months overnight. Shares of Australian-listed miner Capstone Copper Corp tumbled nearly 6% to an eight-month low. The US dollar was perched near its highest point since April 2025 on Nov 17, helped by growing bets on more aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes as inflationary pressures in the world’s largest economy persist. Against a basket of currencies, the dollar was a touch higher at 103.69 . Markets now see a slim chance of a 50-basis-point Fed hike in December, with recent hawkish remarks from policymakers reinforcing expectations of tighter monetary policy. “There will be another superfluity of Fed speakers this week, with almost zero probability for a turn back toward ‘dovishness’,” said Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group. “After all, nothing in the economic data since last week would warrant such a turn following the hawkish calls by the senior Fed staffers offered last week.” The strength in the dollar left the yen struggling near the key 160 level, leaving traders on alert for any intervention from the Japanese authorities to shore up the currency. The euro bottomed out at US$1.0985, its lowest level since April 2025. The Australian dollar edged 0.02% higher to US$0.6739 (S$0.87) , little changed after minutes from the Reserve Bank of Australia’s November board meeting released on Nov 17 showed the majority of members judged that a hike in November was needed as inflation risks were still skewed to the upside and financial conditions might not be as restrictive as required.

events.title: Medical students should ‘learn the hard way,’ AI startup CEO says
events.summary: The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI. “The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to “train classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,” he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie. Nadler’s company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians. The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI. He noted that all of his company’s engineers use “dozens and dozens of AI buddies.” Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry “AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.” Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers “did more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,” he told Sergie that “some people underestimate how big pharma is.” “We’re early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier — and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,” Liu said. — Jake Angelo

Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest. Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks. list 1 of 4 Houthis advance in Yemen as government forces move to defend Aden list 2 of 4 The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state list 3 of 4 Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis list 4 of 4 Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications. The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
