events.title: Microsoft bug undetected since July triggered worldwide outage
events.summary: The bug that crippled Microsoft productivity software last week had been lurking undetected in the company’s data centres since July. When the software maker did some routine rerouting of user traffic on Nov 11, the system malfunctioned. Then servers critical to Outlook, Teams, the Copilot AI assistant and several other services, began to fail – ultimately triggering outages for people around the world. For the next 15 hours, amid scattered server failures, the software maker had little inkling it had a bigger problem brewing, according to a preliminary report the company issued to customers late Nov 15. Microsoft then spent another 15 hours identifying and starting to roll out the fix – an eternity for a wired world that relies heavily on the company’s software. Microsoft shares were down about 1% at 2.29pm on Nov 16. Just after 8pm New York time on Nov 11, traffic from the Teams videoconference and chat service was automatically rerouted to the separate system of servers that also handle Outlook traffic. That, combined with a loss of server capacity caused by an unrelated issue earlier in the week, triggered the bug, which prompted servers to exhaust their memory after an unexpected surge in traffic. Servers began to fail. The problem was worsened by automated systems that rerouted emails and user traffic to what Microsoft’s system thought were other, healthy servers, causing the bug to show up there, too. By 11.30am on Nov 12 – just as traffic from business in the US was reaching its peak – Microsoft realised it had a problem. It took the company another 15 hours of troubleshooting to start deploying a fix for the issue. In the meantime, work at many of Microsoft’s corporate and government clients ground to a halt , as email inboxes failed to load, Teams invitations went missing and workers resorted to phone calls and pen and paper. The outage was an embarrassment for Microsoft, and a reminder of the risks of relying so heavily on a single technology vendor. Charles Lamanna, the Microsoft executive vice president who oversees the company’s workplace software, apologised early Nov 16 for the outage in a post on the X social media site that offered more detail on what went wrong. A more comprehensive timeline, included in an update for technologists who use the Microsoft 365 bundle of software, showed how the company’s automated efforts to keep its software running helped spark a cascading failure. At the nadir on Nov 12, more than 80% of the servers behind Outlook were unresponsive. Such outages often last just a few hours at most. In this case, it took longer because as soon as servers returned to service, they were overwhelmed by waiting traffic and failed again. And because the bug had gone unnoticed for months, efforts to stabilize the system by rolling back recent updates had no effect. Microsoft tests changes to its network in labs and on small portions of its network before deploying them widely, standard protocol for companies that support large online services. This bug wasn’t caught, Lamanna said, because the simulated traffic patterns and hardware in the company’s labs didn’t reflect the real-world conditions the servers later encountered. Microsoft’s testing typically focuses on older and weaker systems to assess whether updates will trip up the weakest link in the company’s cloud. The bug that caused servers to seize up is more destructive on newer hardware with more processing power. BLOOMBERG

events.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for putting public safety at risk by failing to contain AI models in testing environments. Bonta cited the incident in which OpenAI models broke out of a testing platform to hack Hugging Face in July. The suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges violations of California's Unfair Competition Law, and accuses OpenAI of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said at a press conference. Bonta cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face . OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models. Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity." "We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said. Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes. In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits alleging that the company's ChatGPT platform led users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. California's lawsuit comes almost three months after a suit by Bonta and a coalition of other state attorneys general ended with Meta agreeing to pay $16.7 billion after being accused of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by its apps, including Facebook and Instagram. California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion from that agreement. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, setting the stage for a potentially massive initial public offering in 2027.

events.title: Chase software bug wreaks havoc on online banking
events.summary: PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images Chase says a software bug is to blame for widespread online banking issues on Monday. Reports on DownDetector showed disruptions with Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted," Chase said. A JPMorgan Chase software bug is wreaking havoc on online banking services on Monday, leading to delayed transactions. The company said it was working to resolve the issue — which impacted transactions with other banks — by the end of the day. "JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems — there is no evidence this is cyber-related," the bank said in a statement posted online . "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers." "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," it added. "Customers still have access to their accounts and funds." Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank reported thousands of combined issues as of the afternoon, according to the third-party website DownDetector.com . Some customers reported issues with being unable to access information on their accounts. DownDetector also showed reports of issues with Zelle and Capital One. The site showed a much smaller spike in reports across Citibank and TD Bank. Other US banks said the issue was not on their end. "Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time," a spokesperson told Business Insider. A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems are not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the spokesperson added. A Zelle spokesperson said that the payments app is not down and is operating as it should. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers," the spokesperson said. The bank disruptions follow a tumultuous few days of high-profile disruptions, including a massive Microsoft outage and an FAA technical failure that sparked a nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight delays and cancellations. While some online have questioned whether the crop of incidents in the last week could be connected, there is no evidence at the moment to suggest that. events.title: Sam Altman says he's not worried about OpenAI's IPO plan
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn't worried about the reception when OpenAI eventually goes public. Heather Diehl/Getty Images Sam Altman gave an update on his thinking about OpenAI's IPO. Altman said journalists seem concerned about the AI industry but "investors are pretty bullish." The OpenAI CEO also downplayed any ripple effects from Nvidia's upheaval. Sam Altman shrugged off the idea that OpenAI could become the Lyft to Anthropic's Uber. "That is not a worry," Altman said on Monday during a live interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. Altman's response to the question about OpenAI's chief rival generated audible laughter in the room. In 2019, Lyft went public before Uber, and its shares outperformed its ride-share rival's on their respective first days of trading. But Uber got the last laugh and today is worth roughly 22 times Lyft by market cap. Altman said that the narrative about investor demand is different than what he's seeing. He said that "there is a lot of skepticism from journalists" but that investors remain "pretty bullish." "I get that you have to write something every day, and there's got to be all this, you know, this fight and that one, and this winner, and this loser, and what's happening here and there — but the macro trend and the value being created, I'm not at all worried about there not being a huge amount," he said. The OpenAI chief reiterated his view that the ChatGPT maker will eventually go public. Anthropic publicly released its S-1 on October 26 and is expected to debut on Nasdaq later this week. That doesn't mean that being a public company will be easy, Altman said. "I think there are real downsides to being public," he said. "And it's a very volatile time in our industry with high-stakes, consequential decisions to make around safety and how society is going to interact with this technology. And there are doubtless things that are easier as a private company." Altman said it's "directionally a good thing" that more investors want exposure to the AI boom. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar recently said that bringing the company public is in line with OpenAI's mission to bring super intelligence to everyone. Friar also said that OpenAI is still targeting a 2027 IPO and that the tech backlash that helped power the blue tsunami in the midterms hasn't "dramatically changed" the company's thinking. "Look, we are paid as operators to manage scenarios," Friar told CNBC earlier this month. "I don't think there was something that dramatically changed for us." events.title: Honeywell Technologies CEO says 50 years of automation have gotten too complex for the humans running it
events.summary: The automation that runs hospitals, data centers, and refineries got its start in the 1970s. Honeywell Technologies chairman and CEO Vimal Kapur says it has since grown too complex for the people still watching over it. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kapur said those facilities run themselves for the most part, “maybe 95%,” with a person left in the loop to handle the exceptions. “Over the last 50 years since this got created, the systems have become highly complex because we kept adding more and more software and physical infrastructure to it,” he said. “So human cannot keep up with that at this point of time.” He pointed to recent news as an example. “What happened in the last two weeks is an example of complexity,” Kapur said, where “humans are not able to keep up with it,” producing an “undesired incident.” He didn’t say which one, but the options are almost too numerous to count. On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency was focused on a copper-to-fiber upgrade by contractor L3Harris in El Dorado, Ark., that flooded routers with connection attempts and disrupted some radar feeds, while adding, “we don’t actually have the root cause.” On Nov. 12, Microsoft 365 began an outage that lasted more than a day. As of press time, many Americans were unable to access their bank accounts . Physical AI, minus the robots Kapur’s answer is what the industry calls “physical AI,” of which he said humanoid robots are a “very small portion.” His version goes into “every large asset which exists: hospital, data center, life sciences facilities, refineries.” It adds “a layer of learning system, the human knowledge” on top of the existing automation “so that you are able to make human more productive.” The obstacle is data: “We assume that data is available abundantly on [the] internet,” Kapur said. “But when you look at a physical system, the data is in some system which is in this building or in this hospital. Those data [are] not in public domain.” Turning it into something useful takes people “who have deep domain knowledge,” he said. He called data access “the first friction” in an April talk at Goldman Sachs . Honeywell sells automation to building, industrial, and process customers, and now sells the AI layer that goes on top. When it spun off its aerospace business on June 29, completing its three-way split, the company said it was positioned to lead “the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy.” In October it launched Forge Cognition , an AI platform built with Nvidia and Dell that can run buildings in an autonomous mode, which haven’t been fully switched on, its CTO told Fortune at the time. On stage, Kapur put it more modestly: “Physical AI is not about job replacement; it’s about making humans more productive.” At Goldman in April, he said, “we’ll likely build systems which are more augmented and less autonomous.” The back-office version Dave Bozeman, CEO of freight broker C.H. Robinson, who shared the stage with Kapur, described the same problem from the paperwork side. “Variability is now structural,” he said, and supply chains “continue to be super complex.” His company’s answer is what it calls “Lean AI”: AI agents built to do “bespoke, very specific tasks,” with “orchestrating type of agents” on top. The first target is order-to-cash, which he called “a very manual process. Millions of transactions.” Bozeman also pitched it as help for workers, who he said don’t want to do “those mundane tasks every day” and would rather “go up that value stack.” He cited “over 60% productivity gains since the end of 2022.” The company’s Oct. 28 earnings release measures that as shipments per person, per day in its North American Surface Transportation unit, up more than 65% over the same stretch. The other half of that ratio is people. C.H. Robinson had about 17,400 employees at the end of 2022 and about 11,900 at the end of 2025, according to its filings, a drop of nearly a third that FreightWaves tied to automation and AI. “That doesn’t mean that it won’t be hard from a change perspective,” Bozeman said. The 1983 warning The problem Kapur describes was laid out more than 40 years ago. In 1983, Lisanne Bainbridge, a psychologist at University College London, published “ Ironies of Automation ” in the journal Automatica . She argued that designers automate what they can and leave the operator “to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate.” Those leftover tasks include taking over when conditions turn abnormal. Her central irony was that “the more advanced a control system is, so the more crucial may be the contribution of the human operator.” She also warned about what watching does to people. Operators’ “physical skills deteriorate when they are not used,” she wrote, and of the person reduced to monitoring a system: “The human monitor has been given an impossible task.” Her paper argued that automation “may expand rather than eliminate problems with the human operator.” That’s the test for an AI layer added to the stack. Fewer hands to go around Kapur said the shortage of skilled workers is what makes this urgent. “The skill shortage is the biggest problem we all face,” he said. “Anywhere there’s a touch labor where the humans need to work with hand, those workforce is becoming less and less available.” In the Goldman talk, he blamed retirement in part. A 2024 study puts numbers on it for manufacturing. Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute found U.S. manufacturers could need as many as 3.8 million additional workers between 2024 and 2033, and that 1.9 million of those jobs could go unfilled if workforce problems aren’t addressed. Sixty-five percent of manufacturers surveyed called attracting and keeping talent their primary business challenge. Kapur gave his own company a much shorter clock than 50 years. Honeywell Technologies has more than 50,000 employees, and he said he personally took training on Copilot. “Next 18 to 24 months, we all have to reskill ourselves,” he said. events.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
events.summary: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang. Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees. Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer. Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him. An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang. So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back. China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China. But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025. Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact. So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up. China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money. The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China. Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals ?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans. Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come , has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Customers report difficulty accessing online services at major US banks
events.summary: Bank of America, Chase, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Truist were listed by users who have been experiencing issues Customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said the technical problems were not a systemic issue and were not the result of a cyber-attack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online. “Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” The disruption comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage. Also on Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. The Trump administration later said the four-hour ground stop stemmed from routine maintenance. At a briefing on Saturday, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began after “a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber” and a newly installed router “started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system”. The FAA, he said, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”. Monday’s technical issues seem to center on Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services. A spokesman for US Bank said its systems are not directly affected but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.” Zelle, the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money near-instantly to friends and family, is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo . A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” they said. Some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

events.title: OpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company's safety work
events.summary: OpenAI announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support its safety work. Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, with plans to deepen the work going forward. Independent evaluators have taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile AI safety and security incidents. OpenAI on Monday announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators to help support the artificial intelligence company's safety work. The evaluators, Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire, will initially conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, OpenAI said. The company will give the organizations "deep access" to its internal systems as part of the agreements, adding that it plans to use what it learns to expand its work with independent experts going forward. "We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases," OpenAI said in a blog post . Independent evaluators have occupied a quiet corner of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry thus far, but they've taken on outsized importance following a series of high-profile safety and security incidents this year. The nascent ecosystem is still ironing out best practices, including how its work should be funded and what the reporting structures should ultimately look like. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators " employee-like access " to the company in September, shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company would do so as part of his call to slow down the pace of advanced model development. Anthropic has since announced agreements with evaluators including Accenture and METR, and it said in October that it's engaging in discussions with others. Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first How Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face . Following the incident, OpenAI said it would invest more in its safeguards and alignment work, which is the process by which the company works to ensure that its models act in accordance with human interests and values. The company said Monday that its pilot assessment with Apollo Research will explore whether its models covertly work against their developers' intentions, and whether its safeguards detect that behavior. Meanwhile, Goodfire will embed researchers within OpenAI to focus on training run monitoring, debugging and alignment, and METR intends to carry out two assessments focused on model alignment and monitoring. OpenAI said Transluce will conduct an initial assessment of its post-training alignment evaluations, and that the organization plans to conduct an eight-week-long follow-on assessment with broader access to additional models and information next year. The evaluators will get access to some of the "same internal resources" that OpenAI's own researchers use, including its source code, model checkpoints, training data and other documentation, according to the release. The organizations will also have access to relevant researchers and engineers within the company. OpenAI said Apollo Research and Goodfire "accept financial compensation for their work," but that it is not contingent on the results of their evaluations. METR and Transluce do not accept compensation for their assessments, OpenAI said, but they might accept compute or API credits to help support their work. "We do not believe that accepting financial compensation prevents assessors from maintaining independence — but we believe it is important to disclose this," OpenAI said. The evaluators will be able to publish their findings, but OpenAI said it reserves the right to redact confidential information. Disputes that arise between the company and the third parties will be overseen by OpenAI's Safety Advisory Group, which is a group of senior officials from across the company that assesses model capabilities and safeguards, and other OpenAI executives. If disagreements are not resolved, they'll be escalated to the Safety and Security Committee, an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation's board. "We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it," OpenAI said. WATCH: OpenAI unveils ChatGPT Wallet: Here’s what you need to know

"Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register . According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. events.title: Nvidia fallout: Commerce targets loophole for China's data center use
events.summary: The Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries. Commerce's action is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week. It came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China . The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it. How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Trump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends Lutnick Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictions Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exit The tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growing Nvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignation Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule. The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says. The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia." "Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China." Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported. Rep. John Mooelnaar, the Michigan Republican who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement on the new rule that it "sends a message to the Chinese Communist Party that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years." "Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy," Moolenaar said. "This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race." Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips.

events.title: China's rare earth curbs put new emphasis on Latin American investment
events.summary: Latin America is seeking to become a viable destination for investment in critical minerals , as western governments seek alternative supplies to reduce dependency on Chinese imports. China is the dominant player in the global critical minerals supply chain. It holds a market share of 70 per cent or greater for 19 of 20 minerals listed as strategically important by the International Energy Agency, and accounts for about 90 per cent of global rare-earth processing. China imposed sweeping export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements in April 2025, before increasing that list in October. The IEA estimates those controls would cost $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China if fully introduced. Beijing last week announced it was extending a pause on the curbs until January. "I think we're learning the hard way that we need to be more competitive in these environments," said Andrew Wilson, executive director at the Centre for International Private Enterprise. Mr Wilson spoke to The National on the sidelines of a critical minerals summit in Washington. Latin America and the Caribbean hold 38.3 per cent of global lithium reserves and 32.5 per cent of copper reserves, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Experts argue this places Latin America as a key centre in supply diversification, with lithium demand expected to triple by 2040. The region also holds major shares of silver and graphite, well as other metals and speciality minerals used for advanced technologies, aerospace and defence. Foreign direct investment in the region is volatile, despite averaging 11 per cent in recent decades, according to the OECD. "The question is, how do we regain those markets, regain the security guarantees, the economic guarantees, without sacrificing standards, compliance, rule of law and otherwise?" Mr Wilson asked. "It's important for us to be pushing countries where we want to invest to up their game through our own leadership, our own corporate requirements, than it is to lose those opportunities to investors who cornered the market. But the region faces challenges including high financing costs, infrastructure gaps, skill constraints and trust with local stakeholders, according to the IEA's 2026 global critical minerals outlook. It only refines about 20 per cent of its mined output of key energy minerals, except for lithium. The IEA estimates if lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths were refined locally and two-thirds of copper production were processed in the region, the economic value generated would increase by nearly 50 per cent from current levels and reach bout $220 billion by 2035, the IEA said. Gulf states are also been deepening their investment ties into the Americas. Abu Dhabi's ADQ and US-based investment firm Orion Resource Partners in January announced a joint venture to invest in companies in Latin America, Africa and Asia. US President Donald Trump 's administration also entered into bilateral preliminary agreements with Argentina and Peru in February. The UAE and Brazil signed a $2.5 billion preliminary agreement last year to explore and develop strategic minerals essential for the global energy transition. Brazil released a list of 27 critical and strategic minerals last week in an effort to boost investment and increase domestic processing. Copper, lithium, uranium and rare earths were among metals listed as a top priority for government support. The UAE and Argentina also began talks on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to increase investment access across mining and minerals, AI and other sectors. Saudi Arabia also signed non-binding agreements with Brazil and Chile during the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh this year, as the kingdom looks to expand its international partnerships and investment co-operation in the mining and minerals sector.

events.title: US stocks close sharply lower on AI jitters ahead of Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO
events.summary: The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2% and the Dow falling more than 1.4%. NEW YORK - A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Nov 16 as fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks, raising the stakes for the chipmaker’s earnings report on Nov 17 and Anthropic’s initial public offering later in the week. The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2% and the Dow falling more than 1.4%. The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, tumbling 2.5%, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index. The SOX lost 5.3%. “It’s the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade,” said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. “Over the last couple of weeks, it’s like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they’re in a freefall.” “There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren’t panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market,” Mayfield added. Nvidia slid 4.1%, extending its losses after Huang’s resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy , adding to concerns over the emerging technology’s rapid expansion and potential risks. Huang’s departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China’s access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US President Donald Trump’s expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June the SOX index was up 106.6% year-to-date. But that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43%, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year. That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10% below its all-time closing high reached on Oct 6, confirming the index is in a correction. Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4% year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion (S$140 billion). The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41%, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 lost 145.08 points, or 1.92%, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49%, to 24,509.76. Warsh remarks, rate-hike probability US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Nov 16 that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy , but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee’s latest meeting, due for release on Nov 18, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month’s interest-rate decision. Markets are pricing in a near-certain 95.7% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. Among individual stocks, chipmakers Intel and Micron both dropped more than 7%. Neocloud provider CoreWeave dipped 6.1% and rival Nebius dropped 7.6%. Hyperscalers Alphabet, Amazon and Meta slid between 2.4% and 4.1%. Server maker Dell dropped 7.0%, while Super Micro Computer fell 6.9%. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.45-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 68 new highs and 590 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 1,131 stocks rose and 3,697 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.27-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 21 new 52-week highs and seven new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 489 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 17.91 billion shares, compared with the 18.66 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Michigan’s next governor hasn’t talked to Trump yet—but wants to work with him on a 50% auto tariff set for her first day
events.summary: Michigan Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson hasn’t spoken to President Donald Trump since winning the state’s governor’s race as part of the blue tsunami that swept across the nation earlier this month. “Not yet, but I intend to,” Benson said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit in an interview with Fortune editorial director Kristin Stoller. “We’ve all got to work together to better our economy, to better Michigan.”  Top of mind, though, is a tariff that could land on her first day in office. After negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks, and parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027. That’s the same day Benson takes over from term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Benson said she hopes for opportunities to collaborate, “first and foremost, in reducing the impact of these tariffs.” She recalled touring auto parts distributor Detroit Axle in October, where she said the owner told her: “I’m sending millions of dollars into paying these tariffs, and it’s money that I had saved to expand my business, to create more jobs.” Last year, Detroit Axle said it might have to shut down a warehouse and lay off more than 100 workers, although it later backtracked. But owner Mike Musheinesh told the Associated Press, “It’s a market of who is able to survive; it’s not a matter of who can thrive.” Benson said a governor can uniquely go to Canada and broker a Michigan-specific agreement to protect jobs and lower costs, something she promised to pursue on the campaign trail. She also said she intends to negotiate “aggressively” with the federal government for carve-outs that lessen the tariffs’ impact. While campaigning, she argued levies on Canadian imports had set the average Michigan household back $5,600—more than any other state. Tariffs are just one piece of Benson’s broader plan to fix affordability.  “Our campaign was about affordability through the lens of costs down, wages up, knowing that there’s two sides of that coin,” Benson told Fortune . Michigan’s per capita incomes “have also been stagnant for far too long,” she said, adding that most jobs in the state’s economy pay $60,000 or less. In 2025, Michigan ranked in the lower half of median wages in the U.S., according to the Michigan Center for Data and Analytics. Benson said part of the governor’s job is bringing in new, higher-paying jobs and training workers to fill those roles so paychecks will “go up and not stay stagnant.” On the cost side, she pitched herself as “the CEO of state government,” saying she plans to streamline how the state delivers health care, housing development, and childcare to save money. “You’re actually running an institution, and you have metrics and a strategic plan and delivering results,” she said regarding referring to herself as the CEO of Michigan. As Michigan’s secretary of state, she overhauled the state’s DMV offices, which she said eliminated wait times and made the agency “a poster child for efficiency.” Michigan voters also sent progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate over Republican Mike Rogers. Benson said the commonality between the two wins was “costs down and wages up,” along with ending corruption.  “It’s a team effort,” she said of lowering costs. “It’s partnerships, but there’s a lot you can do as the CEO of the state to drive down costs and bring more well-paying jobs in.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking
events.summary: The lawsuit stems from an earlier incident where the tech company’s products hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind. The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement. The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties. California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company probing other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security. In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”. Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity . Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. He said most cases identified have been low severity with limited-to-no impact. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” During a press conference, Bonta said OpenAI violated the law and that his suit is meant to ensure the company puts proper safeguards in place. He noted that the possibility exists for AI agents to hack into the power grid and medical and financial institutions. “These risks are no longer hypothetical,” Bonta said. “Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase.”

events.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
events.summary: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect." events.title: Top Chamber of Commerce official says the midterms weren’t just about prices: They were about 20 years of 2% growth
events.summary: Less than two weeks after voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress in an election defined by frustration over the cost of living and perceived corruption , the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s top policy official warned a room of executives that Washington might already be misreading the message. Neil Bradley, the Chamber’s executive vice president, chief policy officer and head of strategic advocacy, said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit that the affordability anger is real. He also argued it sits on top of something voters have been signaling for two decades that “no one has been paying attention to”: 20 years of roughly 2% real GDP growth, after 60 years of more than 3%. That gap is the difference between a kid who grows up richer than their parents and one who doesn’t. Harvard economist Raj Chetty and his co-authors found in a 2017 paper that the share of Americans earning more than their parents fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s. “The concept of the American dream isn’t 3% growth, but it’s highly correlated to it,” Bradley said. The easy button Bradley’s real target was what Congress does next. “There’s a real temptation to hit the easy button,” he said, like capping credit card interest rates, price controls on pharmaceuticals, or limits on stock buybacks and dividends. These are “proposals that both ends of the political horseshoes are coming together on” and they might ease voters’ angst “for a brief period of time,” he said, “but they won’t solve our long-term challenges.” The horseshoe part is accurate. President Trump called for a one-year, 10% cap on credit card rates in January, and Sens. Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley have a bill to do it. The Senate’s version of this year’s defense bill carries new restrictions on buybacks and dividends by defense contractors. The list also lines up with the Chamber’s membership. Card issuers, drugmakers and any public company with a buyback program would pay for each of those buttons. Bradley’s alternative is growth: expand supply, expand trade, and expand the labor force “through legal immigration reform.” The growth math holds up Bradley’s numbers check out against the government’s. Real GDP grew at a compound rate of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 2005 and about 2% a year from 2005 to 2025, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data compiled by the St. Louis Fed . At 3%, an economy doubles in about 23 years, roughly the time from birth to a first job. At 2%, it takes about 35. His election count holds, too. In the 11 national elections since 2006, voters took control of the House, the Senate or the White House away from the party holding it every time except 2012. Chetty’s research complicates Bradley’s argument when it comes to the remedy. The paper found that “increasing GDP growth rates alone cannot restore absolute mobility” to the levels of the 1940s cohort. Shifting the distribution of growth back to the more equal pattern that cohort saw “would reverse more than 70% of the decline.” Bradley acknowledged this point, too: “Of course, a doubling in pie doesn’t guarantee that anyone’s individual slice will be bigger.” A record, with an asterisk Bradley’s case for optimism was what he called “a little-known record”: 5.68 million new business starts last year. “No one’s an entrepreneur if they’re pessimistic about the future,” he said. Census tracks those as business applications , meaning requests to the IRS for an employer ID number, not businesses that opened. Summed from the bureau’s monthly data, applications came to about 5.67 million in 2025 before seasonal adjustment, the most for any full year since the series began in 2004. The applications that Census flags as likely to become businesses with payroll tell a different story. Those totaled about 1.69 million in 2025 on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 1.86 million in 2023 and lower for a second straight year. More Americans are filing to start something, and fewer of the filings look like future employers. About nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, according to The AP Voter Poll . The new Congress is sworn in in January. The Congressional Budget Office’s January outlook has real GDP growing 1.8% a year in 2027 and 2028. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Sam Altman doesn’t 'know enough' to answer whether Jensen Huang should pull a Sam Altman
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Godofredo A. Vásquez/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman isn't sure about calling for Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's return. Altman said at a Semafor event that he didn't know enough about Huang's situation to answer about such a scenario. The OpenAI leader called Huang one of his heroes while adding, "heroes have flaws." Don't put Sam Altman 's name on the list of tech luminaries calling for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return just yet. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," Altman said Monday during an interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and several prominent Nvidia employees have called for Huang's reinstatement after the Nvidia board of directors announced last week that he had resigned following multiple reported affairs. On Monday, President Donald Trump said he too was supportive of the idea of Huang returning. Altman called Huang one of his heroes and said the Nvidia founder has had a major impact on the AI boom. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine," Altman said. "I am grateful for the company he has built." The OpenAI CEO also said he has "empathy" for Huang's situation, acknowledging how some have compared Huang's ouster to the brief period in 2023 when Altman was forced out of OpenAI. Altman was famously reinstated after a short number of days. "I do have, like, personal, strong empathy to a situation like this," Altman said. "I remember what it was like, although it feels like forever ago." Some on Wall Street and in tech have questioned what the AI boom will look like if Huang remains outside the company he led to become one of the industry's biggest champions. Altman said it is "hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen." At the same time, Altman expressed confidence that the industry will avoid any ripple effects from the Nvidia turmoil. "Look, at this point, I think there is so much demand, and it's so clear that AI is real and people want to use it," he said, "and revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine." Tech challenges have been plaguing US companies and entities in recent weeks. Zelle, the payments system overseen by Early Warning Services and owned by banks, was also among the apps listed as customers flagged problems. A representative for Bank of America declined to comment, while a Wells Fargo spokesperson had no immediate comment. A Zelle spokesperson said its system isn’t down and is operating as it should. JPMorgan shares fell 2.6% to $337.26 at 2.45pm in New York, narrowing this year’s gain to 4.7%. Bank of America was down 2.4%, while Wells Fargo dropped 2.2%. events.title: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
events.summary: Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The expansion comes as Kalshi faces growing legal challenges from states about its sports contracts. Leading prediction market platform Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The platform's move to offer equity trading is the boldest so far in its ongoing push into traditional financial markets and comes amid an escalating fight by states and lawmakers against its sports trading business. Sports contracts continue to account for a large share of trading on the platform. In September, the platform introduced perpetual futures tied to precious metals such as gold and silver after it had originally filed in July to offer beyond prediction market event contracts with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal regulator overseeing derivatives contracts. Perpetual futures are futures-style contracts that have no expiration date. Kalshi also received approval to list perpetual futures tied to cryptocurrencies in late May. The prediction market's stock trading offering was enabled by its purchase of broker-dealer FB Securities in July, the source said. FB Securities was founded in Delaware in 2024 and became registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in December 2025. The broker did not respond to a request for comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported that Kalshi plans to introduce stock trading. events.title: SNL's 'Sister' sketch captures the hidden burden of caring for aging parents
events.summary: Elder care often falls more on women than on men. NBC A new SNL sketch highlighted the gender gap in elder care. It focused on sisters taking on the care of aging parents. Women, in general, are more likely to do care work, whether paid or unpaid. A dark SNL sketch from this weekend about the gender gap in elder care struck a nerve — and there's a strong element of truth behind the joke. Comedian and host John Mulaney featured in the "Sister" segment, intended as a parody ad. The ad positions actor Jane Wickline as a "24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister." Other men in the ad talk about the perks of having their sister take on caring for aging parents . "My dad means the world to me. So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible," Mulaney says in the ad. "I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn. That's when I heard about Sister." The parody ad resonated sharply with viewers, garnering over 2 million views on YouTube since airing. Comments overwhelmingly agreed that this arrangement was "too real," "so true," and "triggering." Business Insider has been covering the challenges facing long-term caregivers over the past year and how the burden of care often falls on women. Business Insider is looking for people to tell us about how much they've paid for caregiving. Fill out this survey if you're interested in sharing. The SNL skit taps into that trend. Waterlily, an AI-powered financial planning platform, found that "America's family care system runs on daughters ," based on its own data and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services data. They are about twice as likely to provide hands-on care, such as helping with dressing and bathing. Among those providing care, daughters typically spend more hours a week helping provide care than sons. In interviews, well over a dozen women caregivers have told Business Insider that they wish their siblings, often male, did more for their loved one's care. Many said that their parents had expected their daughters would care for them so their sons could focus more on their careers or families. It was on them to handle their loved ones' finances, take them to appointments, and, in some cases, quit their jobs to be a live-in caregiver. However, most refused to talk about their siblings on the record. They feared retaliation from their siblings and didn't want to make it seem as though caring for their loved ones was a burden, though they said so in private. The burden of elder care often falls on women Women accounted for 55% of the 38 million unpaid elder care providers in the US, based on 2023 and 2024 Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Unpaid caregivers tend to be older, with over 11 million women elder care providers being 55 and older. While the majority of providers are women, many men are primary caregivers to their aging parents. Dina Mabry's grandmother lived alone in her mobile home until she poured boiling water on herself, after which she moved into a skilled nursing facility. Mabry's mom became her primary caregiver, as her two brothers said they couldn't take her in or help pay for her care. It caused a rift between the siblings, which took years to heal. Mabry's parents had set aside thousands to retire and travel, but $6,000 to $8,000 each month of this went to her mom's six years in care facilities. It pushed back their retirement by years. Mabry, 58, works in long-term care and disability insurance and used this experience to inform her clients about the benefits of planning ahead. She advises her clients to discuss care preferences with loved ones years before a crisis, ensuring there is enough money to hire home care nurses or move into an assisted living facility. One of the worst-case scenarios, Mabry said, is a daughter suddenly being responsible for full-time care. Are you taking care of an elderly loved one? How much does that compare to your siblings? Reach out to these reporters to share at nsheidlower@businessinsider.com and mhoff@businessinsider.com . The prices of nursing homes and adult day services have risen faster than overall consumer prices since the '90s and can end up costing families six figures. AARP found caregivers spend over $11,000 on average a year out of pocket. A large share of that is due to household expenses like food and housing. Sana Sheraz is the youngest of five siblings, but caring for her aging parents mainly falls on her. She suspects it's because of her earnings and financial stability rather than having the free time to balance caring for her parents and her children. "When it comes to medical expenses or big decisions, the weight tends to shift toward me," Sheraz said. "Sometimes it's a direct request. Sometimes it's simply the expectation in the air, the pause after a cost is mentioned, the assumption that I'll handle it — because I can." Care can be like taking on a second job Angelina Grigoryeva, associate professor of sociology at the University of Toronto, has researched the division of labor among siblings caring for elderly parents . She said it comes at a cost — financially and emotionally, with women often having to adjust their relationship to the workforce. Grigoryeva said women provide more care and are also the ones receiving more care, likely because they might feel more comfortable getting dressed, bathing, or similar activities with the help of their daughter. "When working caregivers reduce their hours or need to quit their job entirely, they lose not only their current salary and benefits but also opportunities to save for retirement and build future Social Security benefits," Debra Whitman, executive vice president and chief public policy officer at AARP, said in a press release. Carla Romagnano, who is in her 60s, had her mom, who is in her 80s and has dementia, move in with her. Romagnano said caregiving is the hardest job she's ever had. "When I come home from work, I sit in the driveway to decompress and go into the house because my second job starts," Romagnano previously told Business Insider in an as-told-to essay. "I take care of the needs of my mom, whatever I need to do, take care of my two border collies, and then figure out what's going to go on for the rest of the day. It's two full-time jobs, and I would not wish this on anybody." Grigoryeva said that while caregiving duties can involve daily living activities, they can also involve organizing paid care, such as arranging for caregivers that their parents feel happy with and paying for it. That paid care also often falls on the shoulders of women; 86% of home health aides and 87% of nursing assistants in 2025 were women. events.title: US Fed’s Warsh says emerging technologies to have ‘significant impact,’ but there are risks
events.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh the risks, including higher unemployment and the use of AI by “bad actors,” could be “highly disruptive and economically costly.” SAN FRANCISCO - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said on Nov 16 that emerging technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. Warsh refers to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” the language preferred by President Donald Trump, and said it could prove distinct from earlier technologies as a force to “supercharge idea generation.” In the best scenario, Warsh told a Fed conference on AI in San Francisco, the technology could lead “to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly across labour and the owners of capital. “In that event, real GDP growth rises persistently above its long-run average, and the US stays close to full employment.” But Warsh said the risks, including higher unemployment and the use of AI by “bad actors,” could also be “highly disruptive and economically costly.” “Our job is to prepare for whatever comes next,” he said of the Fed’s convening of a group of AI experts to explore the implications of the technology for the economy and central banking. “Our role in all this is neither advocacy nor opposition. Our responsibility is to recognise that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road,” Warsh said. “The big questions are about magnitude, scope, and timing.” The discussion between Warsh and tech industry leaders and academics took place in a San Francisco Fed auditorium before a small invitation-only audience. Those in attendance included Fed Governor Lisa Cook, venture capitalists, money managers, philanthropists, CEOs of technology, healthcare, and other companies, as well as an assortment of economists from across the Fed system, private companies and universities. While Warsh said the current moment was a “paradigm shift,” much of the conversation remained speculative. Panelists discussed how AI might allow the US economy to outpace economies in the rest of the world because of the speed with which new technology and methods are being applied in the US, but also raised concerns that it could undermine learning among students as they become too dependent on the technology. events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram
