events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. events.title: North Korea outreach in the mix for Trump’s Asia swing
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia may include a sitdown with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Though Trump floated that possibility today, telling reporters that Kim “might come,” one senior US official said days ago that there are “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.” The White House declined to comment further on the prospect, pointing to Trump’s earlier comments. While the president met with Kim during his first term, he has yet to organize a second-term meeting. Trump’s trip will culminate with an unprecedented trilateral meeting between the US, China, and Russia. Trump is not expected to discuss Ukraine at that sitdown, the senior US official said. Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are instead expected to discuss “the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Advocates dub midterms the ‘care election’
events.summary: This month’s midterms were the “care election,” according to a sweeping new report by Care Can’t Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor . The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout — citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach — as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care. “There’s this undeniable sense of momentum,” leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is “looking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.” Seven in 10 voters said it’s important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action. Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government “immediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,” including by tackling child care. Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 95% of Democrats and 69% of men. “Democrats won on these issues, and now they need to take action within the first 100 days of this new Congress,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, told Semafor. She called for lawmakers to “put them on the president’s desk, and then force him to decide whether he wants to veto.” GOP cuts to Medicaid funding helped mobilize “many first-time care-worker activists,” SEIU Executive Vice President Leslie Frane said. Advocates are hopeful the Trump administration agrees to repeal some of those cuts — but they’re not holding their breath on other issues. “When the time comes to be smart about making choices and tradeoffs, we will. But I think we’re really far from that time,” Poo said. “So this is a moment where we have the momentum to do big things, and there’s no reason why we should not.” Democrats had tried to enact paid leave and universal pre-K amid the pandemic , but fell short given their narrow Senate majority. Advocates are now optimistic that the latest wave of policymakers will see more success. “We have a whole crop of new leaders coming in with a clear mandate on these policies — and that was intentional,” Poo said. “That was a big lesson from Build Back Better, is that we need a whole different level of consensus.”

events.title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
events.summary: Robert Pattinson will star in the 26th James Bond film, the first installment since Amazon MGM took control of the franchise. Denis Villeneuve will direct the film with producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman. Pattinson has been in major films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," and will soon appear in "Dune: Part Three." Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise. Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement . "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team." Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime ," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic. The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin." In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios , which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion . Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

events.title: Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
events.summary: As promised last month , Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.” “Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers. Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf. While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models. To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making. For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections. To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders. The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes. Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche. There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option. The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making. Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.” Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update. events.title: ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers
events.summary: As U.S.-Canadian relations go frosty, one American food brand is having to be more intentional about appealing to its northern neighbors. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane said the made-in-the-U.S.A. moniker doesn’t carry the same positive connotation as it did in decades past. As a result, he said, the Chicago- and Pittsburgh-based food giant—behind Jell-O, Lunchables, and Heinz ketchup—is having to tweak its messaging. “Brand America is not as strong as it once was, and that’s been the case for some time,” Cahillane told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “We’re having to overcome brand America. Whereas, in the ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, into the ‘80s, brand America was a badge of honor, it’s a little bit more complicated today.”  Ongoing trade tensions, including a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods , have chilled Canadian attitudes towards American productions, as have repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump about making Canada the “ 51st state ,” claiming it relies too heavily on the U.S. economically. While Canadians have continued to pour money into U.S. investments , many have also made a concerted effort to boycott American goods in favor of Canadian counterparts.  In some areas, these boycotts are taking a toll on the U.S. economy. A report from the Canadian government published last month found that despite Canadian visitations to the U.S. beginning to increase, visitations from Canadians are 29% lower as of September 2026 than they were two years ago. According to the U.S. Travel Association, those decreases in visits cost the U.S. economy $4.5 billion last year. Kraft Heinz has worked to adapt to Canadians’ changing attitudes toward American goods by giving its consumers reassurance their products are being made in the Great White North, according to Cahillane. In March, subsidiary Kraft Heinz Canada announced a $250 million investment to bolster operations at its Montreal production facility. “We had to remind the Canadian consumer that all of the Heinz ketchup that they’re consuming in Canada is made in Canada,” Cahillane said. “We have a couple of big plants up there, and so when we talk to people about the local nature of our products, it may be brand America, but it’s produced in your backyard by your friends and neighbors, grown locally,” he added.  As Kraft Heinz navigates a turnaround after a 10-year slump, the company is beginning to find more solid footing outside the U.S. Despite reporting falling revenue last quarter, it was particularly offset by growing sales in Canada. Its Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen debuted in Canada in July, and, according to Cahillane, it sold out three months of inventory in a week. Kraft Heinz is also finding ways to navigate tariffs after initially being hit hard by the implementation of the import taxes. The food giant reported in May 2025 it would need to shift suppliers and potentially reformulate products as a result of the levies. “We’re already local. We have to be hyperlocal,” Cahillane told Fortune . “We have to build in redundancy. We have to build in the ability to do things faster than we ever have before, and that becomes hyperlocal for us.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Online bookmaker targets netball club for inducements, signs up 18yos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT Wagering Commission fines bookmaker $83k over Instagram inducements The scheme targeted a community football and netball club, with young women making up the majority of new sign-ups. ( AAP: Scott Barbour ) A bookmaker has been hit with a hefty fine over an inducement scheme targeting a community sporting club. The scheme saw about a dozen 18-year-olds sign up to bookmaker Amused Group's promotional offer. The NT-registered bookmaker has since collapsed into liquidation, owing an estimated $5 million to creditors. An Australian online bookmaker has been fined more than $83,000 after an inducement scheme targeting a community football and netball club drew in about a dozen 18-year-olds. It came after an official from the sports club uploaded an Instagram post announcing BetDeluxe as a new club sponsor offering a promotional deal to players who signed up with the company. The promotion, which promised new sign-ups access to $300 and other benefits, saw about 15 people create new accounts with BetDeluxe, an arm of Northern Territory-registered bookmaker Amused Group. More than 10 18-year-old women were among those found to have responded to the promotion. A sporting club official promoted the deal in a post on the club's Instagram page. ( Reuters: Thomas White ) In a decision last month by the online gambling regulator NT Wagering Commission, Amused Group was found to have been involved in "a sustained, employee-facilitated inducement scheme operating over several weeks" involving the club. A series of text messages between a senior Amused Group employee and the sporting club official who made the post were aired in the findings, although none of the people or the club were named. The texts showed that the gambling employee, cited as Mr R, "actively encouraged [the sporting club official] Mr K, to solicit further sign-ups from his personal network" over several weeks in 2025. "Can see a couple sign-ups so far, but not many have come through," read one text by Mr R. The NT Wagering Commission regulates online gambling in the NT, but is also Australia's de facto regulator for the sector. ( ABC News: Jasmine Hines ) The commission found the Instagram post uploaded by Mr K for the club was done without the knowledge of the gambling company, which then tried to get the post immediately removed once it became aware of it. "Under 1,000 views and we have avoided a major issue," Mr R told Mr K in a text. The post was also shared on Facebook groups and via private WhatsApp messages. The Facebook and Instagram posts were later deleted. New bill could restrict major gambling companies An independent politician is set to introduce a private member's bill to the NT parliament, which if passed would impose a string of new laws on some of Australia's largest online gambling companies. However, the commission rejected Amused Group's submission that the "conduct was not intentional" and ruled the post should have been detected by the company's "internal compliance controls". "[Amused Group's] persistence and the involvement of a senior employee place it materially above an administrative or technical failure," the decision read. The commission said the fact that between 10 and 15 "individuals at the lower end of the legal wagering age were among those that responded to the promotional arrangement" was a "matter of concern in context of the licensee's responsible gaming operations". The company was fined $83,250, which the commission said reflected the "serious and knowing character of the breach, the consumer harm that occurred, the aggravating and mitigating circumstance and the objectives of general and specific deterrence". The commission also found none of those who signed up "suffered any financial loss". Amused Group collapses, owing creditors millions Since the commission's decision was handed down, Amused Group has been placed under administration, with corporate documents showing the company owes millions to creditors. In a report released on November 13 by appointed administrator Costa Nicodemou, he said, "To date, I have identified 54 unsecured creditors with claims totalling $5 million". Mr Nicodemou's report said the unsecured creditors included "a number of racing bodies". Alastair Shields says Matchday is now operating Amused's former business and "has assumed responsibility for all client funds". ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) NT Wagering Commission chair Alastair Shields told the ABC that "the wagering business previously operated by Amused Australia Pty Ltd is now being operated by another company, Matchday Entertainment Pty Ltd (Matchday)".

events.title: Days after Microsoft and the FAA went dark, Chase and Wells Fargo customers can’t get to their money
events.summary: If you had trouble logging into your bank’s website on Monday, you’re not alone. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of the day unable to log in or move money, with the bank saying the outage spread from it’s website and app to some branches and to outside apps that connect to Chase accounts. Wells Fargo , Capital One, and Zelle also had problems with their online banking platforms as customers reported trouble. Reports started Monday morning and climbed quickly. Downdetector logged nearly 4,500 Chase reports shortly after 1:30 p.m., most of them about website logins. By 2:22 p.m., the count had passed 20,000. “Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told Fortune . “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” Customers described a wider disruption than that statement suggests. Comments on Downdetector mentioned problems with ATMs and in-person systems as well as online banking and Zelle. Some customers opening the Chase app got a message reading , “Some services aren’t available.” Ashley Lutz The problems also reached apps outside the bank. Plaid, which links bank accounts to payment, investing and budgeting apps, said its own network was working normally but that it was seeing connection problems with Chase accounts. Customers trying to link or refresh a Chase account through another app may have gotten errors as a result. Downdetector listed Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Bank of America among the banks with spikes in outage reports, along with U.S. Bank, Truist and Zelle. By 2 p.m. Eastern, Bank of America saw about 2,000 with U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo seeing about 1,000 each. Wells Fargo did not confirm the outage. It’s also affecting local branches. On the subreddit r/ TalesFromYourBank , one person wrote: “I’m at work and haven’t been able to take a single client.” Three others corroborated to their bank phone systems being down. Bank of America and U.S. Bank had not explained their customers’ problems as of Monday afternoon. Downdetector counts user complaints, not confirmed outages, and it was not clear whether the Chase and Wells Fargo failures shared a cause. The outages follow several other technology failures in recent days. Microsoft restored service on Saturday after a global outage took down Outlook and Teams, and said a technical problem, not a cyberattack or AI, was the cause. No bank has tied Monday’s problems to the Microsoft outage. Meanwhile, a Federal Aviation Administration comminications problem grounded flights across the country on Friday, with service not fully restored until Monday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cables at one location that caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later. Chase has had large online outages before . In 2010, its online banking was down for more than a day, and CEO Jamie Dimon apologized publicly. The bank said then that it would refund late fees to customers who missed payments during the outage, as long as they called to ask. events.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
events.summary: OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public. At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure. “OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.” The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court. It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed. In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.” In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” Updated 12:23 p.m. PT: Added OpenAI statement. events.title: Nvidia has plenty of reasons not to bring back Jensen Huang
events.summary: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia. Bloomberg/Getty Images Jensen Huang's boosters are trying to get Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO. There's some pattern recognition here: In 2023, OpenAI fired Sam Altman, and he returned days later. But there are real differences in the two stories. Which is why it's not surprising that Nvidia is saying — for now — that Huang won't come back . Sam Altman came back . Can Jensen Huang do it, too? After all, it was just three years ago when the leader of an enormously important AI company was pushed out by his board, then returned days later after an outcry from employees and Silicon Valley power players. But Huang in 2026 is not Altman in 2023. That doesn't mean we won't see the same story played out. It does mean it seems less likely: Right now, Nvidia's position is that it's not happening . To understand why, we need a brief recap: The story began with China: in 2025, The New York Times reported that federal officials were investigating whether Singapore-based Megaspeed was diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. Last month, the Times reported that officials suspected Megaspeed executive Alice Huang of being a "Chinese intelligence asset" and that she had a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO and his company dismissed the concerns. Then it metastasized into a story about Huang's conduct. He acknowledged being unfaithful , and Nvidia said it would investigate whether he had been targeted by foreign intelligence, while expressing support for him . Days later, after the Times alerted Nvidia to a story about Huang's relationship with a direct report , the board met. Huang resigned the next morning. Since then, reports have described disagreement in Washington over Alice Huang's role, and long-running suspicions of Jensen Huang among China hawks including Marco Rubio . Some of that tension is now public, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling out Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia policy. And yes, that's the short version of the recap. But it's important to go over it. Because in some narratives — especially the ones promoted by Jensen Huang's vocal supporters — the story is really about Nvidia's foes working to remove a leader they don't like for political reasons. Perhaps it is! But that's why the timeline is important to underline. Maybe Nvidia's board would have pushed Huang to resign if the issue was solely about his relationship to Alice Huang, and/or the way Nvidia chips have been used by China. Last week's newsflow, though, suggests that it was news of the affair with Jensen Huang's employee that pushed the board to ultimately act. So there's a version of a story where Nvidia's board may not have pushed out its visionary leader if the only issue was China. Disclosure of the second affair ( Reuters has subsequently reported yet another affair with another Nvidia employee) is what did it. All of which makes bringing Huang back more complicated than Altman's story. In Altman's case, OpenAI's board was unable to clearly tell a story about why, exactly, they fired Altman. In Huang's case, Nvidia's board can point to multiple instances where Huang reportedly violated his own company's rules. It can also argue that Huang misled his own company about his behavior, as multiple outlets have reported. Those are all fireable offenses in most of corporate America, regardless of national security debates. In the inevitable shareholder lawsuits that will follow Huang's departure ( one has already been filed ), board members will be criticized for not uncovering Huang's acts on their own. They will be able to say, credibly, that once the acts came to light, they acted, which led to Huang's ouster. But bringing Huang back once those facts are known will generate much more risk for the board: Board members couldn't simply say that Huang was the victim of a political plot. They'd have to explain why they thought his transgressions weren't harming the company. And if Nvidia stock fell for any reason after Huang came back, they would face blowback for that, too. What about the fact Huang has boosters throughout Silicon Valley, and in the White House? Donald Trump had reportedly told Huang not to resign last week, and on Monday said he " wouldn't mind " if Huang came back. Perhaps if this were a couple of years ago, after Trump's victory in what was described as a vibe-shift election, Nvidia officials and board members might agree to follow Trump's lead. And they might have expected some kind of political or legal shield for their actions — like the kind that Apple and Google got from the Trump administration when they agreed to keep hosting TikTok in America, contrary to US law . But this time around it's not really clear what the White House position actually is on Huang and Nvidia. Trump has spoken glowingly about Huang and Nvidia, but that's different than pushing a private company to reinstate a disgraced CEO. Meanwhile, the Democrats have won their own supposed vibe shift election, and have promised to spend the next couple years investigating both Trump and his private sector allies. Bringing Huang back at Trump's behest makes Nvidia and its board even bigger targets. That alone may be enough to keep him out of the company for good. Read the original article on Business Insider

Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice.

events.title: Quantum computing, greener data centres: How innovation is helping Singapore and Japan turn shared challenges into opportunities
events.summary: From improving productivity to advancing emerging technologies, Fujitsu is drawing on its Japanese expertise to support Singapore’s digital transformation and sustainable growth The collaboration between Fujitsu and Singapore Pools on a data centre modernisation project won an SBR Technology Excellence Award in 2025. Deliver more. Spend less. Unlock growth. For Singapore and Japan, these are not just organisational demands but national challenges: sustaining competitiveness as populations age and economic growth becomes less dependent on adding workers. Economic uncertainty, technological change and energy transition add pressure. Productivity, skills and resilience underpin both economies’ capacity to grow. As the countries mark 60 years of diplomatic relations, their Strategic Partnership, announced on March 18, 2026, supports cooperation in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, digital infrastructure, supply chain resilience and net zero goals. Drawing on its Japanese heritage, industry experience and commitment to quality and innovation, Fujitsu Asia Pacific serves Singapore’s evolving market needs. The company established its ASEAN operational headquarters here in 1997 and has since expanded its role to include consulting-led transformation. Its contribution centres on three themes: Transform with Innovation, Transform with Impact and Transform with Trust. Alfee Lee, vice-president and head of international business for Singapore and Thailand at Fujitsu, says: “Fujitsu has evolved into an end-to-end technology and business transformation partner. Business-led consulting is at our core: understanding customers’ priorities, then bringing together technology, implementation and operational expertise to deliver meaningful outcomes.” Supporting public sector transformation worldwide For ageing economies, improving productivity starts with everyday tasks. By connecting processes, Fujitsu helps free up employees to focus on service delivery. At a public sector agency with around 1,300 employees, Fujitsu linked human resources, information technology (IT), and facilities and security functions through a streamlined onboarding process. More than 110 officers were onboarded over six months, saving over 550 man-hours and shortening onboarding time by approximately three days. At an educational institution serving more than 16,000 users, Fujitsu helped standardise IT functions to improve support during peak periods. Fujitsu also helped some higher-learning campuses improve service consistency through centralised workflows, benefiting 70,000 students and 7,500 staff. In Australia, Fujitsu implemented a computer-aided dispatch system for Ambulance Tasmania to help coordinate emergency responses. Research partnerships for future growth Fujitsu’s quantum computing research aims to tackle complex problems and open up new possibilities for industries. Fujitsu has a long history of advanced computing research partnerships across countries. In Singapore, its work on the National Supercomputing Centre’s Aspire 1 supercomputer supported data-intensive research. More recently, its quantum centre initiative with the Galicia Supercomputing Centre in Spain has focused on advancing applications and skills. In Japan, Fujitsu developed a 256-qubit superconducting quantum computer with research institute RIKEN in 2025. Its roadmap targets 1,024 qubits in the 2026 financial year and more than 10,000 physical qubits supporting 250 logical qubits by the 2030 financial year. Logical qubits combine multiple physical qubits to protect calculations against errors. Singapore organisations can prepare by developing relevant skills and testing quantum-inspired approaches that use conventional hardware to tackle suitable optimisation and simulation problems. As organisations build new digital capabilities, they must also consider the energy and resources needed to support them. Fujitsu’s data centre modernisation project for Singapore Pools illustrates this balance between innovation and sustainability. The project strengthened resilience, reduced rack space by 31 per cent and was estimated to cut annual carbon emissions by 305 tonnes. Fujitsu’s MONAKA processor, a computer chip built using technology from chip architecture designer Arm, delivers twice the AI inference throughput of other central processing units, potentially halving the number of servers needed and their power consumption for equivalent workloads. Sales of MONAKA servers are scheduled to begin in Japan and Europe from November 2026, targeting data centre operators, enterprises, academic institutions and organisations in high-performance computing and defence. This technology aims to support more energy-efficient AI infrastructure. Designed for high-performance computing, Fujitsu’s MONAKA processor aims to deliver greater computing efficiency while reducing the energy demands of AI workloads.

events.title: From exclusive movie screenings to Asia-only merch: Monster-sized thrills await Japanese entertainment fans in S’pore
events.summary: With Singapore as its regional hub, Toho Entertainment Asia is powering the reach of Japanese films and anime across Asia, led by its cultural icon Godzilla Godzilla made its latest big-screen appearance in Singapore, as Toho Entertainment Asia sets its sights on reaching more fans across the region. Godzilla roared into Singapore on Nov 4, just one day after its latest film debuted in Japan. Now, the Japanese entertainment group behind the legendary kaiju, or ‘monster’, is looking to make a bigger splash in cinemas across Asia. The premiere of Godzilla Minus Zero at selected cinemas made Singapore one of its stops in Asia outside Japan. It also marked an early step in Toho Entertainment Asia’s (TEA) push into direct film distribution across the region. Established in Singapore in 2024, TEA is the Asian regional headquarters of Toho Group, the Japanese entertainment group behind Godzilla and a portfolio of anime titles. Besides distributing and licensing, TEA is also actively exploring business opportunities with local partners on merchandising, marketing, events and promotions. Singapore’s position as a regional hub for business, finance and logistics makes it a strategic base for reaching Asia’s diverse markets, says Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global. “It is also, in many ways, a ‘showcase for Asia’ – a place where the diversity and dynamism of markets across the region come together,” he adds. “To use our resources efficiently while reaching as many markets and fans as possible in an effective way, we determined that Singapore was the ideal location from which to begin expanding our presence across Asia.” Connecting with fans beyond the screen Growing interest in Japanese content across Asia represents an enormous opportunity, Ueda continues. He points out the meteoric growth of Anime Festival Asia (AFA) – one of South-east Asia’s largest annual Japanese pop culture and anime conventions – which has held editions in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia since 2008. Its flagship Singapore edition has drawn more than 120,000 attendees annually over the past four years. Recognising the region’s growing potential, Ueda says Toho’s mission is not just to reach more fans, but also to give fans further ways to connect with their favourite characters and stories offline. Toho Entertainment Asia is looking to bring fans closer to their favourite characters through exclusive merchandise. At this year’s AFA Singapore, happening from Nov 27 to 29, TEA’s booth will feature anime titles, with exclusive Godzilla and anime merchandise and as well as photo opportunities featuring the iconic kaiju and characters from popular series such as The Apothecary Diaries and Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End. TEA also plans to work with regional creators to develop original merchandise shaped by local fans’ needs and preferences. Fabio Takamichi Murayama, managing director of TEA, says: “Our ambition goes far beyond simply bringing content created in Japan to audiences across Asia. We want to work hand in hand with local creators and business partners to create exciting new products and experiences created from Asia.” To engage local and regional fans beyond the screen, Toho Entertainment Asia is bringing popular anime titles to Anime Festival Asia Singapore 2026. PHOTOS: (C) S-SBCR/TP, (C) S,I/ IVP, (C) K.Y,T.A/S/FP, (C) H,II/ADP AND (C) Y.T/S/SEP The company is already making its first-ever expansion into Asian e-commerce markets, progressively launching official stores on regional platforms such as Shopee. Plans also include Asia-exclusive merchandise and the expansion of the TOHO animation store and Godzilla Store into Asian markets. We plan to broaden our line-up and create even more ways for fans to enjoy the worlds of our IP,” says Murayama. “Looking ahead, we will continue exploring new possibilities in entertainment with talented people and partners across Asia.”

events.title: Trump Administration Moves to Block China From Indirect Access to American AI Technology
events.summary: Malware & Threats Cyberwarfare Cybercrime Data Breaches Fraud & Identity Theft Nation-State Ransomware Vulnerabilities Security Operations Threat Intelligence Incident Response Tracking & Law Enforcement Security Architecture Application Security Cloud Security Endpoint Security Identity & Access IoT Security Mobile & Wireless Network Security Risk Management Cyber Insurance Data Protection Privacy & Compliance Supply Chain Security CISO Strategy Cyber Insurance CISO Conversations CISO Forum ICS/OT Industrial Cybersecurity ICS Cybersecurity Conference Funding/M&A Cybersecurity Funding M&A Tracker Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. Flipboard Reddit Whatsapp Whatsapp Email The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. The U.S. bans sales of the country’s most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country’s export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. events.title: Binance chief acknowledges hack ‘shouldn’t have happened’
events.summary: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng acknowledged Monday that the $6.3 billion hack his firm suffered — one which roiled cryptocurrency markets and raised existential questions about industry security — resulted from the company’s own failings. “It shouldn’t have happened,” Teng said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “This was a multi-month, sophisticated campaign,” he continued, referring to the attack, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. (Pyongyang has denied involvement in the hack.) The hack raised questions about what is fundamentally the weakest link in most cybersecurity and business operations: humans themselves. Binance said that it was compromised in part because of a sophisticated phishing attempt that involved a Binance employee undergoing a fictitious interview process that resulted in “malicious software” being loaded onto a corporate machine, Teng noted. Teng also acknowledged Binance’s checkered reputation, involving billions in fines for anti-money laundering violations and the imprisonment of its primary shareholder and founder Changpeng Zhao. “We had really underinvested into the area of compliance,” Teng said. “Since the record fine and settlement, we have really invested a great deal.” Whether that investment is enough is an open question: The New York Times reported in September that Chinese firms continue to use Binance to launder illicit proceeds for the Iranian government . Binance, like most cryptocurrency firms, has also benefitted from a laissez-faire environment in Washington. A pro-crypto mentality adopted by the Trump administration has come up short of what many crypto executives had hoped for, but has still allowed for major regulatory wins for the industry. “We would have hoped that the Clarity [Act] would have passed,” Teng said. “We do hope there will be more transparency and visibility on that front moving forward.” Binance is a sponsor of Silicon Valley & The World. Richard Teng made his comments during Silicon Valley & The World’s partner session. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: The 'Ebenezer' box office numbers prove Johnny Depp's comeback is off to a strong start
events.summary: Johnny Depp. Karwai Tang/Getty Images Johnny Depp starred in the No. 1 movie in the world over the weekend, "Ebenezer." Data shows over 50% of moviegoers this weekend saw the movie because of Depp. The movie made more money overseas, showing that Depp is still a draw internationally. Johnny Depp 's grand return to Hollywood is so far going according to plan. The actor, who has not starred in a major studio movie since 2018, proved he can still be a major box-office draw this weekend when his movie, "Ebenezer," won the weekend box office, bringing in $19 million domestically and $23 million internationally for a worldwide total of $42 million. While those certainly aren't "Pirates of the Caribbean" figures , it's a strong first step for the 63-year-old Depp, who's trying to rehabilitate his image after years of being embroiled in a bitter defamation trial with his his ex-wife Amber Heard . So far, the stats are showing it's working. Not only were the box-office returns heartening for "Ebenezer," Paramount's retelling of the beloved Charles Dickens holiday classic "A Christmas Carol," but audiences scores on Rotten Tomatoes were high, with a 90% rating as of this writing. (Critic scores, however, were more mixed, with a Tomatometer score of 53% as of publication.) Audiences wanted to see Depp — especially women Johnny Depp stars as Ebenezer Scrooge in "Ebenezer." Paramount Pictures Even before "Ebenezer" was released, the warm reception to the movie's early promotion gave Paramount confidence. Over the summer, Depp's surprise appearance at San Diego Comic-Con in-character as Scrooge generated over 152 million social media impressions, the studio said. When the Paramount dropped the movie's first trailer soon after, it brought in over 225 million views in its first seven days. Paramount said the draw wasn't that people love Charles Dickens; it was the anticipation of seeing Depp. According to the studio, 51% of surveyed moviegoers this weekend named Depp as the main reason why they went to see "Ebenezer." Typically, an actor being a film's attendance driver is in the 20% range, according to an industry insider familiar with this kind of survey data. And for the movie's weekend demographic breakdown, women topped men, with 52% of the "Ebenezer" audience being female. Depp is still a major draw overseas The $23 million international total also shows how beloved Depp still is overseas: The movie was No. 1 over the weekend in 63 markets. Of all the international markets, "Ebenezer" had the strongest showing in Dickens' home: The UK, which also hosted the movie's world premiere. It took in $5.4 million. The ones most joyous about Depp's return this holiday season will be Paramount. The movie has already made back its $38 million production budget, and the studio reportedly paid Depp a mere $5 million to star in it (though he'll get some bonuses on box office performance). It's safe to say the Johnny Depp comeback is in full swing. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach
events.summary: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.” When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks. A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks. TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont. When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. events.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
events.summary: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants . After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

events.title: I spent my whole life working toward becoming a lawyer. When I finally made it, I realized I didn't want that life.
events.summary: The author created her own maternity brand. Courtesy of the author I spent years building a successful legal career at a major Chicago law firm. When I decided to leave, my mentors assumed I was burned out and offered to reduce my workload. I cofounded Larken, a maternity apparel company, and found more ambition and fulfillment. In the weeks after I told the partners at my law firm that I was leaving to do something entirely different, many of them took me out for coffee. These were people I loved working with and who had mentored me over the years. They came into the conversations assuming I decided to leave because I was burned out. They offered a reduced schedule and asked whether it was a particular practice group or client they could take off my plate. And at some point in every conversation, there was a warning that they had seen people try to take a step back, and it rarely worked out as they hoped. When I tried to explain that I wasn't burned out but opting out to do something entirely different , they looked at me like I'd started speaking another language. I was told to lean in It was 2019, and the decade I built my career in had one message for women like me: lean in, which meant stay in, ask for more, and never take yourself out of the running. This was before the Great Resignation had a name, before anyone said "portfolio career," before your social media feeds filled with people telling you to quit your 9-to-5, and before entrepreneurship was glamorized. Opting out of a successful career wasn't just unpopular. It was out of character for me in a way that made everyone around me assume something had gone wrong that we could fix. But there wasn't anything about the job that needed fixing. I wanted to be a lawyer since I was a little girl I had decided to be a lawyer when I was 7 years old, stayed committed to that decision long enough that I'd come to think of it as something I actually wanted, and only figured out the difference once I was too far along. The author had always wanted to be a lawyer. Courtesy of the author Every time I said lawyer as what I "wanted to be when I grew up," I received a lot of approval, and I was a kid who ran on approval. So I just kept going. I graduated from college with a 4.0 and spoke at my graduation. I went to Notre Dame Law School, then to a large Chicago firm where I did intellectual property work for some of the world's biggest companies , with a stretch in-house at McDonald's. Every milestone landed with more approval and confirmation, telling me I was on the right path and to keep going. And along the way, the tuition dollars, the years of work, the identity I built around being someone who didn't quit kept accumulating as costs I couldn't abandon. But none of it was proof I wanted the end result. It was just proof I was good at staying on the path. I started my own maternity and postpartum brand Walking away from that looked insane to pretty much everyone I told, and I understood why. The pay was good, and nothing was visibly broken. The same things that made it hard to leave were the exact things that made it impossible for anyone else to understand why I would. But I'd show up to another client meeting or work on another project and be reminded every time that it just wasn't the right fit for me. Law is a great career, and we need excellent lawyers. Many people love the work, but I became a lawyer for a reason that made sense to a child and stayed because every reward along the way made it harder to question. When I left law, I cofounded a maternity and postpartum apparel company with zero industry experience, solving a problem I knew firsthand after struggling with nursing and pumping as a new mom. The author's mom sewed the first prototype. Courtesy of the author My mom sewed the first prototype at her dining room table on Mother's Day. We bootstrapped it, landing on the Inc. 5000 list the last three consecutive years, and figuring out most of it as we went along. I now also advise other consumer businesses and work as much as I did at the firm, if not more. I'm more ambitious than I ever was, but this time I set the ceiling and decide where and how I work, whether that's at my desk, the bus stop, or the soccer field sidelines. That's what I was building toward when I left law. It wasn't a step back, and it wasn't a slower life. It was opting out of one career to build a life on my own terms and ensuring I show my kids by example that they can design a career and life they love without anyone else's approval. The author's company landed in Inc. 5000. Courtesy of the author My 25-year-old self would not have understood any of this. She would have seen leaving a prestigious legal career to start a company from scratch as a woman letting motherhood shrink her ambition. She would have been very wrong. events.title: US moves to stop AI chip-smuggling amid push to reinstate Huang
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Donald Trump says Jensen Huang could return to Nvidia after 'spying' scandal US President Donald Trump says he would not mind if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company. Some Silicon Valley executives are pushing for Mr Huang's comeback just four days after his resignation. The Nvidia board and US authorities are investigating Mr Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Donald Trump says Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has "learned a big lesson" and he would "not mind" seeing the former CEO return to the helm of the AI juggernaut. The US president's comments add weight to a push to reinstate Mr Huang, just four days after his resignation amid fears he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy. It comes as his administration moves to tighten controls on the export of Nvidia's highest-powered AI chips to prevent them being smuggled into China. SpaceX boss Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney are among the tech titans supporting the "Stand with Jensen" campaign. According to its official website, more than 185,000 names have been put to an open letter demanding the Nvidia board reinstate Mr Huang "pending an independent investigation and clear evidence that his removal serves the company". "He could return," Mr Trump told reporters at the White House as he prepared to depart for Asia to meet world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese . "There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Mr Trump said. "I would certainly not mind seeing that." Just days after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, his supporters are urging him to return. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) The Nvidia board has not publicly commented on the campaign, but the Financial Times (FT) reported it was not considering reinstating Mr Huang, citing people familiar with the matter. Similar reports appeared in the Washington Post and on the US business network CNBC. Earlier, the FT reported Mr Huang had discussed the possibility with confidants, and one Huang ally said a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby for his return. The push has alarmed some national security experts and industry analysts, who have criticised Nvidia's alleged failures to comply with US export controls, which are designed to stop the company's most powerful AI chips from being sent to China. Several investigations will consider whether the chips were being smuggled into China by Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset with whom Mr Huang had a relationship. "We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Mr Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told Fox News on Sunday, local time. He said Nvidia needed a "dramatic shake-up" and should "go outside the company" in its search for a new leader. Chinese economic espionage is in the spotlight after the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, and former intelligence officials say the US is not doing enough to combat it. But Mr Trump said he did not believe Mr Huang had put national security at risk. Mr Trump and Mr Huang are known to be close. "It was not put at risk," Mr Trump said. "And, you know, China plays games with us and we play games with China." The Trump administration today said it would bring in new restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips. It means companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil will need to apply for licences to import the chips. Some experts want to see more done to prevent chip-smuggling. Congress is considering multiple bills to crack down on the practice. "The bigger problem illustrated by the Megaspeed case is that advanced AI chips are being smuggled into China and rented by Chinese companies in data centres abroad," Institute for AI Policy and Strategy senior researcher Erich Grunewald told the ABC. "I think the priority should be closing the gaps that allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips. "That means selling to trusted customers like US hyperscalers, rewarding whistleblowers who report smuggling, and restricting Chinese companies from renting advanced AI chips in data centres abroad.
