events.title: The push for Jensen Huang's comeback isn't a Sam Altman-style rerun
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Heather Diehl/Getty Images; Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Calls for Jensen Huang's return echo Sam Altman's comeback to OpenAI in 2023. But the parallels only go so far. One corporate leadership expert said Huang's return was "unlikely in the near term." Don't call it a Sam Altman comeback . As calls grow among Nvidia employees, investors, and Silicon Valley leaders for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO, some observers are comparing it to Altman's ouster and subsequent reinstatement as OpenAI's CEO in 2023. Huang and Altman left abruptly after their respective boards raised concerns. Each company appointed insiders as interim CEOs. And both leaders have attracted widespread support: More than 700 OpenAI employees demanded Altman's return, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered over 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia employees. The parallels only go so far. One key difference: Nvidia is a public company, so it has to meet tougher reporting requirements and answer to shareholders in ways that OpenAI, a private company, does not. Crucially, the reasons given for each leader's departure are also different — and could make a Huang comeback more complicated than Altman's. OpenAI said almost exactly three years ago that Altman was not "consistently candid in his communications with the board." Huang's Nvidia exit is mired in his admission of being unfaithful to his wife and questions over whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." "In short, one board had a disagreement; the other has open questions of fact that only an investigation can answer," David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership advisory firm RHR, told Business Insider. Huang resigned on Thursday after reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs , including one with a direct report and one with a woman who US officials believe was passing information to Beijing, according to reporting from The New York Times. Nvidia's stock has taken a beating in the days since the scandal started; it's down another 4% today. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, called the Altman comparison "an imperfect analogy." "Jensen's situation involves internal and external factors that OpenAI's did not," he said, adding that Huang's situation was closer to Apple's firing in 1985 of Steve Jobs, who returned to Apple a decade later to lead its historic comeback. "The lesson is the same: Founders cannot be replaced," he said. 'Silicon Valley loves a good comeback story' On Monday, the Jensen defenders had a blow to their comeback hopes. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider. That follows fierce speculation among investors and on prediction platforms. Gene Munster, a managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, put the odds of a Jensen return at 51%, up from 10% on Friday, he said in an X post on Sunday. He said the "bring back Jensen" movement was gaining momentum and that Huang's resignation, rather than a formal firing, could give Nvidia's board "air cover" to bring him back. Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, took the opposite view, arguing that legal, board, Washington, and China-related scrutiny had permanently changed Huang's standing. "The old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," Ives wrote in an X post on Sunday. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO." Meanwhile, prediction platform Kalshi said in an X post on Sunday that Huang's odds had doubled to 21%, while Polymarket put his chances of rejoining Nvidia at 7% by November 30, 12% by year-end, and 38% by the end of 2027. Astorino said Huang's return was "unlikely in the near term." "If they reinstated the CEO before the investigation ends, that would likely be a difficult decision to defend," he said. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and co-head of global HR practice at ZRG Partners, told Business Insider that Nvidia's board must protect the company Huang built, rather than the founder himself, and that employee and investor loyalty cannot substitute for the investigation's findings . He also poured cold water on the Altman-Huang comparisons. "The circumstances are different, and you can't simply replay the Altman comeback, no matter how much Silicon Valley loves a good comeback story," Kaplan said. events.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback as campaign for his return grows
events.summary: A display reading "Taiwan heart Jensen" is illuminated on Taipei 101 in Taipei, Taiwan, on Nov 16. Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Jensen Huang as CEO, three people told Reuters, despite a growing campaign for his return days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation. More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort , and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks. The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees – some fiercely loyal to the former CEO – and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwan supply chain and Washington. Taiwan’s tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Nov 16 with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen”. Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him before all the facts were known. “The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back,” one of the people familiar with the matter said. The support for the former CEO, who acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman , comes as US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Alice Huang’s relationship with China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said. The uncertainty has divided investors over Huang’s future and complicated the board’s search for a successor. Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% on Nov 16 , a day before the chipmaker is due third-quarter earnings. Since news of Huang’s intimate relationship broke, Nvidia has lost US$800 billion ( S$1.03 billion ) in market value and the stock’s price-to-earnings ratio has dropped to 11.54 from 15.59, well below the 20.8 average for the Nasdaq Composite. The “Stand With Jensen” campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. The campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, though it cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified. “We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: Bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” an open letter on the website said. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. “I think he learnt a big lesson,” Trump said on Nov 16. Trump’s reported trades in 2026 suggest he held between US$13 million and US$62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Nov 16, citing a review of his financial disclosures. The Trump administration said on Nov 16 it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, tightening controls as President Donald Trump headed to China for talks with President Xi Jinping. Large investors may prove harder to persuade about reinstating Huang. One institutional investor in Nvidia stock, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they would be wary of Huang returning to Nvidia, adding that other big companies, including Apple and Microsoft, had thrived after their visionary CEOs had left. Richard Windsor, an independent technology researcher, said he expected large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Huang’s return while investigations remained unresolved because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. “They’re very risk-averse,” Windsor said, but said his own view was that Nvidia shareholders would ultimately be better served by Huang’s return because of the relationships he has built with the company’s customers and suppliers, particularly TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced chips. T Rowe Price analysts said in a note that a transition of power may call for a new organisational structure rather than simply a new executive. Huang’s reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed “Jensanity”.

events.title: Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser sees 'demand-side problem' for AI
events.summary: Recent jitters in the markets about AI represents a shift among investors towards becoming more selective about where they allocate their money, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup said Monday — and she’s not worried about it. “In a market priced to perfection, getting the air out of the tires is not a bad thing,” Fraser said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that investors are absorbing huge amounts of change even over the past two weeks — the FAA shutdown, a high inflation reading, and the US midterm elections. “I’m hoping for a boring week,” she said. On the fallout of Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, Fraser said she’s “not going to pile on” to the commentary, but that the company is in “very capable hands” with his successor, Colette Kress, which was met with applause in the room. Fraser told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman that she sees AI companies being “thoughtful about their capital stack,” and that it’s not terrible that any pullback is “a demand-side rather than a supply-side problem.” Partner with China Citi just recently got its China securities license and told rivals to “watch out.” The bank is prioritizing relationships in the country, Fraser said, while emphasizing the importance of a stable relationship, as well. Citi has been in China for 124 years, and Fraser said she’d work with Chinese companies if they are complementary to the bank’s client base. As for AI and China, she noted that the tech supports a more service-driven economy in the US, whereas in China, the focus is more about physical AI and robotics. “The two are very complementary,” she said. “There’s far too much for both sides to lose,” Fraser said. The sheer number of meetings between the countries’ presidents is unprecedented and can only mean “good things.” US President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China this week. Fraser feels the bank is prepared for a Democratic-controlled Congress, as Citi has taken pains to de-risk and modernize. “We’ve put ourselves in a position for a global bank to operate and be a source of strength in choppy times rather than a source of problems.” The same goes for cybersecurity risk, said Fraser, adding that banks don’t compete on protecting against hacks and cyberattacks; they have collaborated to make sure the financial system is safe. “We’ve been in a window where we can do a lot of hardening,” she said. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: A new James Bond has always been a chance to reinvent the series
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sean Connery set the benchmark for the character of James Bond with his debut in Dr No. ( Supplied: MGM ) Into every generation, a James Bond is born. And with every new actor playing the British super spy, the franchise has had a reset. A new Bond typically means a new look, a new tone and a chance to reinvent the 64-year-old film series for a new audience, and catch up with new trends. It remains to be seen what the Robert Pattinson era will look like. But here's how the anointing of a new Bond has worked out for the series previously, and how the changing face of 007 provides an insight into the history of action movies. Sean Connery as James Bond in Dr. No. ( Supplied: IMDb ) The first Bond film, Dr. No (1962), created a new template for spy films. Its mix of humour, violence, sex and high-stakes action against a backdrop of world-shaping ramifications set the series apart. Until then, spy films tended to focus on the cloak-and-dagger spycraft, and tried to keep both feet grounded in reality. The big screen ambition of Dr. No was more akin to Alfred Hitchcock's groundbreaking North By Northwest (1959), where spectacle was preferable to plausible. Sean Connery was the original James Bond and, for many, the best. ( Supplied: MGM ) The Connery era of Bond quickly established the language of the films, such as the signature opening credits sequence, the dynamic score, the over-the-top villains with their over-the-top plans, the gadgets, the exotic settings, the highly questionable attitudes toward women, and the hero's mix of brawn, brains and babe magnetism. Dr. No hit big at the box office, and Sean Connery was a big part of that — it's said that the phrase "men want to be him, women want to be with him" emerged because of him. Within two years, a Bond parody was released (Carry On Spying), TV shows were aping the series (The Man From U.N.C.L.E.), and homages like Our Man Flint were in production. Connery and co pumped out four films in four years, some of which are among the best and most successful movies of the series, notably Goldfinger (1964) and Thunderball (1965). When Connery stepped aside after five films, George Lazenby took over for one ill-fated turn (On Her Majesty's Secret Service, 1969), which wasn't much of a reset, but more of a misfire. Australian actor George Lazenby made just one appearance as James Bond. ( Supplied: MGM ) Truckloads of money were thrown at Connery to ensure his return, and he re-teamed one last time with Goldfinger director Guy Hamilton for Diamonds Are Forever (1971). But the magic was gone and something needed to change. Roger Moore starred as Bond in the most films, clocking up seven outings as 007. ( Supplied: MGM ) Just two years after Connery's Diamonds Are Forever, Roger Moore picked up the Walther PPK for Live And Let Die (1973). It is one of the best of the series, helped in no small part by Moore's ability to effortlessly slip into the role of Bond. But as with Diamonds Are Forever, there are a few too many corny one-liners — a script tic that would come to be associated with Moore's stint as 007. By Moore's second outing (1974's The Man With The Golden Gun), outside influences had started to creep into the series, which had previously defined itself as a trendsetter, not a follower. Roger Moore was the third actor to play James Bond in the official 007 films. ( Supplied: MGM ) The recent death of Bruce Lee and a rising interest in martial arts meant some cheesy Hollywood-style kung fu made an appearance, and this would not be the last example of Zeitgeist-chasing in the franchise. In 1977, a little film called Star Wars became the biggest movie of all time, and everyone in Hollywood took notice, including the producers of the Bond franchise. In response, 007 was launched into space in 1979 for Moonraker, the nadir of the franchise. It was the biggest box office earner of the Moore era, but many critics were unkind, and opinions cooled even further as time went on. Moonraker was cited as the kind of film Mike Myers was thinking of when he created the Austin Powers series. Moore and co would redeem themselves with For Your Eyes Only (1981), but after Moonraker, the franchise endured a steady decline at the box office. By the time Moore bowed out with A View to a Kill in 1985, questions were being asked about where Bond fit in the world of 80s action. Timothy Dalton took over from long-running James Bond actor Roger Moore.

events.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
events.summary: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath. The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas. Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism. “The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X . Here be dragons As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should , and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized . And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn. The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS ), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures. Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment…and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” but that he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
events.summary: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide. Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel. Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said , with thousands more delayed. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday. Read more below. What caused the nationwide groundstop? What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds." Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal . The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris , has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide. After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement. How did a router disrupt flights nationwide? How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft. The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft. A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications. The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights. What to know about radio frequency outages One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions. Some reports described this as a " rolling frequency outage ," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time. This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers. Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy. What happens to pilots during the outages? Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail. These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual . The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage. Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities. Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected. What does this mean for flights? Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions. Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports. Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft. What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris. The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

events.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
events.summary: One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup. With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade. To be clear, this feature is not Face ID. Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay. The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity. The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it. Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images. The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness. Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month . Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify. Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game . U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles. The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete. events.title: SCOTUS gives DEI a boost after national assault
events.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion , leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech. The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates. One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants. Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints. A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints." That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group. What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject." A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives." Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation. Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage. Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings. The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity. Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito. Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena , disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come. But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now. Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

events.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment
events.summary: Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”. The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions. Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill. That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable. On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people. Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work. In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line. After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity. Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them. “Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.” He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard. Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip. Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead. Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market. Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment. His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”. The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term. The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have. His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs. So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people.

events.title: There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs. How it could impact your bill
events.summary: As Americans wrestle with inflation, there's a growing "property tax revolt" to reduce or limit property taxes amid rising home values. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025, according to the National Association of Realtors. During the midterm election, property taxes were on the ballot in several states, including Florida, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Wyoming. Property tax relief could impact local government services and infrastructure, experts say. Affordable housing was a key midterm election issue , and as Americans wrestle with rising home costs , there's a growing movement to reduce or limit property taxes. Amid soaring home values , some states want to cap how much local governments can collect from homeowners. Experts have described the trend as a " property tax revolt ." During the Nov. 3 midterm election, Florida voters approved Amendment 3 , which increases the portion of primary residences exempt from property tax for non-school levies and lowers the cap on yearly assessments for certain properties. North Carolina voters approved an amendment to require the state legislature to enact limits on property tax increases, while voters in Oklahoma and Wyoming rejected other property tax measures. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 In Ohio, an amendment to abolish property taxes didn't have enough signatures to make the November ballot, but supporters plan to try again in 2027. Despite the "mixed bag" on midterm ballot initiative results, "I think we'll continue to see property tax reforms," said Matthew Chase, CEO of the National Association of Counties, or NACo, a nonprofit organization that represents county governments. Property taxes are levied as a percentage of a home's assessed value, based on its estimated market rate. Some municipalities use a millage rate — with one mill equaling $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable assessed value — to calculate property tax bills. That rate can adjust up or down based on changes in home values and the local government's budget needs. In some cases, property tax bills can be bigger due to higher assessments, even when local governments lower the millage rate, experts say. Property taxes vary widely throughout the U.S., with yearly bills ranging from less than $250 in some rural counties to more than $10,000 in areas near large cities, according to 2026 data from the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization. Affordability concerns prompt tax cuts Nationwide, the property tax cut movement has been "driven by affordability," according to NACo's Chase. As "home values have gone up, property taxes have gone up with it," he said. In 2020, the median sales price for U.S. single-family homes was about $300,000, compared with roughly $419,000 in 2025 , according to the National Association of Realtors. Last year, the median property tax bill for owner-occupied homes was around $3,300 , the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey reported. Higher property tax bills have been a burden, experts say, as homeowners have wrestled with rising costs for groceries, gasoline and other living expenses. That's sparked more demand for property tax relief. From January 2020 to June 2026, state lawmakers enacted at least 168 property tax measures — including exemptions, credits, refunds and more — across 40 states and the District of Columbia, according to an October report from NACo. Property tax cut proponents argue local governments should rein in spending . But other experts say the relief will cause revenue shortfalls that impact local schools, police and fire services, roads and other infrastructure. "There's no realistic way to replace property taxes in most states," said Jared Walczak, a senior fellow at the Tax Foundation. Typically, property taxes are a more stable revenue source compared to income or sales taxes, which can decline during an economic downturn as consumers earn and spend less, experts say. Reliance on the tax varies, but property taxes are the single largest local levy revenue source for most local governments, accounting for about 28% of local funding nationally in 2024, according to the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, an independent, nonpartisan foundation and think tank. "It's easy to savor property tax cuts in abstract," Walczak said. "It can often be much more challenging to define a replacement system that anyone actually likes.

events.title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
events.summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement. The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers. In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.” But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union. Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already. Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said. “We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Army airstrike kills at least 13 in West Kordofan, says rights group Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal. Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely. Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration. “We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said. In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later. But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court. events.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: US won’t restrict foreign tech companies in allied countries, State Dept. official says
events.summary: The US government has “no plans” to target or “orchestrate the deep pruning” of technology companies headquartered in allied countries from American supply chains, Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said Monday. Speaking alongside ASML’s President and CEO Christophe Fouquet at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Helberg rejected “top-down government-mandated plans that intentionally discriminate” against companies based on their country of origin in comments to Semafor’s Ashley Gold. He named ASML, Samsung, and SK Hynix as key partners to US firms in the technology supply chain. Discussing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains, Helberg said that the Trump administration wants to ensure companies across allied economies benefit from a “level playing field.” He described the initiative as a “capability-centric coalition” that draws on the comparative strength of participating countries. Helberg also argued that Washington must balance technological leadership with global market share of AI-focused companies, warning that innovation alone will not secure America’s dominance in the fast-growing technology field. “We need both in order to win the AI race,” Helberg said. “We need to lead the world qualitatively and have the best innovation out there. But we also need market share, and those two things need to happen in conjunction.” Helberg also stopped short of endorsing three bipartisan bills that lawmakers are considering including in the year-end defense bill that would tighten AI chip export controls following the Nvidia controversy. Asked about the investigation involving Nvidia, Helberg described the company as critical to US technological leadership, saying “there is a really compelling argument for national security to have Nvidia continue to be a leading beacon of innovation.” He called for investigations to establish the facts quickly, adding, “Our hope is obviously to see serious work being done through the investigations to uncover the facts and get to the truth quickly in order to get to the right outcome.” Nvidia has attracted scrutiny from Congress as well as the administration amid revelations that now-former CEO Jensen Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%
events.summary: Odds of a merger of Elon Musk's SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, have risen on multiple Kalshi markets since late last week. On Friday, Walter Isaacson, a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that he is confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a potential catalyst. Odds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 have climbed to 62% from 27% on Kalshi since Thursday. Chances that Elon Musk's two companies, SpaceX, a satellite and rocket maker, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, will soon integrate have jumped since late last week across multiple Kalshi markets. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and would be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. On Friday, Walter Isaacson , a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " he's confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a catalyst. "I think you have to have a merger. Makes no sense otherwise," Isaacson said. Tesla's 2026 annual shareholder meeting, set for Dec. 3, may provide more insight into a potential linkup, Isaacson said. While speculators are anticipating an announcement of a merger this year, a research note from Jefferies last week said a deal will likely face backlash after the Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships in the midterm elections earlier this month. "We understand there is higher risk of scrutiny post elections, but the vision of a combined SpaceX and Tesla as proxies for longer-term U.S. national strategies of independence and leadership in space, energy, manufacturing or semiconductors, in our view, remain highly relevant regardless of which party controls Congress," wrote Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois. Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, said a possible merger between Musk's two companies would face "tremendous scrutiny," Bloomberg reported Thursday. events.title: This Anthropic proxy play is getting traders' attention – here's where they see it going
events.summary: The Destiny Tech100 fund is experiencing 30 times its average-daily volume, with 41,000 calls versus 150 puts traded. 14% of the Destiny Tech100 assets are tied to Anthropic. Anthropic perpetual futures imply a big first-day pop. Who says you can't tailgate an IPO? Traders are preparing for this week's blockbuster Anthropic IPO in different ways, including buying options on one publicly-traded fund that invests in private assets. The Destiny Tech100 (DXYZ) is a publicly-traded, closed-end fund that invests in equity, equity-linked instruments, or shares of private funds and venture companies to gain exposure to private companies. Currently, 14% of the fund's assets are tied to Anthropic, according to the company's website. Options volume on the fund jumped to more than 10x the 30-day average Monday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Of the 42,300 contracts traded by midday, 41,800 were calls, with just 141 puts likely opened by buyers. Just shy of $5.5 million in options premium on DXYZ traded on Monday, with almost all of it tied to calls, but just marginally more spent buying than selling calls, according to SpotGamma. The highest-volume contract is currently the 30-strike call expiring Friday, a 90-cent contract that needs the fund to rally 19% into the weekend to pay off. Traders may want to be wary of how the fund traded around the SpaceX IPO: DXYZ surged almost 150% in May before unwinding all the gains in the weeks ahead of SpaceX's debut. Since then, the fund has barely moved, trading around $26. There are other bullish signs surrounding Anthropic's IPO in the derivatives markets. Current prices for perpetual futures on the blockchain exchange Hyperliquid are implying an opening price of $98, a big pop from the $70-$78 price range quoted in the company's amended S1 filing. The AI giant is expected to price Wednesday evening and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

events.title: I started a handbag company at 22 and grew it into a fashion sportswear brand with partners like MLB. Here's what I've learned.
events.summary: Zara Terez Tisch is the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. Natalie Keyssar for BI At 22, Zara Terez Tisch launched a handbag company called Terez from her parents' home. Terez evolved into a fashion and sportswear brand with MLB partnerships. Her advice is to build an excellent product with a distinct point of view — not just a story. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zara Terez Tisch, the founder of Terez, a fashion sportswear company based in New York City. It has been edited for length and clarity. I started Terez as a handbag company, from my parents' home on Long Island when I was 22. After college, I was fortunate to live at home without paying rent, which allowed me to save money while my friends moved to Manhattan. I worked in marketing and branding and had always been a creative person, but I was going through a difficult period in my life. I had experienced a lot of loss and was trying to get on my feet. I knew I wanted to create something that made me feel good about myself, and Terez was born. The business has taken several turns over the years. After handbags, I moved into activewear and eventually found an opportunity to bring fashion to professional sports by partnering with major leagues. Today, Terez sits at the intersection of sports and fashion. Natalie Keyssar for BI The early days of building Terez In 2008, when I was still working in marketing, which I quit later that year, I was walking through the West Village in Manhattan on an errand. I came across a leather shop with a sign that said, "Customize your own leather handbags." I walked in and asked, "Do I just draw a handbag and you make it?" I also asked whether they could make 500 bags, or even 1,000. They thought I was crazy, but said they could do it. I decided to work with them to start a business. I started with handbags with fun interiors, including comic-book strips and disco sequins. I wanted to get the happiness inside me out again while representing New York City. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch I started gaining some traction I was doing it all myself, carrying samples with me. I didn't sell them on a website. Instead, I did trunk shows at people's homes. The first one was at my sister's friend's house on Long Island. Not long after I started, I asked my father to come back with me to meet the manufacturers. I thought it would help them take me more seriously. Zara's father, Richard Zimmerman, and sister, Darlene Barzilay, at his Budget Dress showroom during Darlene's 21st birthday celebration in 1986. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My dad was a garment manufacturer — a 'garmento,' as people in the industry called it. He had worked in the industry in the 1970s, 1980s, and into the 1990s. As manufacturing moved to China and overseas, he had to close his company. I witnessed that, and bringing manufacturing back to New York became part of my story. In 2012, the business took another turn The linings I used in my handbags were made of spandex. I was wearing leggings all the time, so I started making them out of the same spandex at a factory in Queens. Image courtesy of Zara Terez Tisch My parents had started a business manufacturing clothing for tweens. I brought the leggings to one of their children's trade shows to see if it would stick. A store called Lester's picked them up and put them in its store over Thanksgiving weekend. The buyer called me on Monday and said, "You really have something here." The leggings started taking off. We became a popular brand for tweens and teens We created prints and styles that made them feel confident in who they were. We started with galaxy leggings and star-themed designs, then added emojis to them. We would drop new designs every month. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next decade was a period of significant growth for Terez. As demand for activewear grew, department-store buyers began creating dedicated categories for it, and Terez became a key brand in that expansion. We partnered with SoulCycle on limited-edition drops and with Bloomingdale's. We opened our first store in 2022 In the fall of 2022, we opened our first physical store on the Upper East Side. It's the smallest part of the business in terms of revenue, but it's the heart and soul of the brand. Soon after the store opened, a woman came in, and I helped her shop. I showed her our whole collection and told her everything about the brand. When she was checking out, she asked, "Have you ever thought about working with Major League Baseball?" I hadn't. She pointed out that nobody was really focusing on women's clothing for the fans. The options were mostly bubblegum V-neck T-shirts with sequin script logos. Natalie Keyssar for BI The next day, I got a text from an exec at Major League Baseball. The woman who had come into the store was associated with the organization. He told me they wanted Terez to shape the look of the women's collection. I immediately called our head of design and said, " We have to stop everything that we're doing right now and focus on a women's collection for Major League Baseball." Working with professional sports opened up new ways to reach customers Today, we work with multiple professional sports teams and leagues. We sell through our own site, our Upper East Side store, licensed sports channels, and fashion retail partners like Revolve. Natalie Keyssar for BI Partnering with sports has opened up completely new channels for us. Since making our debut with Major League Baseball, our revenue has tripled. I've learned that hiring more people doesn't necessarily make a business more efficient When we were first doing activewear, we had a period of high growth, and the company grew to around 40-something people in 2018 and 2019. Up until that point, I hadn't felt confident enough in myself to run the business side and manage the company's numbers. I always thought I should surround myself with people who were smarter than me. What I realized was that people weren't always efficient in their roles, so we would hire more people to do the same job, sometimes two or three times. I called them Band-Aids. By the end of 2020, we narrowed down to a team of around 10 people. I picked up all the pieces after a rocky situation with one employee and told everyone, "We're either going to do this all together, and we're going to succeed together, or we're going to fail together." Natalie Keyssar for BI Since then, I haven't wanted to grow our team. The majority of the people on my team now were on my team 10 years ago. To have people on your team who care as much as you do is extremely rare. I want the business to reflect what we believe in When people ask me for advice about starting a business, I always come back to the product and deeply caring about your team. events.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
events.summary: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale. In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame. With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade. Not the benchmark it used to be The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them. SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL. It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor. The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship. It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time. The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer. The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them. We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner. It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI. AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search. High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®

events.title: Every actor who has played James Bond, ranked from worst to best
events.summary: Daniel Craig, Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan as James Bond. MGM Robert Pattinson is the newest James Bond. Before he gets his license to kill, let's celebrate who came before him. Business Insider ranked all seven actors who have portrayed Bond in film. Over 60 years and 25 movies, seven actors have played the legendary spy James Bond on screen. Daniel Craig was the latest to take on the character created by novelist Ian Fleming, bringing a darker, grittier tone to the franchise. His run came to an end in 2021's " No Time To Die ," when his Bond, well, died. Now a new 007 has emerged. Robert Pattinson is officially the next James Bond . Before he debuts his version of Bond, here's where all the best Bonds rank. Zac Ntim, Eammon Jacobs, and Ayomikun Adekaiyero contributed to previous versions of this story. David Niven (1967-1967) David Niven as James Bond in 1967's "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures While most audiences automatically think of Daniel Craig when thinking of " Casino Royale ," there was actually another version of the story that arrived on the big screen back in 1967. (Yes, in the same year as Sean Connery's "You Only Live Twice.") Columbia Pictures' "Casino Royale" starred David Niven as James Bond, and takes a more comedic approach to Ian Fleming's book of the same name. The parody movie isn't connected to any of the other films, nor was it made by Eon Productions and Albert Broccoli. It was only made because Fleming sold the singular rights to the book before it was published in 1953. Niven's Bond is a much older agent who's brought out of retirement to fight a nefarious organization called S.M.E.R.S.H. The Oscar-winning actor brings some charm to the role, but the absurd story — which ends with him going to heaven — ruins the character and sucks all the suave out of 007. George Lazenby (1969-1969) George Lansbury as James Bond. MGM Australian actor George Lazenby is on this list as another matter of courtesy. He was drafted by Eon Productions, the film's producers, to play Bond once in 1969's "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" after Sean Connery decided to step away. He was promptly replaced by Roger Moore when the series resumed in 1973 with "Live and Let Die."  Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002) Pierce Brosnan filming "007" in 1997. Markus Beck/picture alliance via Getty Images After 15 years of Daniel Craig — who is eulogized later in this list — it is easy to forget the damage Pierce Brosnan did to the James Bond franchise. But it's important to revisit our lowest moments so we can grow. So here, I humbly ask, do we remember the unfortunate orange spray tan Brosnan sported throughout his time as 007? Or the awkward hyperpop theme songs like Madonna's awful "Die Another Day"? It's important to note that Brosnan's first Bond film, "GoldenEye," was also the first film in the franchise not produced by Albert R. Broccoli: His daughter, Barbara Broccoli, and his stepson, Michael G. Wilson, took over. But it's been reported that Brosnan was favored by Albert Broccoli. Nonetheless, across his four-film run, Brosnan pushed Bond away from its steely, cool origins to something more Hollywood and less interesting.   Roger Moore (1973-1985) British actor Roger Moore, playing the title role of secret service agent 007, James Bond, is shown on location in England in 1972. AP Photo Roger Moore suited up as James Bond a record seven times. The bulk of his films were helmed by the British director John Glen, who had an unparalleled skill for capturing pure chaos on screen. And that is what Moore's Bond was best known for. In his seven-film run, Moore went to space, fought off a pack of crocodiles, and defused a nuclear bomb. While Moore's Bond was charismatic and entertaining, there was rarely any substance to what he said, and there was even less plot to hold together the big-budget stunts. For this reason, Moore's seven films don't make for great rewatching.  Timothy Dalton (1987-1989) Timothy Dalton as James Bond. MGM The sole reason Timothy Dalton is not at the top of this list is that he portrayed Bond only twice. This wasn't due to bad ratings or box-office numbers, however. His films, "The Living Daylights" (1987) and "Licence to Kill" (1989), are two of the most beloved Bond films, and Dalton's dark and often serious take on 007 is widely considered the most accurate interpretation of Fleming's books.  "I wanted to make him human," Dalton said of his interpretation of Bond during an interview in 2008 . "He's not a superman; you can't identify with a superman. You can identify with the James Bond of the books. He's a tarnished man, really. I wanted to capture that occasional sense of vulnerability and I wanted to capture the spirit of Ian Fleming." As many people have stated before, Dalton's grounding of Bond paved the way for the franchise's most profitable period of releases with Daniel Craig's 007. Dalton's tenure, however, was cut short due to complex legal wrangling between the film's producers MGM and Eon Productions, which halted production until 1994, when his contract expired.  Sean Connery (1962-1967) Sean Connery as the original movie James Bond. United Artists Sean Connery had a legendary acting career that spanned over 50 movies and included appearances in some of Hollywood's most iconic films like 1964's "Marnie," 1989's "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade," and 1987's "The Untouchables," for which he won an Oscar for best supporting actor. But when he died in 2020, he was best remembered as the first 007.  According to Connery, however, his interpretation of 007 managed to charm everyone but Fleming. "I never got introduced to Fleming until I was well into the movie, but I know he was not happy with me as the choice," Connery said on "The South Bank Show" in 2008. Despite Fleming's reservations, Connery played the secret agent in seven films from 1962 to 1983, and his version is remembered as not only the coolest in the franchise but one of the coolest characters in cinematic history.  Connery's powers as 007 came from his own charisma. As Barbara Walters described him in a 1987 interview, the Scotsman was someone who didn't try to be sexy; he simply oozed class. Connery can also claim to be the only Bond actor who actually managed to pull off the famous catchphrase, "Martini, shaken, not stirred" and make it sound cool. Best: Daniel Craig (2006-2021) Daniel Craig as James Bond in "No Time to Die" MGM Daniel Craig's Bond films are dark, physical, and entertaining. But it is Craig's commercial success that has landed him atop this list. The numbers simply don't lie: 2012's "Skyfall," Craig's third outing as Bond and first collaboration with the British director Sam Mendes ("American Beauty"), raked in $1.1 billion at the worldwide box office, making it the most commercially successful Bond film of all time.  Craig's portrait of the top-secret British spy helped to revive th
