events.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
events.summary: A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content. This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft. Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit. Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying. “Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be. “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.” With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves. “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said. What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning. Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks. The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience , which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps. Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch , Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj. Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer. The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed. The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year. events.title: Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar said. A petition for Huang's return has circulated online, with signatures from people like Elon Musk. Huang resigned as CEO last week. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider. The confirmation comes as support mounts for Huang's return both inside and outside the company, including an online petition that has garnered more than 180,000 signatures from bold-faced names like Elon Musk and Garry Tan. CNBC first reported the board's position on Monday, adding that it remained focused on the ongoing investigation. Nvidia announced last Thursday that Huang had resigned from his role. It follows an extramarital affair scandal and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia's board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct that investigation, with former federal prosecutor Joon Kim leading it. The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Huang had discussed the possibility of returning to Nvidia, and that fellow Silicon Valley executives were supporting him, including trying to rally support from the White House. President Donald Trump said Monday that he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at the chip giant's helm. Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim CEO on Thursday. The board's new chair, Harvey Jones, said that the company would seek a permanent succeessor, and that it was considering both internal and external candidates. Have a tip? events.title: The man with the golden touch: James Bond franchise is a money-spinner
events.summary: Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dream New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson Robert Pattinson’s journey to James Bond J ames Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship. The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007. This means that by the time Pattinson makes his first appearance it will have been the longest gap in instalments in the 64-year history of the film franchise, an agonisingly long hiatus for the centrepiece of a sprawling commercial enterprise. While Ian Fleming initially struggled to get Hollywood interested in his debonair, womanising British novel creation, the big-screen debut of Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No marked the start of a marketing dream. The 25 feature films to date – the world’s second longest-running film franchise after Godzilla – have taken almost $8bn (£6bn) at the global box office, making it the fifth most successful property in cinema history, behind only the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, Star Wars, Harry Potter and Spider-Man. When Amazon acquired the famed Hollywood studio MGM – home to 4,000 film titles including the Rocky and Bond franchises, as well as 17,000 hours of TV programming – four years ago, some analysts estimated that the superspy could be worth half of the $8.5bn price tag of the whole library. The estimate of the on-screen value of Bond was underscored last year when Amazon paid more than $1bn to take full “creative control” of the franchise from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the longtime stewards of the films who had retained significant power, unlocking the potential to develop a Star Wars or Marvel-like “universe” of film and TV spin-offs. Plans for one potential spin-off in 2002 – a movie based on the character Jinx, played by Halle Berry in Die Another Day – were scrapped the following year, while the highly successful Young Bond series of books for young adults has never made it beyond print. Beyond the box office, the carefully cultivated prestige image of Bond has proven a brand association dream, a marketing juggernaut impervious even to Daniel Craig’s critical assessment a decade ago that the spy was a “lonely, sexist misogynist” . Charlotte Mair, the founder of The Fitting Room, a communications and culture agency, says: “Bond is a brand in its own right, with associations of sophistication, adventure, luxury and craftsmanship, timelessness and, of course, Britishness. “Bond is a standalone entertainment property, with its own identity, heritage, mythology and extraordinary brand equity. Its partners aren’t simply buying exposure around a film release. They are aligning themselves with a brand that has been building its own cultural currency and influence for more than 60 years.” The 141-year-old Turnbull & Asser, the personal shirtmaker to the king – who bestowed the company with his first royal warrant as the Prince of Wales in 1980 – has created shirts for Bond actors since Connery appeared in the first film. Lock & Co, the world’s oldest hatters, with roots dating to 1676, started its Bond relationship with one of its hats appearing in the now-famous opening credit gun barrel scene that debuted in Dr No. Aston Martin has long been considered Bond’s sports car of choice, debuting in 1964’s Goldfinger, and a bespoke DB10 was created for 2015’s Spectre to celebrate a 50-year partnership with the franchise, but deals remain on a film-by-film basis. The N.Peal cashmere turtleneck worn by Daniel Craig in the poster for Spectre sold out almost immediately. A grey, custom-made Tom Ford suit worn by the actor in Skyfall went to auction last month with hopes it would fetch as much as £40,000 . The “Bond effect” lures big sponsorship deals, reportedly worth anywhere from $45m, with deep-pocketed corporates. Heineken, which has partnered Bond films since 1997, has spent as much as $100m on sponsorship, product placement and global marketing supporting a single film – even if many fans were outraged to see 007’s “shaken not stirred” Martini staple replaced by a pint. Omega’s long-running sponsorship, dating back to 1995 when it replaced Rolex as Bond’s timepiece of choice, included being directly namechecked by the superspy in Casino Royale. Various guesstimates have been put on the value of sponsorships, from as much as $5bn over the lifetime of the franchise to date, to about $200m a film in the modern era. “If the Super Bowl is advertising’s biggest stage, James Bond is the ultimate brand partnership platform,” Mair says. “Some brands have become so intrinsically linked to the franchise that they are part of Bond’s DNA.

events.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

events.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing A t the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU. They are right to be wary, and not just because that debate will come with domestic political risks attached. Some form of closer relationship with the UK’s largest trading partner is desired by a majority of the British public. But however warm its rhetoric, Brussels is going to have other matters on its mind during a momentous period of elections that will test the EU’s internal unity. Mr Macron will be gone by the spring. It seems increasingly likely that his replacement will be a far‑right president committed to national preference policies that are contrary to EU law, and the cutting of support for Ukraine. Pedro Sánchez, the leader closest to Mr Burnham’s own centre-left politics, could be gone by the end of the month. Polls suggest that Spain’s snap election is set to deliver a coalition government including the far right for the first time since Franco. Poland, beset by constitutional turmoil , could also lurch to the far right in 2027. Such political storms breaking would limit EU headspace for Mr Burnham’s overtures and may give the prime minister himself pause for thought. But volatile times also offer political opportunities. Russia’s war in Ukraine, and the wider threat posed to the EU’s eastern flank by Vladimir Putin’s revanchism, mean that a big British offer on defence would be well received and possibly open doors on other issues. Similarly, the febrile geopolitics of energy contributed to five European leaders this month calling for Britain’s re-entry into the bloc’s internal electricity market. On both sides of the channel, the rapid emergence of an unforgiving multipolar world has served to underline the need for strengthened cooperation. Should the UK seek to rejoin the single market, recognition of that reality will not alter Brussels’ red lines in relation to core principles such as the free movement of people. But we are no longer in the world of 2016 and its aftermath. Covid, Ukraine , Donald Trump and Chinese competition have altered the landscape of EU politics and shifted priorities. Possible far-right breakthroughs threaten imminent further disruption. The direction of travel chosen by Mr Burnham is the right one. But predicting the final destination is, for now, a futile exercise. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
events.summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune. The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts . The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.” In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.” “This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.” Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share. The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation. The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation , the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why 13 days ago 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 27 days ago '123456' password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people October 13, 2026 UK.gov begins killing off passwords for 23 million users September 14, 2026 From watches to passwords on paper, everything that's old is new again August 31, 2026 It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg , the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ® Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? events.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’ Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead. The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.” The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang. The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded. Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved. Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress , Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws. Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”. Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

events.title: Personal wealth boom helps Four Seasons to record-breaking year
events.summary: The CEO of Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts said Monday that the company was on track for another record-breaking earnings year. “’25 was our best year on record. ’26 will be the best year on record,” Alejandro Reynal said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He added that 2027 is on track to surpass the previous two years, too. The prediction matches the one Reynal made last year, when he told Semafor that “ this year is going to be our best year ” in terms of revenue and profit margins — and that advance bookings were suggesting that 2026 “is going to be better than 2025.” Reynal has been the CEO of Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts since 2022. 70% of the private company is owned by Bill Gates’ Cascade Investments; Four Seasons founder Isadore Sharp and an affiliate of Prince Alwaleed bin Talal’s Kingdom Holding hold minority stakes. Reynal told Semafor’s Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson that “the wealth creation that has happened” post-pandemic has brought in more guests. “The truth is that we have experienced a lot of tailwinds. Luxury hospitality has gone very well,” he said. There continues to be strong spending on luxury experiences, he added. Since taking over the company in 2022, Reynal has invested in the company’s data infrastructure. And beyond hotels, he has focused on brand launches, such as the Four Seasons yacht, which set sail in March. The company’s dozens of branded residences reported some $2.1 billion in sales in 2024. Service is the top priority: “That moment of connection you have with one of our employees is super important,” he said. “That’s how you build the connection with the brand.” — Lora Kelley

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Flaw can take down an entire host, even when the vulnerable service is running inside a container Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet 18 hours ago Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads 22 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 3 days ago Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens 5 days ago Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session 7 days ago The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim , who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag , a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important , assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted.

events.title: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin gigafactory expansion
events.summary: Just two months after putting its first Cybercabs on the road, Tesla is making a multibillion-dollar bet on mass production of the golden-hued, two-seat autonomous vehicles. The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn. Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added. Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker. The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas. Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace. Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised). The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September , is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.) Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help provide its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify. Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents. That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas. events.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration B oardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. It was only when the likes of Google (now Alphabet) and Facebook (now Meta) appeared with their “mission” statements that dual class structures – and unequal voting rights – got a fresh lease of life. The corporate missions, went the argument, were so important that the founding geniuses needed to be able to pursue them in free-wheeling, risk-taking style without distraction from the tiresome short-term demands of ordinary shareholders. In an extreme example, Snap, the Snapchat company, was even able to pitch its overblown ambition of “reinventing the camera” as so vital that shares could be issued with zero voting rights , as opposed to merely weakened rights. Now we come to Anthropic, the Claude AI developer whose $1.4tn blockbuster listing happens this week. The governance setup here is, to put it mildly, different. In essence, there are two centres of power and neither is the ordinary shareholders. One is the seven founders, who collectively have one vote that commands 50.1% of the ultimate voting power – the collective aspect is designed to force them to come to a consensus. The other is a financially disinterested trust, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which nominates four of the seven directors and looks out for the balance between making money and benefiting humanity. The trustees are a cast of the great and the good, including Ben Bernanke, former chair of the US Federal Reserve. And the whole structure is given an overlay as “public benefit corporation”, nodding to Anthropic’s commitment to develop AI responsibly and safely. There are two positive things to say about this setup. First, the motivation is plainly more complicated than a simple power-grab by the founders, led by Dario Amodei. Rather, Anthropic’s backing for the Long-Term Benefit Trust seems to be designed to create some form of constitutional balance of power. Second, Anthropic probably has a stronger justification than most to divert from the norm of equal rights for equal economic risk. If the development of AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the listing document puts it, a few unconventional governance structures are probably in order. We’re not talking about Snap’s fluffy videos for social media. All the same, Anthropic is offering an untested experiment. For all the fine words, the company may simply have recreated an inward-looking “trust us” setup, just with more elaborate clothing. Here’s a nuanced point from Stuart Riddick, sustainable investment manager at fund manager Aberdeen. “Agreement with a mission in principle does not equate to agreement over how it is interpreted and implemented by the directors.” Riddick notes that Mustafa Suleyman, the chief executive of Microsoft’s AI division, even as he acknowledged Anthropic’s seriousness about AI safety, has made strong and detailed criticisms of the company’s thinking on so-called “model welfare” , arguing that AI models must not be trained to act as if they have rights or consciousness. How, in practice, are such challenges handled within Anthropic’s supposedly responsible governance arrangements? It’s hard to tell unless the Long-Term Benefit Trust starts to throw its independence around, or not. What happens if the trustees are at loggerheads with the founders on a basic safety question? Will they tell the outside world? Or will they reflect that ultimate voting still sits with the founders, so best not to rock the boat? If the shareholders are denied any role in holding the executives to account, what is the true level of challenge? It is surprising after events at Nvidia that Anthropic’s governance has received so little attention. Yes, the setup is supposed to be high-minded and responsible. But it still represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals.

events.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
events.summary: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes You report ( 11 November ) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock. It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle. Our helpline already hears from too many older people on low incomes having to cut back on essentials to pay their bills. With poverty in later life on the rise, and healthy life expectancy reversing (with lows of 50.9 years for men and 51.8 years for women, both in Blackpool at the last count, according to the Office for National Statistics ) we need to think very hard indeed about how to mitigate these impacts if we contemplate further rises. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Opt-in Edge archive gives Pro subscribers early access before full testing, while normal updates remain human-validated Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 34 minutes ago US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 5 hours ago California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety 6 hours ago Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach 8 hours ago Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn 10 hours ago Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive , an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company . At the previous such event in June , the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. Ubuntu Summit 26.10 Thursday keynotes – Pierre Guillemin's begins at 27 minutes in. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism ). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022 , Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30 , surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world. Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money .

events.title: Rudd's mining tax could have delivered years of surpluses, analysis finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kevin Rudd-era mining 'super profits' tax could have improved budget by $135b Kevin Rudd (left) attempted to introduce a tax on resources super profits, but it led in part to his removal as prime minister. ( Alan Porritt: AAP ) Parliamentary Budget Office analysis commissioned by the Greens has found a mining super profits tax proposed by former PM Kevin Rudd could have raised $135 billion if it had been kept. The proposed tax became deeply unpopular and led to Mr Rudd's removal as prime minister in 2010. The Greens continue to call for a tax on gas export profits, saying the public is missing out. Labor's abandoned mining tax, which led to the 2010 toppling of then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, could have improved the budget by $135 billion if it had been kept, a Parliamentary Budget Office analysis has concluded. Mr Rudd's proposal to tax 40 per cent of mining company "super profits" sparked a fierce $22 million industry campaign against the tax that continued until he was ousted by his then-deputy, Julia Gillard. The unpopularity of the Resources Super Profits Tax partly prompted the leadership challenge by Ms Gillard, who replaced the super profits tax with a lighter-taxing scheme. That was also eventually scrapped when the Coalition — under Tony Abbott — won government at the 2013 election. Since 2012, when the super profits tax was meant to begin, the federal budget has been in deficit most years. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned the pressures on the budget are mounting, with borrowing costs growing and aged care and other social payments becoming more expensive, even with measures to save $38 billion over four years from the National Disability Insurance Scheme. The federal government is also under pressure to slow down spending, as the Reserve Bank warns a lack of "domestic capacity" is driving up inflation, alongside international pressures including the war in Iran. The Greens have called for a 25 per cent tax on gas export profits and an increase in the rent tax levied on offshore petroleum companies, saying both could help to fund the budget. Senator Steph Hodgins-May said the PBO modelling showed the missed opportunity by not pursuing revenue from the resources giants. "We were interested to see what other revenue has been lost as a consequence of our government not being willing to stare down those big gas exporters, those big resources industry players, to make them pay what they owe," the senator said. "They jump with fright as soon as there are a couple of billboards at the airport warning them off going after these profits. "We're sick of the government telling us we can't have nice things, nice essential things, like free early childhood education, like wiping HECS debt, like having a well-funded National Disability Insurance Scheme, and being told those things aren't possible when they are leaving in the realm of $135 billion on the table because they are unwilling to stare down a few mining and gas corporations." Steph Hodgins-May says the government could have raised tens of billions of dollars if it had held firm against resources industry lobbying. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) On Monday, Resources Minister Madeleine King dismissed the Greens' gas tax push. "Our focus is on getting more gas available to Australians at affordable prices. I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she said. The government has previously warned a gas export tax could also damage Australia's relationships with Asia, which depends on Australian gas, and which Australia depends on for petrol and diesel. The PBO suggested the mining tax would have raised a net $24 billion last financial year if it had been kept, which would have eliminated the government's $22.3 billion budget deficit, with all else being equal. It found over the 14 years that the tax would have operated, it could have improved the overall budget position by $135 billion — assuming that the major reform would not impact mining company behaviour. Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who was a senior adviser to then-treasurer Wayne Swan when the resources super profits tax was introduced, declined to comment. But the ABC was told the government was not considering reinstating the resource rent tax.

events.title: Australian doctors warn of millions of deaths from antibiotic resistance
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Antibiotic resistance on track to kill 39 million people in coming decades, doctors warn Antibiotic resistance means standard medical procedures can become high-risk or life threatening. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) The peak body for doctors says increasing antibiotic resistance in Australia could threaten the foundations of modern medicine. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats. Doctors and experts are calling for governments to act and scale up solutions. Millions of people are expected to die because of rising antimicrobial resistance over the coming decades, the peak body for Australian doctors has warned. The latest Australian figures show reports of critical resistance jumped by more than 25 per cent in 2024 alone, and if current trends continue, antimicrobial resistance will cause the deaths of 39 million people globally by 2050 — more than the total deaths projected for all cancers. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats and occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites adapt to the medicines designed to treat them, most commonly, antibiotics. It means infections become difficult or impossible to treat, which increases the risk of disease spread and death. A new report released today by the Australian Medical Association (AMA) said the scale of the threat in Australia was rising and resistance was outpacing the national response. AMA president Michael Bonning said antibiotic resistance was already having devastating consequences and threatened to undermine the foundations of modern medicine. Michael Bonning says antibiotic resistance is already having serious impacts. ( ABC News: Rahni Sadler ) The World Health Organization (WHO) last year warned resistance to essential antibiotics was "widespread, increasing and unevenly distributed". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a similarly stark warning last month, saying drug-resistant germs caused an estimated 50,800 deaths in the country each year. The latest figures showed that in 2020, more than 1,000 Australians died because of infections caused by five common antimicrobial-resistant bacteria. Although antimicrobial stewardship, which is specialised programs to promote responsible use of antimicrobials in the health system, has reduced overall antibiotic use by about 21 per cent in the past decade, prescribing has risen in residential aged care. Dr Bonning said such stewardship needed to be scaled up across hospitals, primary care and aged care, as well as agriculture and the environment. "We know what needs to be done. What we need now is coordinated action from governments and proper investment to implement those commitments and turn plans into results," he said. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria and parasites adapt to the drugs meant to kill them. ( Pixabay ) The AMA report also took aim at state and federal initiatives allowing pharmacies to prescribe antibiotics for urinary tract infections without a script from a GP. It said evidence showed E. coli, which causes urinary tract infections, had developed resistance to trimethoprim, an antibiotic available through some pharmacy prescribing programs. A spokesperson for the Pharmacy Guild of Australia said suggestions that pharmacies were independently choosing which antibiotics to prescribe were wrong, as they followed the same therapeutic guidelines as doctors. "Antimicrobial resistance is a whole-of-health-system challenge. The answer is strong antimicrobial stewardship by every prescriber …. not scaremongering and old turf wars," they said. Only a 'handful' of new antibiotics being explored Molecular biologist Amy Cain, who has dedicated her career to finding solutions for antimicrobial resistance, said the situation was getting increasingly "dangerous" and the world was "looking off a cliff". "I think anyone that's had a really nasty infection, especially one that hasn't responded to treatment, will understand how scary it is." Dr Cain, who works to find new antibiotics at the Galleria Research Facility at Macquarie University, said there were only a "handful" of new antibiotics in the pipeline globally and urgent funding was needed to turbocharge development. She said the pressure to develop new treatments fell heavily on academics and small research organisations, with pharmaceutical companies unmotivated to find breakthroughs as they did not stand to make significant financial gains from new antibiotics. Amy Cain wants to see a reduction in antibiotic use in agriculture.

events.title: Several companies are using Trump tariff refunds for corporate bonuses
events.summary: Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump ’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found. After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership. Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same. A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now has “accrue incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said. In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker did not immediately respond to request for comment. The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $131bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval. Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica. Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds. In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws. Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs. Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, about half of the number of 2022 midterm voters who said the same thing about former president Joe Biden.

events.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
events.summary: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country T his week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here. It is the central purpose and the meaning of Tuesday’s report by Alan Milburn, commissioned by Keir Starmer and keenly adopted by Andy Burnham. This is the hardest of social projects, yet the government nonetheless sets itself to be judged by it, despite the high upfront cost, with no payback for years. How will this land? There will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.” Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area. Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool , Merseyside Youth Association . Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free. GPs will not mourn the passing of the “fit notes” with which they were expected to sign people off work. That task goes to hubs’ community teams of occupational therapists, work coaches, mental health and job advisers, who offer counselling and personal “return to work plans” instead. Neets will be fast-tracked through NHS mental health queues. Milburn is searching for obstacles to knock down. Care leavers will get back the education maintenance allowances (EMA) for staying in school or college, with plans to spread this to all who used to qualify before the Tories axed them – that is, every sixth-former on free school meals. “Just paying for buses to stay in college is £4 a day, £20 a week: too much for those families,” he tells me. Abolishing another obstacle, the government will end young people’s loss of 55p from their benefit for every £1 they earn when they do get a job. A good omen is the optimism of FE colleges, after years of despair at turning away 16- and 17-year-olds for lack of spaces and teachers. These neglected gardens of second chances for all those failed by Gove-stricken schools are the mainstay of this whole plan. Today, they celebrate being told they can now take as many students as they want. David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, closely involved in the Milburn plan, expects colleges to be funded to take tens of thousands more. He wants funding for colleges to do their own social outreach to missing young people. “We can go and find them,” he says. “Many have no adult to ask what to do.

events.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
events.summary: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry. In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks. Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.” The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease. Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people. The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers. The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim. Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials. “Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen. A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers. After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks. It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea. events.title: Silicon Valley’s head-on collision
events.summary: The timing of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World this week, which brings together global business and political leaders at the intersection of technology and geopolitics, could not feel more urgent. When we came up with the name of the California convening this spring, the phrase was meant to represent a broad sense that AI and geopolitics were on a collision course. Policymakers and CEOs were starting to come to terms with the pressing need to talk to one another. Then, here in the US, they spent a long bitter summer campaigning for and against each other. Thirteen days ago, that collision course became a head-on collision. The US is preparing to inaugurate a new Congress deeply skeptical of the tech industry and its leaders, and — perhaps more consequential — new governors from Texas to Ohio who have pledged to stop data center construction. Similar sentiments are rising in Europe, but much of the rest of the world is rushing to get in on the action, and eager to pick up data-center investments forced out of North America. And now Washington is facing questions about how it managed the interactions between its main geostrategic rival, China, and one of the world’s most valuable companies, Nvidia, and what, if any, involvement it had in the undoing of the CEO atop an American chip champion. There are, of course, far more than two sides to this story: Silicon Valley is divided on the fundamental questions of how fast to develop new technology, on open- versus closed-weight models, on the role of startups and hyperscalers, and on the correct place for regulation. Washington, too, is balancing the promise of AI against the impact it could have on citizens. And senior officials from Singapore to South Africa bring their own pressing agendas. You can join us live here for conversations with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, and dozens of other CEOs and world leaders. We don’t have all the answers, but you can be sure we’ll be asking the right questions.
