Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter). "This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing." Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said. Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release . Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage. Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July . On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 " permanently vulnerable ." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear. Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability." Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week. Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ® Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? events.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
events.summary: Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York. I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him. It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”) You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year. But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.) Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”). Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice. It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer). But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard. Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built? It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically. Is this effectively trained on you? It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made. How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together? Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own. Who are your customers, and how do they use it? We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale.

events.title: Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
events.summary: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X , referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

events.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
events.summary: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

events.title: Exclusive: White House requires signoff before staffers testify to Congress
events.summary: The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said. Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries. "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish ' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned. "Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary," the letter said. Between the lines: Partisans will likely differ on what's "legitimate," but it's clear that Scharf's office will use its interpretation in deciding whether to allow executive branch employees to testify. "We are ready to engage with Congress," the White House official said, "This process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work." In his Monday memo, Scharf said the administration "will remain disciplined in pursuing the work and service the American people deserve by ensuring that all Executive Departments and Agencies follow the established White House consultation process ... before any agency personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee." Zoom out: For more than a year, Trump's administration has planned for the day congressional investigations ramp up. Trump knows he also faces the prospect of impeachment. But advisers say that's no longer threatening to Trump, and he doesn't believe there would be the 67 votes needed in the Senate to remove him. "The president can count, and he won't be cowed," a Trump adviser said. Trump also has promised to pre-emptively pardon staffers and allies he believes will be unfairly targeted by Congress or prosecutors in future Democratic administrations.

events.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
events.summary: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement. The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM. OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI. OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children . The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens . events.title: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts
events.summary: Instagram announced on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content. While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned company told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio. By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content. Instagram says adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees. Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products. When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL. Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon. The new integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform. events.title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
events.summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia . The S & P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss . The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time. Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership . Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow. Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities. It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.” Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%. The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations. Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation. Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier. The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S & P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet. It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates . Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks.

events.title: US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
events.summary: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration , signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times . "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms. American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration , and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership . A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs. It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
events.summary: I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind. These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy. WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event , and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind? LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025. It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has. Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way. There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”? It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into. Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable. I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise. What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate. You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board? I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue. I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company.

events.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
events.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

events.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
events.summary: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail. Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity. NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails. Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path. Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement . events.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
events.summary: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need. Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform: CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server . A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard. CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months. CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation. The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink. At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built. Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies . events.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
events.summary: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time. AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research. Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster. MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks. For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure , Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus , Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE , Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida . Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance. Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week. Dive deeper into the results in the MLPerf Training and MLPerf Endpoints technical blogs. events.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever. Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results. Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron -powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design. Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research , accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions. NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER , NAMD , GROMACS , LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows. Cadence , Fathom Therapeutics , Topos Bio , Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery. Daviator , a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs. At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory , the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments. The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center , with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs. Codeveloped with scverse , the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights. And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research , benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models. Explore NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries. Learn more in this technical blog on GPU-powered black hole reconstruction. events.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
events.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. Honoring the Architects of Progress Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution . These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more. Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26 . events.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
events.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates. Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028. events.title: NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computing
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA and IBM announce a growing quantum supercomputing collaboration combining NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to advance quantum error-correction research, scientific applications and integration into supercomputing workflows. NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will connect with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful processor IBM has yet built. A quantum computing codesign platform with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, alongside IBM and NVIDIA, will support quantum error-correction and applications research for future systems. NVIDIA releases TCBP-JOBS, a new decoding algorithm part of the CUDA-Q platform, that delivers up to a 13,000x speedup for quantum error-correction research, accelerating fault-tolerant quantum computation. NVIDIA is expanding Slurm to simplify scheduling quantum processors within supercomputing workflows, with IBM contributing integration through its Quantum Resource Management Interface. NVIDIA today announced plans for new collaborations with IBM and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory that will span research into next-generation modular architectures for quantum computers, scientific applications and supercomputing integration. These efforts, including a new modular quantum computing codesign platform with IBM and Fermilab, combine NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to help researchers scale quantum computers and explore their scientific capabilities. Separately, NVIDIA also announced a new quantum algorithm that delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms — cutting the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes. The collaboration with IBM also brings together new Slurm capabilities integrations to simplify how quantum computers can be added into supercomputing workflows. Modular Quantum Computing Codesign Platform IBM and NVIDIA are colocating NVIDIA DGX™ B200 systems with state-of-the-art IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the fastest quantum processor IBM has ever delivered. This integrated system is supporting a jointly developed IBM, Fermilab and NVIDIA modular quantum codesign platform. The codesign platform will allow researchers to develop and evaluate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms and quantum-classical applications driving scientific discoveries in high-energy and nuclear physics (HENP), as well as how classical systems can scale alongside multiple linked quantum processors within modular architectures. Fermilab’s expertise will allow work at the platform to focus on quantum error correction and HENP applications — helping define requirements for future fault-tolerant quantum computers and the science that can be achieved with them. “Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together,” said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA’s research software and our collaboration with IBM give scientists more powerful tools to investigate quantum designs and develop applications across these systems.” “Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach without access to quantum computing. Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric computing. “With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we plan to explore how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing.” “The future of quantum computing depends on more than advances in quantum hardware alone,” said Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and director of the SQMS Center. “Accelerated computing and superintelligence will play an important role in how we design algorithms, study errors and coordinate increasingly complex quantum systems. This proposed platform would combine NVIDIA’s computing capabilities with IBM’s quantum technologies and Fermilab’s scientific expertise, and would enable researchers to explore new approaches to codesigning quantum computers that meet the needs of challenging HENP science problems.” Advancing Quantum Error-Correction Research Errors inherent to quantum processors limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform. Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it across multiple physical qubits. A classical algorithm called a decoder interprets measurement data to identify likely errors so they can be corrected. Available through the NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ QEC 0.9.0 library today, NVIDIA’s new TCBP-JOBS decoding algorithm accelerates the computationally intensive parts of quantum error-correction research by up to 13,000x while delivering high accuracy. Faster decoding in research workloads allows scientists to evaluate candidate error-correction approaches more efficiently and explore how different codes and decoder configurations perform. The new decoding algorithm provides researchers with tools to identify designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, and better measure their performance improvements, shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing. Advancing Quantum Chemistry  IBM and RIKEN are advancing quantum-classical chemistry research powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. The work, which combines IBM’s quantum computer with RIKEN’s JHPC-quantum GPU supercomputer ROQUO, has been named a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The researchers calculated binding energies for two protein-ligand complexes to study interactions relevant to drug discovery. By dividing the systems into fragments and combining quantum sampling with GPU-accelerated calculations, they modeled complexes containing up to 12,635 atoms — more than 40x the size of the previous 303-atom quantum-classical benchmark.  ROQUO uses NVIDIA GB200 systems and NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to support research in quantum algorithms, simulation and hybrid computing. This research is supported by NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization), an organization under the jurisdiction of Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s “Research and Development of Quantum-Supercomputers Hybrid Platform for Exploration of Uncharted Computable Capabilities.” Bringing Quantum Into Supercomputing Workflows NVIDIA is expanding the open source Slurm workload

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Vera CPU Platform to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: The NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform combines NVIDIA processors, NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking and breakthrough scientific software to boost weather, climate and molecular simulations. DKRZ has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer for climate science. The full Vera CPU platform is coming from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro. NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for state-of-the-art scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science. The rack-scale platform brings together 192 Vera CPUs interconnected by NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to meet the massive performance demands of climate modeling, molecular dynamics and other unaccelerated, next-generation scientific workloads. The liquid-cooled system delivers more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth to support scientific simulation and AI workflows. “Scientific simulations need CPUs that can keep large datasets moving and sustain performance as applications scale,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Vera brings custom CPU cores, high-bandwidth memory and InfiniBand networking together to address those bottlenecks. With compilers and libraries optimized for Vera, researchers can run demanding simulations more efficiently and explore more complex scientific problems.” Engineered for Memory-Intensive HPC Each Vera CPU features 88 custom NVIDIA Olympus cores, 176 threads and compact, serviceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory delivering up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth to accelerate data-intensive scientific applications. The rack combines 192 Vera CPUs with approximately 300TB of memory and 1 petabyte of storage in a fully liquid-cooled NVIDIA MGX™ design. Each 1U tray integrates eight Vera CPUs, and NVMe storage and management. The platform reuses NVL72 rack components, including chassis, power distribution and cooling infrastructure, to simplify deployment and service. NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking connects the system, and NVIDIA SHARP™ In-Network Computing helps scientists finish complex simulations faster by reducing the time processors spend coordinating their work. In NVIDIA’s tests, Vera delivered 1.9x the performance and 2.4x the performance per watt of x86 systems on OpenFOAM’s motorBike Large airflow simulation. Advancing Climate Science Research NVIDIA has benchmarked the open source Weather Research and Forecasting model on Vera CPUs, with projected performance gains of 1.6x and energy-efficiency gains of 2x compared with x86. DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, alongside NVIDIA GB200 Grace Blackwell systems and NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking. Built by Bull and expected to be available in early 2028, the system will support climate simulation and AI research, enabling global kilometer-scale climate simulations with lower energy consumption than on the current system. Software and Availability To help researchers speed scientific applications, NVIDIA HPC SDK 26.11 is available now, providing compilers and libraries optimized for Vera. NVIDIA is also introducing a public beta of its next-generation Fortran compiler, which was built in collaboration with leading HPC centers and national labs. The new compiler gives developers a way to run their existing programs built on Fortran — the language that scientific computing was built on — with greater speed on NVIDIA platforms, without needing to rewrite their code. Vera CPU racks are expected to be available from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro beginning in early 2027. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU . For detailed benchmark results and test configurations, read the NVIDIA Vera CPU HPC performance brief . About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing.
