events.title: NVIDIA Introduces Nemotron for Science to Accelerate Discoveries With Agents
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA Nemotron for Science brings together the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model, scientific evaluations, a new open chemistry dataset and recipes to help researchers build domain-specific science agents. LitmusBench v0.2 supports both evaluation and post-training for chemistry reasoning, helping researchers assess model capabilities and adapt models to scientific tasks. NVIDIA DGX Spark and data center infrastructure take Nemotron 3.5 Super VL from researchers’ desktops to supercomputing centers, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. Leading global research institutions, including the U.S. Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory, are using Nemotron to build agents to speed scientific discovery. NVIDIA today introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, bringing together scientific applications of its NVIDIA Nemotron™ 3.5 Super VL open model, a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes to help researchers build specialized agents for scientific discovery. Built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Nemotron for Science helps researchers develop agents that reason through scientific problems and put specialized research tools to work. With post-training, scientists can adapt the model to specialized tasks such as conducting experiments for chemistry, protein design and more. Part of Nemotron for Science, LitmusBench v0.2 is a new open dataset with nearly 50,000 questions for training and evaluating language models on chemistry reasoning. Drawing on molecular properties and experimental drug discovery data, it helps researchers improve models’ ability to predict how molecules behave, including their solubility and how the human body processes them. Life sciences companies Lila Sciences, Terray Therapeutics and Therna are using and customizing NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for science applications. Use cases include extracting chemical knowledge, planning experiments and designing therapeutics and laboratory protocols. Major research centers like Argonne and Jülich Supercomputing Centre are integrating it into their drug and scientific discovery AI agents. “Accelerated computing is transforming how scientists tackle the world’s most complex challenges,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries.” Post-Training Nemotron Open Models for Scientific Discovery Researchers can post-train Nemotron open models with domain-specific data to improve performance on specialized scientific tasks. They can integrate the resulting model into agent workflows that interpret scientific information, generate code and call computational tools. These workflows can use NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ accelerated tools to perform scientific computation. Terray Therapeutics post-trained Nemotron to extract reactants, products and reaction conditions from scientific diagrams, surpassing previously published results on two benchmarks. On the RxnScribe test, it recovered about 76% of annotated reactions under the benchmark’s matching criteria, helping turn published chemistry discoveries into structured data for synthesis planning and scientific agents. Lila Sciences used Nemotron to design execution-ready laboratory protocols for its automated labs, matching frontier-level performance without requiring additional fine-tuning. Post-training with laboratory feedback nearly doubled the model’s accuracy for making quantum dots — nanoscale crystals used in screens and solar panels — to 61%, exceeding GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at 10-20x lower inference cost. These gains help agents and materials scientists translate desired material properties into synthesis recipes, advancing the discovery of new materials. Therna collaborated with NVIDIA to post-train Nemotron for agentic mRNA therapeutic design, nearly doubling accuracy in predicting protein-expression ranges over frontier models. Scientists preferred its explanations over those from the base model in 96% of comparisons. These gains could help scientists tailor mRNA designs for the desired protein production in specific cell types as they scale to human use. Researchers Speed Science With Nemotron Models and Datasets Leading research institutions are using NVIDIA Nemotron models and datasets to advance scientific discovery at every scale, from individual researchers’ desktops to labs and supercomputing centers. By helping researchers rapidly design and evaluate novel molecules across the periodic table, the work has the potential to open new pathways for applications in critical materials and minerals, national security and cancer treatment. Argonne is integrating Nemotron into its StructBioReasoner multi-agent system to design and evaluate protein-based therapeutic candidates for treatment of cancer and other diseases. KTH Royal Institute of Technology has built an AI agent on Nemotron that repairs broken GROMACS molecular dynamics setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark ™ system, the agent fixed 81% of test cases with reasoning enabled, and every fix was checked independently by GROMACS itself. RIKEN has made NVIDIA Nemotron, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, available on its RIKYU AI supercomputing platform through RiVault, its inference gateway, enabling researchers to access the models for scientific research and the development of accelerated applications. Availability NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and the LitmusBench v0.2 chemistry dataset are available now on Hugging Face. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model was also optimized to run locally on a 128GB NVIDIA DGX Spark system . events.title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
events.summary: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do. A new approach to securing your code CodeRabbit Secure uses s emantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes. Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC: reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks; finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan; rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime. Find vulnerabilities already in committed code Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it. I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable. Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep Review incoming changes before merge PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application. CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff. On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved. Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them. For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed. Carry the investigation through to a fix Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file. events.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
events.summary: Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample. The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says. The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews. The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets. Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews. But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.) Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata. The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books. The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said. “Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added. events.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
events.summary: Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland. Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”. Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays. It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021. Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped. All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade. That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday. The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households. But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make? EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made. In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies. The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker. But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules. A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. The reset means they will be dismantled. The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves". He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included. Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said. But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules. He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found. UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D. Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations. Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area. Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK. "I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said. Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said. Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations. "The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

events.title: U.S. attorney targets another Democrat over congressional investigtions
events.summary: A U.S. attorney put likely incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on notice about her intent to investigate corporations and expected probes into the president's inner circle. Why it matters: The letter demanding Warren preserve documents related to her congressional oversight is the latest in a string of threats levied against congressional Democrats ahead of the party assuming the congressional majority — and gavels — next year. Congress' authority to investigate, hold hearings and gather testimony is a core legislative power. Analysts have long forecasted a Democratic subpoena storm into President Trump's lucrative presidency. But Democrats' plan to exercise that power and hone their focus on the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption," as reported by Axios' Hans Nichols, is already facing Justice Department pushback. Driving the news: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas contended in his Sunday letter that Warren appeared "eager to wield" her "gavel like a tomahawk," instructing her to preserve oversight records. In the strongly worded letter, he warned Warren about targeting private citizens close to the president and reiterated that any probes must serve a legislative purpose or risk violating those individuals' First Amendment rights. Those arguments echo his prior letters to Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller , shared Reitz's letter and referenced two civil rights statutes. Warren's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Reitz's letter referenced Warren, Blumenthal and incoming Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia's (D-Calif.) recent inquiry into Trump fundraiser Meredith O'Rourke's role in coordinating contributions for the president's ballroom and other projects. It also referenced letters Warren, with Slotkin and other lawmakers, sent to tech CEOs probing the extent to which their AI investments were subsidized by GOP-led tax breaks. What they're saying: The White House did not respond to detailed questions but referred Axios to White House counsel Will Scharf's letter to Garcia that argued Democratic threats of investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality." Asked if Warren was the subject of a criminal probe or other proceedings, a Justice Department spokesperson told Axios that "the Department does not confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations." "The Department has both the statutory authority and the responsibility to examine potential violations of the law," the spokesperson added. Asked if DOJ leadership authorized or reviewed the letter, the DOJ referred Axios to Attorney General Todd Blanche's prior statement that "DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations." Friction point: Blanche refused to rule out prosecuting Democrats set on investigating administration officials in an interview earlier this month, claiming lawmakers' rhetoric had overstepped their authority. That came after Trump demanded the DOJ look into what he labeled as "Weaponization and Lawfare" from his political opponents. What we're watching: Reitz asked Warren to respond to his letter by next Monday. He described the letter as his "first arrow shot." Go deeper: Corporate America's Trump trap

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters France's data protection authority is looking into the intrusion after the postal service reported itself Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 35 minutes ago 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer 2 hours ago US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 5 hours ago California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety 6 hours ago Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach 8 hours ago The contact details of 22 million people were accessed after a cyberattack on a subsidiary of France's postal service, officials say. La Poste confirmed to The Register that an attack in September had resulted in full names and postal addresses being stolen by cybercriminals.The attack targeted the systems of Maileva, a business mail platform that's part of Docaposte, the digital services arm of La Poste. Customers use Maileva for hybrid post services. They upload the documents they need to send to Maileva, which then prints and posts the letters on behalf of the customer. According to Maileva itself, the service has more than 70,000 registered users and is trusted to send more than 180 million documents per year. The digital assault was first reported by French cyberattack-tracking website Cyberattaque late last week, revealing that Maileva notified customers of an attempted intrusion in late September. The letters mentioned the cybercriminal attempting to send emails using customers' official, trusted addresses, a situation which resulted in Maileva service disruption for six days. A number of Maileva customers issued public statements confirming the attack in October. Cornouaille's occupational health and safety service, for example, said the attack targeted Maileva's tracking database. It went on to say that senders' usernames and email addresses were also compromised, and that recipients' genders were exposed too, adding to the potentially affected data types that La Poste confirmed over the weekend. Maileva told the organization it was not aware of any compromise of documents uploaded to the platform, nor did the attacker alter or destroy any data. However, the disclosures of other customers suggested that each may have been affected differently. In the case of the Foch hospital in Suresnes, whose debt recovery partner Kiwee was a Maileva customer, the names of documents sent to recipients may have been exposed, which may have indirectly revealed details about medical conditions. According to Cyberattaque, the attacker also potentially accessed the contents of payment reminder letters, which in turn revealed additional details such as invoice numbers and amounts, and treatment dates. Another case involving social housing provider Flandre Opale Habitat reportedly exposed details from letters dating back ten years. La Poste said in a statement to The Register : "All teams are working hard to provide the best possible support to Maileva's clients and remain committed to rigorously and professionally implementing the necessary measures to ensure the security of its own operations and those of its clients." The attack on Maileva is the second major cyber-related disruption La Poste has handled in the space of a year. On December 22, 2025, the organization fended off a DDoS attack, which went on to affect mail operations for days, including online parcel tracking and its banking arm’s online services, right at its busiest time of the year. La Poste described the DDoS attack as "unprecedented in its scale and power," and while it had mostly subsided by December 24, the attackers restarted it in the early hours of New Year’s Day. The organization said the second wave comprised "several billion connection attempts per second," sent from several million IP addresses. More than 300 cybersecurity specialists were involved in defending and remediating the attack.

events.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
events.summary: The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others. The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. “This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions. Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S. Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect. Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media. The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies. “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
events.summary: Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users. The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day. Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions. For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop. Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses. The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf. Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone 19 hours ago Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads 23 hours ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 1 day ago Most victims of last week's Microsoft outage lost access to their email, but 15 unlucky guests at a German hotel got a dose of chlorine when a warning about dangerous levels never reached staff. The incident, first reported by German broadcaster WDR, happened on Friday at Hotel Ling Bao, part of the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, Germany, where a malfunctioning automatic dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the swimming pool. The hotel's monitoring system spotted the problem and emailed staff a warning about the excessive chlorine levels. Unfortunately, Microsoft's Outlook service was caught up in a global outage, meaning the warning never arrived. Brühl Fire Department said the problem started when a technical fault caused the pool's dosing equipment to pump in more chlorine than it should have. Chlorine gas then escaped into the swimming area, leaving guests needing medical attention. Paramedics checked over 15 people at the hotel, and five were taken to hospital. Four suffered minor injuries, while one was moderately injured and needed further treatment. The fire department sent about 40 personnel to the scene, and crews spent roughly two hours dealing with the incident. The incident came as Microsoft was battling a major outage that began on Thursday, November 12, and dragged well into Friday. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services were knocked offline, leaving businesses unable to access email and documents. The disruption wasn't confined to office workers unable to check their inboxes, with hospitals, police forces, and government departments reporting problems accessing the Microsoft services they use for day-to-day operations. Redmond has since blamed the outage on a bug introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade . It sat there until a later network change set it off, and the failures then spread across the company's infrastructure. Microsoft ruled out both cybercriminals and AI as culprits, and has issued the customary apology. At Phantasialand, though, a broken inbox was the least of anyone's worries. The chlorine dosing equipment went haywire independently of Microsoft's troubles, but the email warning staff about the problem apparently never arrived. Whether the hotel had a backup alarm, or anything capable of shutting off the chlorine supply automatically, remains unanswered. Why a hotel would rely on Outlook to deliver warnings about dangerous chlorine levels is anyone's guess. Email can be delayed, filtered into spam, or simply disappear when Microsoft's infrastructure throws a tantrum, none of which is particularly helpful when you've got a pool with guests breathing in noxious gas. ® Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? events.title: US moves to close 'remote access' chip loophole
events.summary: The US Commerce Department on Monday issued interim rules aiming to close the so-called remote access loophole by which Chinese AI firms used cutting-edge US-made chips via data centers in third countries. The new rules limit access to advanced AI chips and servers in a limited number of countries, including in the Southeast Asian nations of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand where the practice was most intensely applied. The updated rules come with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick facing increasing pressure over his department’s allegedly poor enforcement of export control rules, particularly when it came to a Singapore-based company accused of smuggling chips into China. The company hit the limelight after one of its executives, alleged by US officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset, had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Private investments in African climate projects tripled in 2024
events.summary: Private sector investment in carbon-cutting and adaptation projects in Africa tripled in four years to reach $26.5 billion in 2023-24, pointing to a shift in the continent’s climate finance landscape. African banks and businesses provided three-quarters of the investment, which overwhelmingly funded energy projects, while household spending on solar PV alone rose nearly fivefold to $3.3 billion a year, according to a report jointly published by the Climate Policy Initiative think tank, development agency FSD Africa, and the UK and Norwegian governments. Africa has the lowest proportion of private climate finance of any region in the world. Public funding provides almost two-thirds of flows, although it is increasingly being used to de-risk and leverage private capital. But the growth is uneven, and CPI’s CEO said many projects were too small and fragmented for investors to reach. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Uncertainty deters green investors from Africa's biggest economies
events.summary: Many of Africa’s biggest economies remain unattractive for major renewables investors because of legislative, regulatory, and security uncertainty, the head of one of the continent’s biggest clean energy developers told Semafor. Infinity Power, a privately owned joint venture between Infinity and the UAE’s Masdar, has been fast expanding its green power generation targets in Egypt, and sees Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal as attractive markets for growth. But Ethiopia, Kenya, and Nigeria — among the continent’s biggest economies — are not as much of a draw, Nayer Fouad, Infinity Power’s co-founder and CEO said in an interview. Kenya had recently renegotiated the terms on its power-purchase agreements, causing unease among prospective investors, while Ethiopia and Nigeria carried security risks.

events.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
events.summary: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event. Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.” Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter. Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray. I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security now Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach 7 hours ago Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn 9 hours ago HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider 9 hours ago ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years 10 hours ago A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report . This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN , CyberStrikeAI , HexStrike AI , and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ® Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? events.title: Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Appliances can share 16 TB of DRAM and half a terabyte of HBM across up to 16 systems Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 35 minutes ago US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 5 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 11 hours ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 13 hours ago Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 17 hours ago Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric. Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth. “What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg. Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity. With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules. If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs. Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity. As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely. Memory godboxes could offer relief from the RAMpocalypse Amid the AI-fueled memory crunch, will Compute Express Link finally have its moment to shine? The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money. In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5. This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale. Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents.

events.title: Americans are eating way less turkey than we used to
events.summary: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer Green One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm , Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays . I find turkeys fascinating , because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway . Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies , researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving . Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken , according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound , while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched . Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken . So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans . And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn . The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds . Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken . In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week . Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours , while a 4-pound chicken takes about two . That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society . In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut . He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one . They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take . I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. events.title: The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors
events.summary: KETTLE Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia after a trio of affairs that include an alleged Chinese spy and two of his subordinates, turning the week into one that's shaken the tech sector. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music, or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? Will other chipmakers take advantage of the chaos to surpass the Geforce maker? Will Jensen be the one to put a pin to the AI bubble? Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, systems editor Tobias Mann , and reporter Dan Robinson to talk about the Jensen Huang affair(s) and how the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names could reshape the entire industry on this week's episode. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hey everyone and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and the big news on the tech industry's mind this week is the ouster of Nvidia founder, CEO, president, and board member Jensen Huang over allegations that he not only had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but also at least two Nvidia employees who were his subordinates. Nvidia's been shaped into one of the most valuable companies in the world over the past thirty-three years, and Huang has played a pivotal, if not the pivotal, role in that ascension, meaning his controversial departure is going to rock the industry, if not the greater world. With me to discuss this is our systems editor Tobias Mann and Reg reporter Dan Robinson. Thanks to you both for coming on. Dan Robinson (00:42) Hi. Tobias Mann (00:43) Good to be here. Brandon (00:43) Quite the week, huh? It seems like we went from Jensen’s just going to survive this spy kerfuffle to the board basically seeming to demand his resignation in the course of a few days, right? So Dan, bring us up to speed on the timeline here, what happened? Dan Robinson (01:01) Well, it all happened over the last couple of weeks. That was when the story first surfaced, or it was first reported in the media, of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who happened to work for this company in Singapore that bought a lot of Nvidia's products. Brandon (01:30) Right, company was Megaspeed, right? And her name's Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, coincidence. Dan Robinson (01:36) So it's all happened fairly quickly, but like you say, at the start of this week, it all seemed like Jensen could weather the storm. We were discussing this in our editorial chat and we thought that basically there isn't really anybody who could replace him, or so we thought. He practically is Nvidia, and it's been his vision that's driven the company for so long. But then he came out and he confessed and said he was sorry to all the Nvidia employees. Then the second affair came to light and very quickly, on November 11th actually, Wednesday, he handed in his resignation and it was accepted by the board. So we got to hear about it yesterday [Thursday] when they announced it and it was filed with the SEC. Brandon (03:03) And since then a third affair has come out, right? The New York Times published a finding. Tobias Mann (03:06) Just a few hours later, yeah. Dan Robinson (03:08) It seems so. Makes you wonder how many others may be about to come out in the following days. Brandon (03:13) We're not going to speculate, but my gosh, it seems like that leather jacket really made him irresistible. It’s kind of crazy, right? It seems like the internal affairs with Nvidia employees are the ones that sort of broke the board's back, right? The spy affair seemed like it was kind of like…. Apparently American authorities have basically said they've found no direct evidence to say she is a spy. Dan Robinson (03:44) Exactly. Brandon (03:45) It could just be that she runs a chip company too, or at least a company that is dealing in servers and datacenters. So she has a business reason beyond politics to potentially want to get involved with Jensen. What do you guys think? Was it the internal elements that finally kind of broke the camel's back here and forced the board to act? Dan Robinson (04:08) I think that was the final straw. I think quite possibly he could have weathered the storm as we were saying, if it had just been the one affair outside the business. Brandon (04:20) Outside the business, right? Because now like you were saying, Tobias, not only do you have potentially an international spy affair, but you also have an HR issue to contend with. Tobias Mann (04:29) Right. And I do think that the board could wave their hands around an alleged honeypot scenario. “He was targeted, this was a deliberate act, they preyed on his insecurity.” Brandon (04:44) “It wasn't as big as it's made out to be in the media.” Tobias Mann (04:47) They could make up any number of excuses that they wanted in order to wave their hands over it and keep him CEO or if their arms were twisted by US intelligence services they could have taken him out of an executive role and pushed him into a chairmanship. They had options. And then you had the HR kerfuffle of him allegedly sleeping with another employee. And at that point now there's a pattern. I do sort of question once the news came out that he had an extramarital affair with an employee, whether or not that had influenced him being targeted by Megaspeed and or the Chinese intelligence service, assuming those allegations prove out. Brandon (05:42) We don't know the timeline on one or the other, do we? Tobias Mann (05:46) Right, no. And so it could be that the Chinese intelligence service became aware that this was an avenue that could be exploited and they took it. It's not lost on anybody that he spent most of the last year and a half lobbying to get his chips back into China. And largely successfully on the US side of things. It's been held up by Beijing, which kind of undermines that theory a little bit. Brandon (06:22) It seems like if she was a spy doing China's bidding and he managed to get the Trump administration to allow those older chips in, then Beijing wouldn't have been like, “No, screw you, we're making our own….” Tobias Mann (06:34) But there's the other allegation here, which was that Alice Huang and Megaspeed were smuggling GPUs. Their operation in Singapore was set up such to bring more modern GPUs into the market. And so it could have been that Beijing all of this is alleged didn't really care for its model labs getting old hardware. So they could appear to be blocking us and promoting their own chips while smuggling in more advanced silicon from Nvidia through Singapore. Brandon (07:10) Through Alice Huang's company, essentially, right? So I know Jensen's going to be appearing before Cong

events.title: Trump arrives in the Philippines, a key ally in resisting Chinese aggression
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to the Philippines ahead of the APEC summit this week takes him to a key US ally on the front lines of resisting alleged Chinese aggression in Asia. Though Trump has upended relations with many longtime partners throughout his second term, ties with Manila have remained sturdy, with joint military drills increasing in scope and sophistication. Washington sees the Philippines — a potential launchpad for American defense of Taiwan were China to attack the self-ruled island — as a key linchpin in projecting its power across the East, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump should expect a warm welcome: Almost 70% of Filipinos said they trusted him to do the right thing, the highest level of 36 countries polled. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: China's economic activity slows more than expected
events.summary: China’s economic activity slowed more than expected last month, a sign that Beijing’s efforts to bolster growth are having limited impact. Retail sales and industrial output missed forecasts, feeding fears that the country could slip into deflation. Meanwhile, investment plummeted in the worst monthly drop outside the COVID-19 pandemic. Policymakers fear conditions will worsen further in 2027 and 2028 , prompting them to hold back some stimulus to weather those headwinds. The disappointing data weakens Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s hand ahead of this week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Elsewhere, Japan’s economy unexpectedly cooled , too, as it reeled from higher energy prices sparked by the war in the Middle East. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
events.summary: Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data. Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy. Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states. Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs. The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited. Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

events.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
events.summary: Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages' National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge. There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show. Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest. Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads". She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages. "I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said. Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters. "I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs." The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full. He has already unveiled some of his proposals including: Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits. Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100. Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase. Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank. Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money. But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing". Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers. "Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said. "The state has a responsibility to help them with that." On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit. People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales. McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029". events.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
events.summary: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.
