events.title: AIX investors urged to register claims before creditors' meeting in December
events.summary: Investors in AIX Investment Group's liquidated unit have been urged to register their claims by December 4, as its liquidators plan to hold the first creditors' meeting four days later. AIX Secure SPV, the Cayman-registered issuer of fixed-income notes linked to Dubai-based AIX Investment Group, was placed into liquidation on October 30 by the Grand Court of the Cayman Islands. The court appointed Angela Barkhouse of Kroll (Cayman) and Michael Byrne of Kroll Middle East Consultancy in the Dubai International Financial Centre as joint official liquidators. Claims must be filed online through the liquidation website, said law firm ALBM Excello Law, whose clients were among the creditors who supported the winding-up petition, in a statement on Monday. The firm is helping AIX investors file claims, appoint proxies and put forward members for the liquidation committee. “Many AIX investors are based in the UAE, and the liquidators have been authorised by the Cayman Islands Court to pursue proceedings before the DIFC Courts and the Dubai courts,” said Sujith Mathew, partner at ALBM Excello Law. “We will continue to monitor developments and keep investors informed as the liquidation progresses.” What went wrong AIX Secure SPV, which was registered in the Cayman Islands on December 9, 2022, was established to issue debt notes to raise funds for investment activities, either directly or through affiliated entities. However, investors alleged that AIX Secure SPV failed to make interest payments when due and filed claims against them. According to the Financial Times , investors have filed claims seeking to recover about $10 million, including two individual claims for almost $2 million and $8 million. The company reportedly suspended payments to thousands of investors after promising annual returns of up to 30 per cent. AIX on its website said that “a period of exceptional geopolitical uncertainty and significant volatility across global financial markets has affected valuations and investment realisation cycles within a limited part of AIX’s product offering”. Last month, the UAE's Capital Market Authority said it was reviewing AIX Financial Consultations' activities after receiving information that the company had delayed or even missed payouts. Without disclosing the details of the information it received or the nature of the review, the CMA said it would keep the matter confidential to ensure a thorough, fair and impartial assessment. Following the Cayman Islands ruling, AIX said it had written to its investors directly, explaining why it was proposing a restructuring rather than a forced sale of assets in the current market conditions. “AIX intends to apply to the court for a stay of the order within the period permitted, and will ask the court to consider in full the alternative to liquidation presented to investors in October,” it said on November 4. Steps for investors The liquidators have “determined that AIX Secure SPV should be treated as insolvent, so the liquidation committee must have between three and five creditors”, the latest statement said. While late claims will still be accepted, those creditors may be shut out of the meeting. “A claim admitted for voting is not yet admitted for payment; the liquidators will assess claims for distribution later,” it added. The liquidators have also asked investors not to visit their offices. According to the letter to creditors, nominations for the liquidation committee close on November 26. Submission of claim information for voting, notice of attendance and proxy forms are due by December 4. The creditors’ meeting will be held virtually on December 8. The committee will advise the liquidators on strategy and approve the basis of their fees.

events.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
events.summary: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

events.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
events.summary: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field Published 16 hours ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 21 October Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

events.title: India feels less threatened by AI than the US, official says
events.summary: Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the “cognitive and office-oriented jobs” that the technology could replace, one of the country’s top tech officials said. Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise that’s only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector. With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that “AI compute is still in short supply and expensive.” Krishnan said India and the US were “pretty close” to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. “We’d prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,” he said. Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasn’t happened in Trump’s second term, he said: “Well, I think they still share a very good relationship.” — J.D. events.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
events.summary: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

events.title: Thrift shop asks shoppers to nominate a charity
events.summary: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. events.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
events.summary: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments. events.title: Taiwan deputy minister on Jensen Huang scandal: ‘We feel sad’
events.summary: The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the island’s deputy digital minister said Sunday. Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. “The relationship is very personal,” she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “The supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.” Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huang’s longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep , drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation. “We feel sad,” she added. The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huang’s years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations. US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese don’t want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy that’s “precise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.” China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwan’s outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs “trusted partners.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US official says government needs to make a better case for AI
events.summary: The US government has a responsibility to explain AI’s benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday. Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an “opportunity.” “The onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,” Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasn’t caused mass job losses, and “we haven’t seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,” using the Trump administration’s preferred alternative term for AI. Competitor obsession Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldn’t “obsess” over China. “Great companies don’t try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,” he said. “One of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.” While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be “an America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.” — J.D. events.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy. The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country. The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.” Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations. Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April. “We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another. One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.” The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings. Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others. “We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.” Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom. He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves. Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion . His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry. "While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said. Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report. events.title: A new generation of media will shape the 2028 Democratic primary
events.summary: The Scoop Last week, while shouting out supporters at the Muslim Public Affairs Council gala in Washington, DC, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed singled out a figure in the crowd for special thanks: the founder of Zeteo, Mehdi Hasan, whose posts and videos pushed back against claims that progressives had underperformed more moderate candidates. Three days later, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told the anti-Trump digital outlet MeidasTouch that the network had given him a key boost at a moment when few people believed Mississippi would be in play for a Democratic candidate. “Thank you for giving me the opportunity very early on, when nobody thought Mississippi would be on the radar, to tell my story, tell my message,” Colom said. The first two years of President Donald Trump’s return to power were a waking nightmare for the Democratic Party. But in Trump’s shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. Creators like Aaron Parnas, Keith Edwards, and Jack Cocchiarella gained millions of followers railing against Trump on YouTube. Independent media companies like The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and Zeteo gained millions of combined subscriptions on Substack, which grew from a platform largely favored by right-leaning or “heterodox” publishers to one dominated by left-leaning new media outlets and voices. Scarred by Trump’s 2024 podcast tours, Democratic donors are pouring money into the independent media space, and Democratic candidates have new media figures on speed dial. And now this ascendant new media ecosystem is positioning itself to help pick the next Democratic presidential nominee — or at least weed out a few of the duds. Progressive outlets are aiming to serve as a check on traditional media that they feel wants to knock out left-wing candidates, while moderate forces are starting up their own media to try and counter a zealous left flank that has shouted down moderates online. “That’s going to be the war more than anything: the attention fight… How can I, with the least amount of friction, get these people to start sharing clips?” Cocchiarella told Semafor. The Left While many legacy outlets that had experienced ratings and subscriptions growth during Trump’s first term have seen little to no meaningful gains in his second go-around, independent media outlets critical of Trump, the mainstream media, and Democratic Party leadership saw huge gains. Since the beginning of Trump’s presidency, Zeteo has added almost 2 million YouTube subscribers. The Bernie Sanders-ite outlet More Perfect Union has added 3 million. Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer who became a midterm campaign fixation, has gained millions of followers on YouTube and increased viewership of his stream. Now, both MPU and Zeteo are hoping to bring different issues — or candidates — to the front of the Democratic presidential primary debate. Over the last two years, Zeteo has provided early coverage and political air cover for left-wing and socialist candidates, particularly those that have expressed aggressive criticism of Israel. In an interview on Thursday, Hasan pointed to the company’s early interviews with then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed as examples; both were able to gain exposure to like-minded voters while other outlets were skeptical of their candidacies. “From Zohran Mamdani’s race, to AOC’s rise, to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory, I think it’s been very clear — I’m not saying they wouldn’t have happened without us; that’s a little bit too arrogant and not accurate — but certainly they were aided and abetted and strengthened and bolstered by the fact that we exist,” he said. Hasan said potential 2028 candidates clearly have taken notice. Before the midterm elections, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a candid rare interview on Zeteo that he was considering running in 2028 , an admission he hadn’t made on-camera anywhere else. Hasan said although his political views are clear, multiple likely candidates who do not necessarily share Zeteo’s progressive, Israel-critical stance had nonetheless been in touch in recent days about appearing on the outlet’s show. “Democratic presidential [hopefuls] and their teams have reached out to us, not the other way around, even people we’ve criticized,” Hasan said, noting that he’s angling for an interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a pro-Israel Democrat. Other outlets are more interested in highlighting specific issues, but could end up tipping the conversation in favor of certain candidates that they choose to spotlight. More Perfect Union, the viral video channel founded by Sanders advisor Faiz Shakir, has not outright endorsed candidates in races, but its story selection and tone have bolstered candidates on the left. During the midterms, the organization published a video on then-Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner titled It was less investigatory (the piece did not uncover the various scandals that later led to Platner’s decision to drop out), and more complimentary; it gave space for Platner to explain his view on various media controversies, and showed working class Platner supporters who were unbothered by the unfolding scandals. Over the last few months, More Perfect Union has interviewed Sanders and Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. In an email, More Perfect Union Editor-in-Chief Josh Miller-Lewis told Semafor that although the organization had not finalized its 2028 plans yet, it was hoping to host multiple events with candidates. The organization also hopes to grow its More Perfect University program, which hosted town halls where candidates faced college student questioners. But primarily, Miller-Lewis said, it plans to create content that would “put candidates in conversation with working class audiences and force substantive policy discussions that are often lacking in election coverage,” citing videos the organization made with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz during the 2024 election and El-Sayed during the 2026 Senate race. “Our goal will be to create spaces where our working class audience has the opportunity to challenge candidates in substantive, solutions driven conversations, candidates can outline the big ideas they’ll prioritize if elected and show viewers how candidates engage with the voters they need to persuade to win,” Miller-Lewis wrote. Beyond highlighting more ideologically aligned candidates, left-wing outlets also plan to highlight shortcomings of centrist and moderate candidates. Ryan Grim, a founder of the foreign policy-centric Drop Site News, noted that the investigative outlet will be expanding its domestic coverage to focus on spotlighting how three powerful interest groups hope to influence the Democratic presidential primary. “Crypto and AI, and to some extent AIPAC, are gonna wanna participate, which is wonderful, and we’re a big democracy, but we’re gonna make sure that the public knows who they’re support

events.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
events.summary: Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day. Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report. The BBC has contacted Intel for comment. In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year. events.title: Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO lead crucial week for AI bulls
events.summary: Nvidia earnings and Anthropic 's public debut are set to lead a blockbuster week on Wall Street as questions mount over the AI bull market that has powered US equities to record highs for the past four years. The two events will cap what has been a turbulent period in a sector rocked by disappointing earnings reports, investor anxiety over rising AI financing and expenditure , the Democrats' stunning sweep in the midterm elections , and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang 's affair with a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. “I think both events have the potential to be positive catalysts for the AI trade, which has otherwise been hitting a lot of bumps in the road over the course of the last two weeks,” said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B Riley Wealth. Nvidia accounts for about 90 per cent of the market for the most advanced chips that run and train AI models. It and Anthropic are at the core of AI. Nvidia is expected to post third-quarter revenue growth of 91.3 per cent to $109 billion, with earnings increasing to $2.47 a share when it reports on Tuesday. Fourth-quarter guidance is expected to show earnings growth of 69.5 per cent to $2.75 a share, with revenue up 84.4 per cent to $125 billion. Shares in the company are down about 14 per cent for the year so far. Nvidia's quarterly reports are highly scrutinised and investors expect the company to not merely meet, but overwhelm expectations. But the company's leadership vacuum is expected to generate as much interest this week, as are questions over the possible diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which have turned Mr Huang's extramarital affair into a political firestorm. Nvidia's board of directors told CNBC on Friday that it is in the process of selecting a search company to find a new chief executive. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has filled the role in an interim basis. Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, said investors should look past Mr Huang's resignation as they pore through this weeks' numbers. “If the financial results remain strong, the market may look past the leadership change,” Mr Valecha wrote in a note. Attention will quickly turn towards Mr Huang's rival Dario Amodei , whose company Anthropic will begin trading on the Nasdaq market on Thursday under the symbol “ANT”, joining SpaceX as among the major AI IPOs this year. OpenAI is expected to stage its IPO next year. Anthropic said in an updated S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it will offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a market valuation of $1.3 trillion to $1.45 trillion. Earlier estimates put the company's valuation as high as $2 trillion, but those have dipped alongside a broader AI slide on Wall Street. Its amended filing also showed how connected the companies powering the AI build are. Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC have agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement. UAE-based technology firm MGX participated in a $65 billion funding round for Anthropic this year. The Silicon Valley company is one of three frontier model front-runners the company has stakes in, along with OpenAI and xAI. Founded in 2021, Anthropic's Claude chatbot and a deep bench of other AI models and services have quickly gained momentum. The company reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 ending September 30, an about 1,200 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Its public listing will also beat rival OpenAI, whose IPO has been delayed. Unlike his rivals, Mr Amodei has pushed for stronger AI regulation, drawing opposition from US President Donald Trump's administration. The Pentagon designated the AI company as a “supply chain risk to national security”, with a legal battle being fought. Mr Amodei has been pushing to restrict certain US semiconductors and technology exports to China. The issue deepened into a potential national security crisis last week after Mr Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked at a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed. Megaspeed is under investigation in the US for allegedly smuggling chips to China, in a charge the company denies. Mr Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have agreed to testify before Congress to answer questions on the extent to which US national security had been compromised. Anthropic's rivalry extends beyond Nvidia and OpenAI, however. The company also faces competition from Alphabet and Microsoft in AI software, as well as newer Chinese businesses. The rivalling AI buildout has also raised fears of cash burn. Anthropic reported a net loss of more than $104 billion in the nine months ending on September 30, 2026, although most of this reflected non-cash accounting adjustments to the value of its financing instruments. Amazon posted a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion when it reported in October, while Alphabet posted $9.1 billion of negative free cash flow in its fourth-quarter report. Those concerns have caused stocks to swing wildly in recent weeks, amplified by concerns about stricter regulation and a potential data centre moratorium after the midterm elections. US equities have broadly recouped their losses, with the major averages ending last week in positive territory. “I think we're still in early innings of this game, and I think the impact of artificial intelligence is going to be massive. That said, I think there's always going to be volatility in the trade because we find something to scare us about the trade,” Mr Hogan said.

events.title: Energy security has been forgotten in Kurdistan’s political squabbles
events.summary: If a house divided against itself cannot stand, what are the chances for a house triply divided? On November 8, explosive drones slammed into the Khor Mor gasfield in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, turning out the lights across the semi-autonomous territory. The Kurdish governing parties are at loggerheads ; their debate with Baghdad continues, and the federal government is conflicted about bringing the perpetrators to justice. The strike is far from the first on Khor Mor, which is run by the Pearl Petroleum consortium that includes Sharjah-based Crescent and Dana Gas . Dana Gas said on Saturday that “great damage has hit the Khor Mor gas facility, and at present no quantity of gas can be produced”. The field is the main producer in Kurdistan and was expanded to 750 million cubic feet per day of gas capacity last October. Without it, Kurdistan has very limited alternative production, and its power plants quickly go dark. Electricity generation plunged to 1,000 megawatts from 3,700MW before the attack. A domestic dispute The attack was not directly a result of the US- Iran war , despite early claims that the drones came from Iran. If Iran wanted to target US interests, it would probably have attacked the Sarsang oilfield, run by American company HKN, led by Ross Perot Junior, son of Ross Perot, who ran as an independent candidate in the 1992 presidential election. Indeed, Sarsang was damaged in March and April, early in the war. Cutting off oil is more to Tehran ’s advantage right now in keeping pressure on global markets and the US administration. The Khor Mor attack stems instead from domestic politics . The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which controls the southern part of the region from Sulaymaniyah, has withdrawn from the regional government. It is threatening to set up its own separate administration, reversing the unification reached under American auspices in 2006. Its leader, Bafel Talabani, son of former Iraqi president Jalal Talabani, denied that he was “in Tehran’s pocket” and called this an “old perception”. His party, which has steadily lost ground to the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), based in Erbil, fears exclusion from its share of the oil industry. Mr Talabani said in October 2024 that “I will never hand over gas to them”. The US is not going to step in to resolve the squabble this time, special envoy Tom Barrack saying, “This is an Iraqi issue; this is not an American decision.” Three sides, no solution The Kurdistan–federal struggle has not gone away either, despite the deal finally reached in March to resume exporting the region’s oil through the pipeline to Turkey, this time under Baghdad’s authority. There are complaints of unauthorised exports from Kurdistan through Iran, and of the region not producing the amounts required. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has made the Kurdistan region’s pipeline to Turkey even more important. It now moves about 500,000 barrels per day, including 200,000 bpd trucked from southern Iraq. The importance of the Kurdish line could diminish if Baghdad fulfills its plans to reconstruct the direct route from Kirkuk. Pro-Iranian forces in federal Iraq are certainly behind the drones – and, before that, rockets – launched at Khor Mor. They have also been implicated in attacks on oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia; these are more clearly linked to the US-Iran war and the conflict of Riyadh with Tehran’s allies in Yemen. The US withdrew its air defences from Kurdistan in September, and the regional government complains that Baghdad has not authorised promised anti-drone systems. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi , who took office in May, is locked in his own struggle with some of the militias, moving lately against lucrative oil smuggling activities run from the town of Jurf Al Sakhar, a base for Kataib Hezbollah. It is widely suspected the central government knows very well the culprits for the attacks on Kurdish oilfields, but cannot arrest them, or only detains some lackeys. The Kurdistan region has no immediate solutions to the loss of its main gasfield. Pearl is developing the large Chemchemal field, with hopes of some output next year. In August, it began sending some Khor Mor gas to the federally governed Taza power plant in Kirkuk province, but the Kurdistan Regional Government complained this was in breach of its contract and not in accordance with the region’s priorities. HKN was awarded Miran, another big field, last May. But its sour gas, with a high concentration of toxic, corrosive hydrogen sulphide, will take years to develop. It has already suffered years of commercial deadlock since discovery in 2009. These and other sizeable resources are all in the PUK-controlled zone. This contrasts with oil, concentrated in the KDP zone, with nature’s usual whims to foster trouble. In the absence of major progress on new developments in Kurdistan, Baghdad has taken the chance to lure away investment. After a historic policy of blacklisting companies that worked in the region, it has welcomed first Crescent and, more recently, HKN into oil and gas projects. Two of the other leading operators in Kurdistan, Shamaran of Canada and the UK’s Gulf Keystone, are in the process of merging and entering HKN’s Hamrin field. The Kurdistan region could greatly improve its strategic position by seizing opportunities. It holds almost the only big gas fields in Iraq that are not associated with oil, and so can be developed flexibly. If it had even one more major gas supplier, it would not be so exposed to the violent blackmail of Khor Mor. Beyond gas dependence Its Runaki initiative has been a worthy effort to ensure people pay their bills and rely on centralised electricity and not on the costly and dirty diesel generators that blight the streets of the rest of Iraq. If it rehabilitated its hydroelectric plants, and advanced large-scale solar power, it would further ease reliance on gas. It could develop a larger power surplus and send gas or electricity to the rest of Iraq. That would be a bargaining chip in further debates over oil. It would also give Baghdad more reason to safeguard Kurdish energy sites if another drone caused blackouts in Kirkuk or even Baghdad. A gas link to Turkey has long been in the works, and the Turks have extended their grid up to the border. A bidirectional connection would further boost Kurdish energy resilience to sabotage. Independent gas exports to Turkey, long a dream, now look checkmated by the oil pipeline negotiations. But the Kurdistan region, if still divided, could at least make itself part of a trilateral trade.

events.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
events.summary: The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company. Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify before the House Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the Foreign Affairs and the Intelligence committees. The committees had threatened to issue subpoenas to Jensen Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Jensen Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. Moolenaar said: "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls." Separately, a group of tech leaders including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive. A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of him being reinstated is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday, 17 November. On Friday, Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by fellow cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

events.title: Amazon loses first batch of broadband satellites launched on custom rocket
events.summary: Amazon’s ambition to operate a constellation of broadband satellites took a hit on Sunday, when 40 of its craft failed to make it into orbit. The failure is significant because it was the first Amazon launch to use a rocket designed especially for the job of carrying its broadband birds to low Earth orbit. The Lockheed/Boeing joint venture United Launch Alliance (ULA) created that rocket, a version of its Vulcan heavy lifter using a six-booster configuration and a Centaur V upper stage optimized to carry payloads into low Earth orbit. Last week, Amazon previewed the launch with a post that noted this mission, code-named LV-01, is the first of 38 planned missions with ULA, and that LV-02 would likely follow within weeks. The two companies planned to test new hardware on the first “several” flights using the custom rocket. Amazon put 40 satellites aboard the Sunday mission and said it is “already planning larger configurations for subsequent missions.” Those plans, and the LV-02 launch, are probably on hold after the rocket suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight. The flight began well, with the Vulcan reaching an altitude of 95 miles (150 km) and completing the first phase of its flight. Six minutes into the mission, the main booster and payload fairing both separated as planned, and ULA lit up the Centaur V’s engines for the first planned firings needed to reach low Earth orbit. Then came the anomaly, which UAL’s live update stream states meant the mission “failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” “Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something,” UAL wrote. “Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.” Amazon already has over 200 satellites in orbit, had hoped to launch its satellite broadband service this year, and plans 20 or more launches in 2027. It is unclear if this mission failure will change those ambitions. ®

At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. events.title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
events.summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. “We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.” The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people. events.title: Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China
events.summary: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China. The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA. As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world. Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike. Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent. Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent. Sega Japan hits double trouble Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage. The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming. Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15. The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe. But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages. Alibaba floats chip unit Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips. T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers. India bans export of dead batteries The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries. “It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.” “Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.” Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites. The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.” Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise. The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan. If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

events.title: Dems' Denver victory party previews 2028 battles
events.summary: DENVER — Thousands of Democrats gathered here this weekend for a giddy postelection summit, reveling in their party's historic midterm victories and touting the center-left strategy they say powered them. But some progressives saw the event as a lavish, out-of-touch affair bankrolled by billionaires — exactly what Democrats just campaigned against. "I'm all for celebration, but perhaps a fancy retreat does not exactly meet the tenor of the moment," said Josh Orton, president of the liberal group Demand Justice and a veteran of Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign. Why it matters: The competing views of What's Next, the buzzy confab held by the influential centrist organization Majority Democrats, offer an early glimpse of the ideological battles over health care, money in politics and other issues that will define the party's 2028 presidential primary. Zoom in: Democrats in the Mile High City were practically vibrating with happiness, still not quite able to believe they'd won back both chambers of Congress and flipped deep-red states such as Mississippi and South Carolina. "The vibes are excellent," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride, a member of the Majority Democrats, said in an interview. "The last high-water mark, we were all in our houses on Zooms," she added, referring to the 2020 presidential election. "This is the first time there's been an undeniable capacity to celebrate widespread wins in the last decade." Free drinks flowed. Political operatives sported bomber jackets embroidered with the phrase "Majority Democrats." Speakers were immortalized in rock concert–style posters on the walls. For a brief moment in Denver's Mission Ballroom, the often-in-disarray Democratic Party looked united. Several presidential hopefuls downplayed the party's divides in speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said onstage that ordinary people don't give "a damn" about "where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum." Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin quipped in her address that elected officials who were fighting over progressives vs. moderates had "missed the plot." The other side: But others in the party weren't interested in all the kumbaya. Young protesters sneaked into the event and heckled House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), shouting "You're a f**king traitor!" while calling for Medicare for All and impeachment. Some audience members were palpably annoyed, yelling "Shut up!" Another flashpoint emerged over high-dollar donors and super PACs. Majority Democrats — which is largely funded by a billionaire couple and describes itself as an alternative to both the "activist left" and a "gerontocratic establishment" — is already in the crosshairs of the Lever, a progressive publication. Majority Democrats' funding has been the focus of reporting by the Lever. The group tussled with the news site over the Denver event, initially denying it press passes and later blocking one of its journalists from interviewing an elected official. David Sirota, founder of the Lever, said the group's actions were "Trump-like attempts at retribution." But there was a silver lining for the outlet: The back-and-forth generated the single biggest influx of new subscribers in its history, he said. What they're saying: "What's Next was an overwhelming success: It brought together 3,500 Democrats from across the political spectrum to talk about what worked this cycle and where we go next," said Majority Democrats spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev. "This cycle, we won seats that had been written off for a generation and proved there is no one way to be a Democrat." The intrigue: Some potential 2028 candidates in Denver tried to portray themselves as unifiers who can bridge the party's divides. New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim, who declined to rule out a 2028 bid, said, "I understand" where the protesters were coming from. "People are furious," he added.

events.title: Some Dems' 2028 strategy: Make America Nice Again
events.summary: Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure. Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure. Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little." In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty." In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire." Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times. "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America." The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side. Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks. In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics. In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time." The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out." He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter." Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents. In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

events.summary: Iran launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, adding to mounting tensions even as Washington signals a reluctance to escalate. US President Donald Trump has told senior advisers he may hold off on striking Iran if the US faces no new provocations, Reuters reported. Yet American military assets continue to flow into the region, while three oil tankers caught fire over the weekend after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. With mediation stalled, continued tit-for-tat attacks raise the risk that limited exchanges could spiral into a wider war: “The current situation in the Strait of Hormuz is inherently unstable and cannot be sustained indefinitely ,” an Israeli analyst wrote on X. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Vance may wait until late spring to reveal 2028 plans
events.summary: Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field. People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however. Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said. The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition. Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network , which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms. As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier. Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028. Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president. But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028. Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions. Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran. The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans. Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him. Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected. Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run. Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance. Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin . But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation. Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis has been particularly outspoken , calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party. What they're saying: A Vance spokesperson declined to comment.
