events.title: ‘Silicon Valley’ showrunner on how the HBO comedy predicted today’s tech drama
events.summary: The Scene A year before the iconic show debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the show’s creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valley’s power and its eccentricity, but it wasn’t working and he wanted a second opinion. Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he can’t afford. Berg told Judge the scene didn’t make sense: “This is not a guy who’s materialistic,” he said. “He’s an artist.” Berg took over the writer’s room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom — and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release. Their moment of realization comes when their AI, Son of Anton, let loose on Pied Piper’s code, concludes that the most efficient way to eliminate bugs is to delete the software. That has, of course, happened . Clips of it now circulate as proof the show “called it.” Even throwaway comic plots, like when a household prank ends up hacking together a rogue swarm of smart refrigerators to keep Pied Piper’s servers running, have come eerily true in the AI-run-amok era . A member of the team getting trapped in an autonomous car that heads to a shipping container bound for a Pacific island foreshadowed a thousand videos of confused Waymos. Berg helped reshape the pilot of the first episode to open with a wild-but-lame party, featuring Kid Rock, thrown by founders who had just cashed out, to contrast the ascetic, mission-driven Richard with a culture obsessed with exits and “three-comma” fortunes. The show “was about how Richard had discovered fire, and he was trying to keep it safe from all of these assholes,” Berg said. “He was ill-prepared to shepherd a company, but he didn’t want to surrender this thing to people who would use it for nefarious purposes.” The writers were obsessed with making the show “photorealistic.” Berg called up a Harvard friend and venture capitalist Marc Bodnick, who connected him with Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg; the team spoke to other Silicon Valley figures and hired a technical consultant, Jonathan Dotan, who assembled a revolving cast of founders, lawyers, VCs, and professors to stress-test storylines. As they were writing the first season, one of their Silicon Valley sources remarked that the Pied Piper crew would be angling for a slot at TechCrunch Disrupt. “We were like, ‘I’ve never heard those words before, but that sounds hilarious. What is that?’” They learned that it was a kind of for startups, and it became the core of the first season. In the climactic scene, the Pied Piper team is holed up in a hotel room the night before the Disrupt finals when one of the team vows to win even if he has to manually pleasure every man in the audience. The engineers calculate “mean jerk time” and sort the crowd by “dick-to-floor” ratio — delivering an unexpected mathematical breakthrough for Richard. As the first few episodes began to build a fan base, the writers giddily anticipated episode eight. “We felt like we were sitting on pocket aces because we knew,” he recalled. “Wait till they see that dick joke. They’re going to lose their minds.” (Berg was nominated an Emmy for the episode.) Dotan introduced the writers to Stanford’s Tsachy Weissman, and the show invented a “Weissman score” for compression efficiency, a metric that computer scientists now actually use . The ultimate compliment, he said, came from tech workers who told him they couldn’t watch the show “because it makes me nauseous.” How Mark Cuban inspired ‘three-comma’ Russ As the show grew, it caricatured real Silicon Valley figures. Perhaps the most recognizable was Russ Hanneman, played by Chris Diamantopoulos, who arrived in season two. The character began with the idea that Richard, under pressure, would be forced to accept an investment from a sinister figure the writers called “Bad Money,” who would break his promises and try to manipulate them. While they were writing, they received an invitation from the star of another show shooting on the Sony lot. Mark Cuban was a fan of Judge, best known for , , and , and had enjoyed season one. An intermediary invited them to the set to meet the billionaire. Berg and Judge arrived excited to meet him, then sat there for an hour waiting. “We walked out of there going, ’What the f*ck was that? We’re supposed to have an audience with the king, and then he f*cks us around for an hour,” they fumed. “We were like, you know what? That motherf*cker is Bad Money.” The character — dumb, aggressive, absurdly macho — wasn’t exactly Cuban. But his signature accomplishment (“I put radio on the internet”) was drawn from Cuban’s perfectly-timed sale of Broadcast.com to Yahoo. “I bear no ill will to Mark Cuban,” Berg hastened to add. “I’m not sure he even knew we were there.” The show’s continued relevance owes much to its 2019 finale, which Berg wrote and directed. Pied Piper is days away from a spectacular launch when the team discovers that its AI has learned to break encryption. Releasing it would make them billionaires — but end privacy. They sabotage the launch, fail, and never tell anyone why. In 2026, the image of founders who conclude their AI is too dangerous to release and silently walk away has become harder to imagine. Berg said he and his friend, showrunner David Mandel, are often asked about reboots of their respective shows. He can’t quite see it. “Both of those shows were created in an era where it’s, like, ‘Can you imagine if what was actually going on behind closed doors was this?’ And now it’s not behind closed doors anymore,” he said. In particular, he sees a tech industry that has lost its earnestness, lost mission-driven founders like Richard, and is instead consumed with vast sums of money and naked power. “It’s just gotten f*cking dark,” Berg said. “I don’t think the kind of fun that we had with it is doable now, in this era.” Notable While could still play the industry for laughs, modern takes on Silicon Valley, including Luca Guadagnino’s , a biopic of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, become “ so frightening it is hard to laugh,” Deadline wrote.

events.title: Center-left previews 2028 in Denver
events.summary: The News DENVER — The race for the next Democratic presidential nomination has begun, with a festival of agreement. There was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, telling the What’s Next conference that voters demanded action, not “shallow litmus tests or where we fall on some political spectrum. ” There was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, explaining that voters did not want “marginal change” and Democrats weren’t in a battle of “progressive versus moderate .” And there was Pete Buttigieg, who’d noticed the Democrats borrowing his formula. They wanted to pass cost-cutting, pro-family bills with their new majority, then convince voters that they would never go back to pre-Trump neoliberalism. “It sounds good. It’s easy to say,” said Buttigieg. “Everybody thinks they already agree with this.” The post-midterms conference, organized by Majority Democrats, was a payoff of a two-year investment by moderate donors. Two years before strategists and elected officials landed in Denver and grabbed their lanyards, the venture capitalist Seth London circulated a memo about how new candidate and media investments could steer the party away from “race and group-based identity politics,” and toward “prosperity for more Americans.” This year’s Democratic landslide carried along every kind of candidate —the ones plugged into the Majority Democrats network, and the ones who worried it was a big-money ploy to defeat the populist left. But the conference elevated the candidates who wanted to build a supermajority, battling big tech and environmental attorneys. Some donors were in; the donors who wanted them to move left were out. “Tell us which ideas you’ll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or didn’t work,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, the pedigreed Massachusetts Democrat who chairs the Majority Democrats PAC. “Tell us which privileges you’ll confront, even if your donors or allies object.” Celebrating the center The donors did know how to throw a party. What’s Next resembled the sort of well-funded, media-friendly conferences that many Democrats have envied on the right, like the multi-day “AmericaFest” put on by Turning Point Action. This was a party for the Democratic mainstream, the staffers most likely to work for center-left presidential candidates than for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY. For two days, blocks of Denver’s River North Art District were cordoned off for Democrats, the people who elected them, and the reporters asking if they were running for president. (Their answers were variations on “not yet.“) There was conflict, but it was largely limited to the argument over who should lead Democrats’ new congressional majorities. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who announced his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Thursday, paused for 10 seconds of applause when he took the stage and explained why he was running. “Candidates from different backgrounds and different parts of our party – they ran on a strikingly similar platform,” said Van Hollen. “They didn’t run on the tired Washington labels of progressive versus moderate. They ran on an economic populist message, on a commitment to fight for working people and take on a rigged economic and political system.” Many of those winners showed up in Denver, like Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. They shared road stories of how they listened to Republican concerns, and would work with the willing ones to lower prices. But it was implied that Democrats should focus on building homes, lowering bills, and expanding health care before they did anything else. Not every attendee agreed. “The organizers here want a big tent, one big enough to even invite anti-establishment voices like me,” said Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Ca., who Democrats see as a competitor for a Sen. Bernie Sanders lane in the primary. “A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.“Apart from Khanna, the likely presidential candidates didn’t quite do that. Mallory McMorrow, who Majority Democrats supported in her unsuccessful U.S. Senate bid in Michigan, told Semafor that her party had just shown that it could have a loud primary argument and then unite on the basics. “It’s anti-corruption, getting money out of politics, protecting democracy, ending wars,” said McMorrow. “The disagreements are around the edges.” David’s view There will be many Democratic “cattle calls,” but I am focusing on how What’s Next was built because it’s the fruit of a two-year effort to ensure that the 2028 primary plays out differently than the 2020 primary. There is widespread agreement among Democratic strategists that their last open primary was defined by left-wing organizations that wanted candidates to commit to their ideas, eyeball to eyeball, on camera. That meant forums organized by groups like Planned Parenthood and MoveOn, and more progressive labor unions like SEIU. That meant the ACLU asking candidates if they would commit to cutting the federal prison population in half, and Movimiento Cosecha bird-dogging Joe Biden at his own events until he committed to stopping most deportations.If the left sees Majority Democrats as an effort to swipe their strongest messaging and junk the rest, they’re right. The economic populism in Denver was more sincere than they might think, but it is against degrowth and for permitting reform; skeptical of single-payer health care, but for incremental steps to “universal” health care; basically, right in the sweet spot of the Democrats’ congressional caucuses. Right now the Schumer-Van Hollen contest is where the fights over ideology and priorities are happening. The 2028 candidates would prefer to agree, for now. Room for Disagreement The left was not letting the rest of the party adopt its ideas without a fight. In the run-up to What’s Next, reporters from three left-leaning outlets that had been critical of Majority Democrats – The Lever, The Intercept, and The American Prospect – announced that they’d been denied access. All were eventually allowed in, becoming a First Amendment nuisance for donors who didn’t want to interrupt happy hours with hard questions. And on Friday, four protesters accessed the Mission Ballroom to interrupt the most powerful Democrat at the conference, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. As liberal pundit Jessica Tarlov asked the likely House Speaker about his agenda, they jumped up, one after another, accusing him of complicity in genocide. A protester with Climate Defiance, pushing back at the bouncers who dragged him out, turned to the stadium seating reserved for reporters and shouted “f— you all!“Nicole Shea Niebler, a 31-year-old organizer with the Sunrise Movement in Denver, said that she interrupted Jeffries because “the conference made it pretty clear that strong progressives are not invited to participate at the scale that centrists were.” That limited the bounds of debate in a room where media taste-makers were starting

events.title: Under pressure, Lutnick joins Trump in China
events.summary: Howard Lutnick is expected to travel on Air Force One with the president to China this week as the commerce secretary fights to regain his footing after clashing with Trump officials over Nvidia and China chip controls, according to people familiar with the matter. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Lutnick has become the target of Washington finger-pointing for slow-walking Commerce Department restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, as well as his close relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia customer suspected of being a Chinese spy, and media reports of two affairs with subordinates. The woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, which the US is investigating for improper chip smuggling into China. Republicans are accusing Lutnick of defying Trump — and warning his job could be on the line — after reports emerged that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had pushed the commerce secretary to place the Nvidia customer, Megaspeed, on a blacklist of companies that pose national security concerns. Treasury “has been pushing for this for months” but Commerce “has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC last week. Bessent, who has directly criticized Lutnick’s handling of the matter, is also expected on the trip. A senior US official told reporters ahead of the China trip that the Nvidia scandal “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the official said. ‘Nine lives’ They have accused Lutnick of allowing the chipmaker to indirectly sell more advanced chips to China than previously known or allowed under US export control laws, through loopholes he has so far declined to close. He’s also been criticized for giving Nvidia unfettered access to rule-making that would impact the entire industry. The White House has said it “maintains complete confidence in the secretary.” Lutnick had been expected to attend Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World convening this week alongside OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Amazon’s Andy Jassy, and hundreds of other CEOs, but will instead be with the president. And while plans could still change, Lutnick’s inclusion in the trip signals that Trump wants to keep Lutnick around long enough to at least accompany the president to China for his visit with Xi. “This guy has nine lives,” a person close to the White House previously told Semafor. “How many does he have left?”

events.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO. Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth. The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market. Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans. Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance." "This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said. For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks. The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others. In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports. As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports. What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

events.title: Trump's border crackdown faces a new blue wall of governors and House members
events.summary: Voters have handed Democrats every House district touching Mexico and all four border-state governorships. Why it matters: Starting next year, the sweep gives Democrats new leverage over state resources, border spending and legal challenges during President Trump's final two years. By the numbers: Democrats last held all four governorships — California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas — in January 1979, according to National Governors Association records . 10 for 10: Democrats swept all 10 House districts touching Mexico for the first time since 2008, according to an Associated Press analysis . Three flips: JoAnna Mendoza ousted Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona. Bobby Pulido and Katy Padilla Stout flipped Republican-held seats in Texas. Four attorneys general: Democrats also won the top legal offices in all four border states, including Texas , where the party hadn't won an attorney general race since 1994. State of play: Trump built his immigration crackdown around the southern border. He declared a national emergency on his first day back, expanded the military's role and border barriers, and launched a sweeping deportation campaign. Southwest border apprehensions dropped roughly 91% in the 12 months through August compared with Biden's final 12 months, according to FactCheck.org's October analysis . The crackdown has also reached further into American communities, with ICE arrests surging during the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott could bring the most immediate border changes. Abbott spent about $11 billion on Operation Lone Star, deploying state police and National Guard troops and building Rio Grande barriers, according to the Texas Tribune . Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect, has questioned that spending. She can rethink state deployments and enforcement priorities, though existing laws and federal authority limit her options. Democrats also flipped the Texas House and elected a Democratic attorney general, giving Hinojosa allies in funding and legal battles. Republicans retained the state Senate. The intrigue: Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed more than 20 lawsuits against Democratic immigration policies and defended Gov. Greg Abbott's border crackdown. His Democratic successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed to challenge unconstitutional federal border tactics — potentially turning the office from a powerful Trump ally into an adversary. What we're watching: Several Democrats newly elected to represent border districts in Washington campaigned on both strong border security and pathways to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants. Bobby Pulido, who flipped a Texas GOP-held seat, said in his launch video : "Yes, we have to get the criminals out and secure the border. But we can do that without destroying families and our South Texas economy." He also told the Texas Tribune that one of his congressional priorities will be codifying a pathway to citizenship. JoAnna Mendoza, who flipped an Arizona seat, also backs a strong border and legal pathways to citizenship. That aligns with many border voters' views: An October N+ Univision/YouGov survey found 56% of Texas Hispanic voters thought immigration enforcement had gone too far. Yet 62% wanted border security and a pathway to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants pursued together — suggesting Democrats can make gains without abandoning enforcement. Zoom out: Trump's tariffs and immigration crackdown have rattled businesses that depend on trade and shoppers from Mexico, giving Democratic governors another reason to challenge Washington. Laredo businesses report fewer customers, while merchants near San Diego's border crossings say tougher immigration enforcement has hurt foot traffic and hiring. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs pressed Washington over tariffs and trade uncertainty. Manufacturers near Santa Teresa, New Mexico, have put projects on hold amid tariff threats and uncertainty over trade rules.

events.title: Trump heads to Asia with hopes of shifting the momentum after midterm setbacks hurt him at home
events.summary: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, hoping to make some big attention-grabbing moves on the world stage after his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections , diminishing his standing at home. The Republican president is using the international trip to try to shift momentum, and he is poised to make a splash with a historic three-way meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. Trump has long boasted about leveraging his relationships with the leaders of two of America’s biggest global adversaries, though he has failed so far to achieve major breakthroughs with them. He first heads to the Philippines to meet on Tuesday with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. Trump will then go to China on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. There, he will have his third face-to-face meeting this year with Xi and see Putin, too. A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028. “I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell , a former deputy secretary of state in Democratic President Joe Biden's administration and chairman of The Asia Group, a consultancy. It's a pattern followed by some of Trump's predecessors. Democratic President Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate in 2014 to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. Republican President George W. Bush went to APEC in Vietnam after the GOP lost control of Congress in 2006, though the Iraq War hung over his travels. The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila as well as a host of commercial deals and will be the “guest of honor” at a leaders' dinner. In Shenzhen, he will focus on trade issues before the meeting with Xi and Putin. Trump is leaving as airlines struggled to get passengers onto flights after a nationwide ground stop on Friday led to thousands of flight cancellations. Trump and his officials have blamed their predecessors, a contractor and Congress for the problems. Trump is about to be bogged down at home in ways that may curb what he can do overseas. His tariffs and war with Iran proved to be poisonous with voters. Going forward, Trump's ability to threaten import taxes or military assaults — two of his major foreign policy tools — will be limited by Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill in the new year. Just last week, in a newfound vulnerability, his push to boost artificial intelligence was complicated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved. Huang had traveled with Trump on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on AI and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. But Trump does not plan to confront Xi on the issue, said administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president’s plans on a call with reporters. The officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip. Even though the administration is discussing ways to close loopholes and further prevent Chinese businesses from using advanced chips made by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, the officials said they do not expect the restrictions to cause retaliation by Beijing. Trump will be accompanied by Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is the world's wealthiest man and a frequent adviser to the president. Musk spent at least $445 million to try to help Republicans keep control of Congress, and Democrats are keen to investigate his ties to the administration. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Trump may find it easier to be in the company of foreign leaders than his own crumbling coalition at home. But his words and actions at the summits are now more likely to draw scrutiny in committee hearings when he returns to Washington. “We’re going to have a very close eye on it," said Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

events.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left last year as it launches internal investigation
events.summary: Megaspeed, the AI infrastructure company linked to the scandal that toppled Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang , has said Alice Huang left the business more than a year ago. “Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” it said in a statement on Sunday. The company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”, including a review of its compliance with US export controls. It said media reports against it were not supported by verifiable evidence. Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese companies get around US restrictions by buying Nvidia’s advanced chips for data centres in South-East Asia and routing them to China. Singapore authorities have said servers containing advanced AI chips were shipped to Malaysia and may have been delivered elsewhere, contrary to declarations made in Singapore. Singapore police said their investigation is continuing. Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China, was at the centre of the scandal that led to Mr Huang’s resignation on Thursday. Mr Huang had admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife after reports of their relationship, and Nvidia’s board opened an inquiry into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence operation. China has denied the spying allegations. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has taken over as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor. The fall-out has intensified scrutiny in Washington of how advanced chips reach China, with politicians from both main parties calling for tighter export controls . Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, its first since Mr Huang’s departure.

events.title: UAE engineering firm Kent heads for record order book despite Iran war
events.summary: Kent, the Dubai-based energy engineering company owned by Saudi Arabia's Nesma & Partners , expects to end the year with a record order backlog as Gulf producers press ahead with major projects despite months of disruption caused by the Iran war. The company is on track to meet its revenue target of about $1.5 billion this year and deliver on earnings, chief executive John Gilley told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. The war involving the US, Israel and Iran, which began in late February, has disrupted energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged critical infrastructure across the Gulf. But it has also generated a wave of work for engineering contractors with a deep presence in the region, from repairing damaged plants to building export routes that avoid the strait. Rystad Energy estimates the cost of restoring energy infrastructure damaged in the conflict could reach $58 billion. Kent is helping energy producers in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE assess damage to plants after the attacks. While some repairs are relatively minor, others require extensive planning before operations can resume. "We're very proud of the fact that we'll probably hit budget this year at a time when supply chains have been massively disrupted," Mr Gilley said. Kent's order backlog was nearly $3 billion by the end of 2025, much of it concentrated in Gulf countries, and was expected to reach a record by December. Its contracts with Adnoc Gas are progressing, including a $1.1 billion deal to expand the Asab and Buhasa gas processing plants under Adnoc Gas's $5 billion Rich Gas Development project . Supply chain bottlenecks have slowed progress, but Kent still aims to deliver on schedule, Mr Gilley said. New urgency for bypass pipelines Gulf producers are accelerating projects that allow them to export crude without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco has started work to expand its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, while Adnoc is fast-tracking a new West-East pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Mr Gilley said he did not see a major change in strategy from oil companies, but the war has transformed how such projects are viewed. "In the past, when these types of projects, which really don't add any production, are talked about, they're always on a slow burn," he said. "Now the risk rating and the benefit for the project have increased exponentially, so they're much more likely to go ahead." Kent does not expect to significantly increase capital spending next year, relying instead on its 5,000 to 6,000 engineers worldwide, including teams across five offices in India. Iraq emerges as major market Iraq is becoming a "very, very large" market for Kent as international oil companies expand their involvement in the country's energy sector. The company has a major framework agreement with Basrah Gas Company, works with BP at the Rumaila oilfield and with China's Sinopec, and has secured a new contract with BP at Kirkuk. Mr Gilley expects ExxonMobil , and potentially Chevron, to return to Iraq, creating opportunities for contractors at major fields, including Majnoon. LNG a key growth area Mr Gilley expects liquefied natural gas to remain a major growth area over the next decade, and Kent is pursuing opportunities linked to Mozambique's LNG developments. However, volatile prices complicate the long-term supply agreements needed to finance projects costing billions of dollars, he said, and contractors rarely share in the upside when commodity prices rise. "When the prices of gas and oil reduce, our customers ask us to reduce our rates," he said. "But they never get us to increase our rates when they make such profits." Kent is also expanding into data centre engineering, advising operators on grid optimisation and renewable electricity supplies. Mr Gilley said the business was "absolutely flying". "The world is addicted to two things: energy and data," he added. "The problem with increased demand for data is the increased demand for power. As an offering, we can do both." Kent has reduced its carbon intensity by 43 per cent, exceeding a 30 per cent reduction target set for 2027, and aims to achieve net zero by 2040. That does not mean retreating from hydrocarbons, particularly in the Gulf, where production costs and emissions intensity are relatively low. "We'll continue to proudly produce fossil fuels," Mr Gilley said.

events.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
events.summary: Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment. Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague". McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed. But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work. His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade. However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year. Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job. He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness. How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted. Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service. Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense' Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this." He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to." He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today". Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added. Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending. But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs". She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing. Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said: a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage. From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently. It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year . How have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Tell us about your experience. events.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
events.summary: Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant. Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates. By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute. Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet. That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said. Zoom in : For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat. For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value. An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity . A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction. Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings. Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself. About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom. If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message. "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added. Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline. "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios. Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter. Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions , which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days. Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops. It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil. Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance. The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

events.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
events.summary: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions . What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts. "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks." By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers. In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year. SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation . Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively. Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview. "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet." The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

events.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
events.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

events.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.  When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family. “Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.” Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground. “I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.” According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.” In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences. The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder. But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell. His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.  In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison. A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.  Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court. “During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”  As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said. Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital. “If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email. Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion. “Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.” Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.  “I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.  She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him. events.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
events.summary: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

events.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds but are they value for money?
events.summary: It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use. "I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid." Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated. High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out. But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier. "I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist. She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product. "For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales." Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products" Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy." Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items" Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing". So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to? "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper Heather Widdows, a beauty expert and philosophy professor at Warwick University, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them. "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it. In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says. events.title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
events.summary: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker. Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday. The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months. The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday. The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon. The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans. The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV. The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius). Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech “It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud. Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him. “They taught us not to drown,” Knab said. Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him. Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. “Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said. The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations. The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment. The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

events.title: Tens of thousands march in Portuguese cities against surging home prices
events.summary: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices LISBON, Portugal -- Tens of thousands of people marched through more than 30 cities and towns across Portugal on Saturday in the largest protest yet against soaring housing costs that many say have put buying or renting a home beyond their reach. The housing crisis has fueled weeks of demonstrations. Some activists have camped in central squares in Lisbon and Porto, the country’s two largest cities. Riot police with dogs have dispersed some protests, drawing accusations of heavy-handed tactics. The demonstrations took inspiration from protests that began in neighboring Spain last month over similar housing concerns. They come amid widespread social unrest across Europe this autumn. Marching under the slogan “We won’t let them steal our right to housing,” participants ranged from teenagers to retirees. Drums, music and chants accompanied the Lisbon march as protesters carried large banners and flags. Susana Pacheco, a 35-year-old data analyst who works part-time as an astrologer to help pay her mortgage, said she worried about whether her younger sister could afford to move out of their parents’ home. “I’m really worried about young people,” Pacheco said. “I don’t know how they’re going to be able to pay” for their own home. “Things have become intolerable,” said Ana Encarnação, 42, citing rising living costs and the widening gap between rich and poor. Activists want ceilings placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61%, followed by the Netherlands with 34%, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week. There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, housing prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68% increase since 2020, according to the government. Foreign buyers and investment funds have fueled price rises by buying Portuguese real estate. The country’s mild climate and long coastline have helped it grow popular with digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees. Tourism has also surged, with many city center apartments switched to short-term rentals. The government has responded with measures such as lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes. But it acknowledges that the effects won’t be immediate. Portuguese President António José Seguro, whose role is mostly ceremonial but who wields political influence, convened a Council of State, an advisory body, to discuss the protests earlier this month and met Friday with some of the protesters. events.title: Retail sales and Fed minutes in focus next week
events.summary: A report on retail sales will anchor the calendar of economic updates this week, which also includes details about the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and the latest take on consumer sentiment NEW YORK -- New data on retail sales will headline U.S. economic updates this week, but there will also be details from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and a new read on consumer sentiment. The latest economic data showed that inflation remains hot . High prices on everything from groceries to clothing and gas have squeezed millions of Americans and cast a shadow over the broader economy. Democrats swept Congress in midterm elections and for many voters, the cost of living was the top issue. Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead. Retail activity may have slowed last month. Economists expect a 0.2% overall increase, easing back from 0.8% in September and 1.3% in August. At the same time that overall retail sales are slowing, spending at gas stations has surged amid persistently higher fuel costs because of the U.S. war with Iran. The war disrupted shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, slashing global oil supplies and raising prices. That has made gasoline more expensive and indirectly raised costs for anything that is shipped. Shoppers have been pulling back on spending just as retailers head into the vital holiday shopping season . The squeeze from stubbornly high inflation is expected to persist as long as the war stifles global oil supplies and tariffs from the U.S. trade war with much of the world keep putting pressure on prices. Details from the Federal Reserve's latest policy meeting will be released Wednesday. The minutes from that meeting could shed more light on the central bank's decision-making process as it tries to cool inflation. It held rates steady at its October meeting following the first rate hike in three years at its September meeting. Raising the benchmark interest rate can help slow economic growth and cool inflation by making borrowing more expensive. Timeline of the FAA nationwide ground stop: How it developed 20- to 30-foot waves pound the West Coast as storms continue India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain Higher interest rates, though, could also stunt job growth, which has been strong but is showing some signs of weakening. Supporting the labor market is also part of the Fed's mandate along with taming inflation and taking action to support one can often be detrimental to the other. Inflation has remained stubbornly above 3%, which puts it well above the central bank's 2% target rate. The Fed is expected to raise rates again at its December meeting and anxiety over stubborn inflation likely means more rate hikes to follow in 2027. The latest weekly update on unemployment claims, which are a proxy for layoffs, will be released Thursday. Economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. Claims have remained at historically low levels amid a broader jobs market that has remained a strong point in an economy pressured by rising inflation. The resilient jobs market has made it easier for the Fed to focus on raising interest rates to cool inflation. The last broad employment update for October showed that U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The reports have shown that the job market remains solid, but unspectacular. Employers have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month throughout the year, which is modest by historic standards. The University of Michigan on Friday will release an update to its November consumer sentiment survey. It is expected to remain unchanged from its initial reading, which continued to show that consumers remain pessimistic as they deal with pressure from inflation on household budgets. Other reports on consumer confidence revealed similar concerns about inflation. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index for October showed some improvement in confidence levels, but they still remain on an overall downward trend. Responses to that survey continued to echo worries about the high costs of gas, goods and services. events.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S. The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop. Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said. Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said. According to numbers from FlightAware , over 4,700 international and domestic flights have been canceled, and over 13,500 delayed, as of 11:50 am ET. Zoom out: Bedford and Duffy both said the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution for the safety of passengers and airplane crews. Bedford added that they have no reason to believe a cyberattack or an AI issue prompted the outage. "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious," Bedford said. Zoom in: Duffy used the press conference to again plead with Congress to fund upgrades for the aging air traffic control system. Duffy has previously said the FAA needs $30 billion to update airports and air traffic control. Congress had previously awarded $12.5 billion in July 2025 for upgrades into 2030. After Friday's outage, Duffy upped the funding request to $50 billion. "For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don't get the resources," Duffy said. "And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait, America and Congress? And I think this is a sign for them to lean in. This is bipartisan." Bedford offered a blunt assessment when reporters asked about the system's function, saying it's the "worst-kept secret in government" that it needs an upgrade. "We have to keep the existing system operating at the very best of our ability," with the funding they have, he said. "But," Bedford continued, "let's not kid ourselves. It will continue to break until we replace it."
